Analyzing 67,976 posts and 305,048 comments from nine communities on the Tor-based darknet forum Dread, we map user trajectories, content distribution, and the adoption of generative AI. Our findings show that structural cohesion within the ecosystem is maintained by a thin layer of `bridgers' who generate the majority of all content. Against a degree-preserving null model, three knowledge-building upstream stages of the value chain form a tightly coupled cluster, whereas the remaining three operational downstream stages resolve into highly specialized populations with small personnel overlap. Finally, we demonstrate that generative AI is being rapidly but unevenly absorbed across the value chain; the technology saturates knowledge-building communities while operational stages remain largely untouched. By quantifying criminal specialization and structural integration, our network-based approach provides a framework for targeted, high-impact law enforcement interventions.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 67,976 posts and 305,048 comments from the darknet forum Dread to map an underground fraud ecosystem across a six-stage value chain. It finds that a thin layer of bridgers maintains cohesion, upstream stages cluster tightly, and generative AI saturates knowledge-building stages but not operational ones.
AI.motivation: Cyber-enabled fraud relies on a specialized underground ecosystem, yet its structural integration, actor trajectories, and uneven adoption of generative AI across operational stages remain poorly quantified.
AI.method: The authors analyze 67,976 posts and 305,048 comments across nine Dread communities using a six-stage value chain (Capability, Data Acquisition, Technique Sharing, Identity Forgery, Execution, Extraction) and compare structural cohesion against a degree-preserving null model.
AI.result: A thin layer of bridgers generates most content and maintains cohesion; three upstream knowledge-building stages form a tightly coupled cluster, whereas three downstream operational stages consist of specialized populations with little overlap. Generative AI saturates upstream knowledge-building communities while operational stages remain largely untouched.
AI.conclusion: Quantifying criminal specialization and structural integration across the fraud value chain provides a framework for targeted law enforcement interventions.

title: Beyond Binary Audits: Does Guideline Grounding Mitigate Decision-Space Framing in LLM Opioid Prescribing?
summary: Audits of LLMs for bias in opioid prescribing have largely relied on binary treatment decisions, a signal that current models have saturated. We introduce Q-Pain++, a full-factorial stress test that holds clinical content fixed while independently varying clinical risk factors and the granularity of the available dosage options. Adding an intermediate dosage option to otherwise unchanged vignettes substantially lowers agreement with expert-annotated dosages for most models, while demographic differences in dosage decisions remain small in all but one configuration once clinical risk factors are added. Grounding models in perioperative guidelines through retrieval reduces this framing effect on average but does not eliminate it, and one model's treatment decisions change when the retrieved passages are reordered. These results suggest that audits should vary the answer format, not only patient identity. We will release our codebase as well as Guideline-RAG-associated resources on GitHub (this https URL).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Q-Pain++, a full-factorial stress test for LLM opioid prescribing that varies clinical risk factors and dosage option granularity. Adding an intermediate dosage option substantially lowers expert agreement, and guideline RAG reduces but does not eliminate this framing effect.
AI.motivation: Binary treatment audits of LLM prescribing bias have saturated, leaving sensitivity to decision-space framing and clinical risk factors unexamined.
AI.method: Q-Pain++ holds clinical content fixed while independently varying clinical risk factors and dosage option granularity, and evaluates the mitigating effect of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounded in perioperative guidelines.
AI.result: Adding an intermediate dosage option substantially reduces agreement with expert-annotated dosages for most models, while demographic differences remain small in all but one configuration once risk factors are included. Guideline RAG reduces this framing effect on average without eliminating it, and reordering retrieved passages alters one model's decisions.
AI.conclusion: Clinical LLM audits should vary answer formats and decision-space granularity, not just patient identity.

title: ReVision: Selective Intrinsic Reasoning for Tool-Augmented, Reasoning-Intensive VQA
summary: External tools substantially expand what multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can retrieve and compute on reasoning-intensive visual questions, and aggregate accuracy typically improves when tools are available. Our empirical study across six VQA benchmarks shows that aggregate accuracy gains under tool access can coexist with answer reversals: questions answered correctly without tools but incorrectly with tools. Trajectory analysis reveals substantially shorter reasoning turns under tool access, suggesting a shift from intrinsic visual reasoning toward reliance on external outputs. We propose ReVision, a training-free test-time method that registers intrinsic reconsideration as an optional action alongside search and code execution. When invoked, a separate tool-free multimodal call re-examines the original image, integrates accumulated evidence, and returns a revised analysis. The MLLM chooses if and when to use it, without fixed reflection stages or paired rollouts. ReVision improves over standard tool use on all six benchmarks (1.28--7.51\%) and outperforms Dual-Rollout Combine on five, with reasoning-token use comparable to standard tool use.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ReVision, a training-free test-time method that registers intrinsic visual reconsideration as an optional tool-free action for tool-augmented MLLMs. ReVision improves over standard tool use on all six VQA benchmarks by 1.28% to 7.51%.
AI.motivation: Tool-augmented MLLMs achieve higher aggregate VQA accuracy but suffer answer reversals—failing questions they previously answered correctly without tools—because shorter reasoning turns shift reliance from intrinsic visual reasoning to external tool outputs.
AI.method: ReVision adds intrinsic reconsideration as an optional action alongside search and code execution; when invoked, a separate tool-free multimodal call re-examines the original image, integrates accumulated evidence, and returns a revised analysis without fixed reflection stages or paired rollouts.
AI.result: ReVision outperforms standard tool use on all six VQA benchmarks (by 1.28% to 7.51%) and beats Dual-Rollout Combine on five benchmarks, while keeping reasoning-token usage comparable to standard tool use.
AI.conclusion: Allowing MLLMs to selectively invoke tool-free visual reconsideration mitigates tool-induced answer reversals efficiently at test time.

title: Winning the Leaderboard, Losing the Distribution: Diagnosing and Mitigating Acoustic Narrowing in Low-Resource ASR
comment: 29 pages, 12 figures. Code, per-utterance outputs and fact ledger: this https URL
summary: For a low-resource language, one public leaderboard is often the only shared measure of progress, so optimizing toward it means optimizing toward a test distribution. Our low-rank fine-tune of whisper-large-v3-turbo ranked first on MediaSpeech, Common Voice 17 and a five-set Turkish community board, at 9.02% word error on MediaSpeech against 11.93% for the best baseline. On its private split it lost to unmodified whisper-large-v3. We treat that split as an alarm, not evidence; the main finding does not depend on it. On a twenty-condition FLEURS-TR benchmark built independently of our model selection, the unmodified base beats every fine-tune in every condition, and all five deficits clear zero under paired bootstrap. We call this acoustic narrowing: fine-tuning contracts the acoustic range a model serves well. The central finding is methodological: our in-house proxy for detecting narrowing concealed it instead, ranking the narrowed fine-tune above the sturdier base. Model selection needs a proxy from an independently produced distribution; more of the same source will not do. A rebuilt pipeline reduces the narrowing: a larger mixture with disclosed provenance, a higher-capacity base, and base-referenced selection with trajectory averaging. It wins three same-provenance axes and draws level on FLEURS-TR, 8.16% against 8.26%, interval spanning zero. Parity holds under a second inference stack and a full epoch, decoder fixed. The recovery is one trajectory, a demonstration rather than a validated recipe. In Kazakh the inversion reappears on corpora we did not build. With matched trainable-parameter shares, fine-tuning raised out-of-pool error by 2.23 points for an attention encoder-decoder and lowered it by 3.46 for a CTC encoder-only model, across three seeds each. Narrowing thus depends on the system adapted. We release TurkSpeak Bench, a robustness-first Turkish ASR leaderboard.

AI.tldr: This paper diagnoses "acoustic narrowing" in low-resource ASR, where fine-tuning whisper-large-v3-turbo wins public Turkish leaderboards (9.02% WER on MediaSpeech) but degrades on an independent 20-condition FLEURS-TR benchmark. A rebuilt pipeline with a higher-capacity base and base-referenced selection mitigates the narrowing.
AI.motivation: Optimizing low-resource ASR for a single public leaderboard risks overfitting to its test distribution, while same-source in-house proxies can conceal resulting out-of-distribution degradation.
AI.method: The authors evaluate fine-tuned models on an independent 20-condition FLEURS-TR benchmark, rebuild the pipeline using a larger disclosed mixture, a higher-capacity base, and base-referenced selection with trajectory averaging, and test cross-architecture behavior on Kazakh.
AI.result: Unmodified whisper-large-v3 beats every fine-tune across all 20 FLEURS-TR conditions, whereas the rebuilt pipeline draws level on FLEURS-TR (8.16% vs. 8.26%) while winning three same-provenance axes. In Kazakh, fine-tuning raises out-of-pool error by 2.23 points for an attention encoder-decoder but lowers it by 3.46 points for a CTC encoder-only model.
AI.conclusion: Model selection requires proxies from independently produced distributions, and the authors release TurkSpeak Bench as a robustness-first Turkish ASR leaderboard.

title: Non-Deterministic Finite Automata for Telugu Letters and Visualizations for Metrical Poetry
summary: Syllabic weight is central to Telugu metrical poetry. Syllabically, every letter (aksharam token) is either light (laghuvu) or heavy (guruvu). Poets classify it using a set of pre-defined rules. This paper formalizes aksharam token, the atomic unit of syllabic classification, as a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with the regular expression$\colon$ $(A_h+A_d+A_p)(\epsilon+V_s)+A_m+H^+G(\epsilon+H+V_s+V_v)$, where $\epsilon$ denotes a null string, $A$ denotes a vowel (achchu), comprising hrasvam ($A_h$), deergham ($A_d$), plutham ($A_p$), and miscellaneous ($A_m$), $H$ a pure consonant (pollu\_hallu), $G$ a vowel diacritic (gunintha\_chihnam), $V_s$ the sunna (anusvara), and $V_v$ the visarga, the latter two being nasal and aspirated sounds respectively. We then present automata diagrams and regular expressions for (i) a necessary condition satisfied by every light letter, and (ii) a sufficient condition for a letter to be heavy. Finally, we propose graphical visualizations for the 9 Telugu poem types.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes Telugu metrical poetry's atomic syllabic unit (aksharam token) as a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with an explicit regular expression, and provides automata for light and heavy syllable conditions alongside visualizations for nine Telugu poem types.
AI.motivation: Telugu metrical poetry relies on classifying every aksharam token as light (laghuvu) or heavy (guruvu) via pre-defined rules that benefit from formal automata-theoretic specification.
AI.method: The authors formalize the aksharam token as an NFA with a regular expression over vowels, pure consonants, diacritics, sunna, and visarga, derive automata and regular expressions for necessary light-letter and sufficient heavy-letter conditions, and design graphical visualizations for nine poem types.
AI.result: The paper delivers a formal NFA specification, regular expressions for light and heavy syllabic conditions, and graphical visualizations covering all nine Telugu poem types.
AI.conclusion: Formalizing Telugu syllabic weight with NFAs provides a precise computational foundation for analyzing and visualizing Telugu metrical poetry.

title: Criterion-Activated Preference Synthesis: Attribution-Preserving Preference Data from Explicit Standards
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is notoriously sensitive to attribution ambiguity: when chosen and rejected responses differ along multiple entangled dimensions, the model cannot identify which behavior the preference label teaches. We propose Criterion-Activated Preference Synthesis (CAPS), a criterion-first framework that turns explicit quality standards into attribution-verified preference pairs. CAPS synthesizes contexts and responses from a target criterion, then applies dual-signal scoring: a rubric-bound judge measures criterion compliance, while a blind general judge measures holistic quality. Two filters close the attribution loop: the Empirical Activation Test (EAT) keeps criterion-context pairs where satisfying the criterion improves blind quality, and the Attribution Ratio (AR) keeps pairs whose quality gap is dominated by the target criterion. Instantiated with general rubrics, medical rubrics, and Chinese legal statutes, CAPS shows strong data efficiency and domain transfer. With 20k general synthetic pairs, it outperforms 35k human-annotated HelpSteer3 pairs on IFEval, IFBench, AlpacaEval, and Creative Writing v3. In domain settings, CAPS improves HealthBench with 2k medical pairs and improves Qwen3-8B/14B by +4.9 to +6.6 points on legal benchmarks using only public statutes, without human preference labels. We additionally construct the CAPS-Legal preference dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Criterion-Activated Preference Synthesis (CAPS), a framework that synthesizes attribution-verified preference pairs from explicit quality standards using dual-signal scoring and two attribution filters. With 20k synthetic pairs, CAPS outperforms 35k human-annotated HelpSteer3 pairs across four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) suffers from attribution ambiguity when chosen and rejected responses differ across multiple entangled dimensions, obscuring which behavior the preference label teaches.
AI.method: CAPS synthesizes contexts and responses from a target criterion, scores them with both a rubric-bound judge and a blind general judge, and applies the Empirical Activation Test (EAT) and Attribution Ratio (AR) filters to ensure the quality gap is driven by the target criterion.
AI.result: Using 20k general synthetic pairs, CAPS outperforms 35k human-annotated HelpSteer3 pairs on IFEval, IFBench, AlpacaEval, and Creative Writing v3. In domain settings, it improves HealthBench with 2k medical pairs and boosts Qwen3-8B/14B by +4.9 to +6.6 points on legal benchmarks using only public statutes, alongside releasing CAPS-Legal.
AI.conclusion: Criterion-first synthesis with attribution filtering yields highly data-efficient, domain-transferable preference data without human preference labels.

title: Wrong with Confidence: Measuring Hallucination, Overconfidence and Identity-Conditioned Behaviour in Large Language Models
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Data and code are included as ancillary files
summary: Large language models answer underspecified questions readily, and accuracy-only evaluation rewards guessing over abstaining. Observational studies link query underspecification to hallucination, but they cannot separate the effect of missing information from item difficulty, and they rarely ask what the model tells the user. We report a pre-registered, paired behavioural study of five open-weight models (Gemma 3 27B, Gemma 4 31B, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B and Nemotron 3 Super). Each of 142 factual questions was posed in a fully specified form and in a referentially underspecified form with the same answer key, and three probes measured identity-conditioned behaviour. Two raters scored 5,620 responses under a fixed rubric; effects were estimated with mixed-effects models. Without the referent, the models sought clarification on 33.7% of prompts and answered the rest. Among attempted answers, the error rate rose from 39.1% to 52.0% (mixed-effects odds ratio 4.12, 95% CI 2.76-6.14), and specialist-domain questions failed more often than general ones in every model. Unelicited verbal uncertainty did not track this risk: 75.3% of wrong answers carried no hedge, wrong answers to underspecified prompts were hedged no more often than wrong answers to clear prompts (27.3% vs 22.3%), and hedging separated correct from incorrect answers only weakly (AUROC 0.56). Gendered pronouns followed occupational stereotypes whenever a model committed to one; any stated user identity lengthened answers by about 45% relative to an anonymous user; claimed expertise did not reduce safety caveats. The models either ask or answer as if the question were well posed, and the wording of a guess does not reveal that it is one. Evaluations should score clarification as a distinct outcome and check label validity as well as rater agreement.

AI.tldr: This pre-registered paired study of five open-weight LLMs (5,620 scored responses) shows that referential underspecification increases error rates from 39.1% to 52.0% while unelicited hedging fails to signal uncertainty. Stated user identity lengthens answers by ~45%, and gendered pronouns follow occupational stereotypes.
AI.motivation: Observational studies link query underspecification to hallucination but cannot separate missing information from item difficulty or examine what models communicate to users.
AI.method: The authors pose 142 factual questions in both fully specified and referentially underspecified forms—plus three identity-conditioned probes—to five open-weight models (Gemma 3 27B, Gemma 4 31B, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, and Nemotron 3 Super), with two raters scoring 5,620 responses analyzed via mixed-effects models.
AI.result: Without the referent, models seek clarification on 33.7% of prompts and answer the rest, raising error rates from 39.1% to 52.0% (odds ratio 4.12). Moreover, 75.3% of wrong answers contain no hedge, hedging barely separates correct from incorrect answers (AUROC 0.56), any stated identity lengthens answers by ~45%, and claimed expertise does not reduce safety caveats.
AI.conclusion: LLMs guess confidently on underspecified prompts without signaling uncertainty in their wording, so evaluations must score clarification as a distinct outcome.

title: Mapping the Afterlife of Future Work Statements in NLP Research
summary: Future work statements are one of the few places in scientific papers where authors explicitly describe what they think should happen next. We study what happens to such statements after publication. We construct a dataset of 72,070 future work items extracted from 23,113 ACL Anthology papers published between 1979 and 2025, categorize them by type, retrieve candidate follow-up papers through citation-based and content-based search, and use LLM-based judgments to assess whether later papers pursue the proposed directions. Using this resource, we analyze patterns across time, venues, categories, themes, and authors. We find that many items are later addressed, often within a few years, with clear differences across types and themes and a largely community-driven pattern. Our results suggest that future work statements provide useful evidence for studying how research directions develop in NLP. To support further research, we release our dataset at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs a dataset of 72,070 future work items from 23,113 ACL Anthology papers (1979–2025) and uses citation/content search with LLM judgments to track whether later papers pursue them. Many proposed directions are addressed within a few years in a largely community-driven pattern.
AI.motivation: Future work statements capture what authors believe should happen next, yet their post-publication trajectory across NLP research has not been systematically mapped.
AI.method: The authors extract 72,070 future work items from 23,113 ACL Anthology papers, categorize them by type, retrieve candidate follow-up papers via citation-based and content-based search, and apply LLM-based judgments to assess whether later work pursues the proposed directions.
AI.result: Analysis across time, venues, categories, themes, and authors shows that many future work items are addressed within a few years, with distinct variations across types and themes and a predominantly community-driven pattern.
AI.conclusion: Future work statements provide valuable empirical evidence for understanding how research directions evolve in NLP, supported by the authors' public dataset release.

title: KUDEX: A Zero-Shot Decompositional Framework for Logical Analysis in Natural Language
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text, they often struggle with multi-step logical reasoning with inferential connections among statements. We introduce KUDEX (Knowledge-Upward-Downward Reasoning Extension), a novel zero-shot, decompositional framework for analyzing and verifying logical relationships in natural language. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on surface-level entailment checks, KUDEX leverages LLMs to decompose reasoning into atomic primitives and constructs transparent reasoning graphs that serve both as execution traces and audit logs. Our framework includes a general prompt adaptation pipeline that adapts to diverse reasoning tasks without additional fine-tuning or domain-specific pipelines. Through comprehensive experiments on benchmarks across four domains, we demonstrate that KUDEX provides superior performance compared to existing methods, offering a more granular and robust framework for assessing logical relationships between statements.

AI.tldr: KUDEX is a zero-shot decompositional framework that uses LLMs to break natural language logical reasoning into atomic primitives and transparent reasoning graphs, outperforming existing methods across four domains.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with multi-step logical reasoning involving inferential connections among statements, and traditional approaches rely on surface-level entailment checks without transparent execution traces.
AI.method: KUDEX decomposes reasoning into atomic primitives, constructs reasoning graphs that serve as execution traces and audit logs, and uses a general prompt adaptation pipeline without fine-tuning or domain-specific pipelines.
AI.result: Experiments on benchmarks across four domains show that KUDEX outperforms existing methods in assessing logical relationships between statements.
AI.conclusion: Decompositional reasoning graphs with zero-shot prompt adaptation provide a granular, auditable, and robust framework for natural language logical analysis.

title: GPBam: A Retrieval-Aware German Public Law Exam Benchmark
comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at the 39th International Conference on Legal Knowledge and Information Systems (JURIX 2026). 43 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables
summary: Legal reasoning in civil-law systems is not rule-lookup: the German state examination asks for a structured opinion (Gutachten) that names the governing norms, applies them to the facts, and argues to a conclusion. We introduce GPBam (German Public Law Bar-style Exam), 81 public-law examination cases with reference solutions, paired with a recitation task over 200 statutory provisions. Drawn from state examination preparation, the cases are broad and rarely repeat, and are not publicly available - we find no evidence of exact-solution memorisation in the models we evaluate, and keeping them private limits contamination. Because each reference solution's cited norms form a retrieval gold set over the very instances the essays are graded on, GPBam scores retrieval and long-form generation jointly, which makes it a benchmark for legal retrieval as well as for legal writing and lets us ask how much retrieval quality a legal opinion actually needs. Across 32 open-weight and proprietary models evaluated without retrieval, scores span 4.81-76.42 out of 100. Supplying the law helps modestly: across seven models and eight retrieval configurations, retrieval performance varies nearly threefold and buys at most 4.1 essay points, and nothing significant for three of the seven, while an oracle with 91% gold-norm recall improves scores by 2-6 points. Essay quality strongly tracks prior knowledge: verbatim statute recall, measured in a separate task, correlates at $\rho = 0.92$ over 32 models.

AI.tldr: GPBam is a private benchmark of 81 German public-law exam cases and 200 statutory provisions that jointly evaluates legal retrieval and long-form opinion writing, showing that prior statutory knowledge correlates strongly with essay quality while retrieval helps only modestly.
AI.motivation: Civil-law legal reasoning requires structured opinions (Gutachten) that identify governing norms, apply them to facts, and argue to a conclusion, rather than simple rule lookup, and existing benchmarks lack joint evaluation of retrieval and long-form legal writing without contamination.
AI.method: The authors introduce GPBam, comprising 81 non-public public-law examination cases with reference solutions whose cited norms form a retrieval gold set, paired with a verbatim recitation task over 200 statutory provisions.
AI.result: Across 32 models without retrieval, scores span 4.81 to 76.42 out of 100 and correlate at rho = 0.92 with verbatim statute recall; across seven models and eight retrieval configurations, retrieval adds at most 4.1 essay points (and nothing significant for three models), while a 91% recall oracle adds 2 to 6 points.
AI.conclusion: Long-form civil-law exam performance depends heavily on internalized statutory knowledge, and current retrieval setups provide limited gains even with near-oracle norm recall.

title: PREFACE: Separating Shared Corrections from Prefix Conditioning in PEFT
comment: 22 pages, 2 figures. Includes supplementary analyses, code, and numerical evaluation artifacts
summary: Does input-conditioned parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) improve because it uses the current input, or because it adds a useful learned correction? We investigate this distinction with PREFACE, a bounded channel controller for PEFT-adapted projections that requires no test-time gradients. The controller reads observed context; in multiple-choice likelihood scoring, its state is independent of the candidate continuation. Our central study freezes IA3, tuned LoRA, and DoRA adapters and matches controller architecture, initialization, batches, and updates across current-prefix and learned-global controls. Across ARC-Challenge and SciQ, current-prefix control improves all six mean accuracies over frozen adapters, but none of its paired contrasts with learned-global control excludes zero. Replacing its corrections with their training-prefix mean changes accuracy by at most 0.34 percentage points; input-varying corrections contribute only 1.8-2.8% of correction RMS. On ARC test, frozen-adapter current/global controls score 25.68%/25.77%, distinct from the earlier jointly trained 23.1% to 26.4% gain over IA3. We derive and evaluate static compilation of fixed corrections, separating deployment simplification from statistical equivalence. Broader GPT-2, Pythia, and Qwen experiments show family-, task-, and scoring-dependent gains, with modest recent-model effects. The study provides an intervention-based evaluation of conditional PEFT: improvements over a static adapter do not by themselves demonstrate a benefit from input matching.

AI.tldr: PREFACE is a bounded channel controller for PEFT-adapted projections used to test whether conditional PEFT gains come from input matching or learned global corrections, finding that current-prefix and learned-global controls perform statistically indistinguishably.
AI.motivation: Existing input-conditioned PEFT methods improve over static adapters, but it is unclear whether gains arise from conditioning on the current input or simply from adding a useful learned correction.
AI.method: The authors propose PREFACE, a gradient-free bounded channel controller, and compare current-prefix control against matched learned-global controls on frozen IA3, LoRA, and DoRA adapters across ARC-Challenge, SciQ, and broader GPT-2, Pythia, and Qwen experiments.
AI.result: On ARC-Challenge and SciQ, current-prefix control improves all six mean accuracies over frozen adapters, but no paired contrast with learned-global control excludes zero; replacing corrections with their training-prefix mean changes accuracy by at most 0.34 percentage points, and input-varying corrections contribute only 1.8 to 2.8% of correction RMS (25.68% vs. 25.77% on ARC test).
AI.conclusion: Improvements over static PEFT adapters do not by themselves establish a benefit from input matching, highlighting the need for intervention-based controls.

title: SurveyWeave: An Agentic Framework for Automated Survey Generation
summary: Surveys help researchers keep up with fast-moving fields, but they take weeks to months to write. Automated survey generation (AutoSurvey) can alleviate this situation, but it is challenging to draw on hundreds to thousands of precisely scoped papers, choose among many valid structures, and stay faithful to its sources while offering insights. We present SurveyWeave, an agentic architecture that decomposes the problem into four tasks coordinated by three agents, each reviewing others' work and conducting revisions based on feedback. We also introduce WeaveEval, a five-dimension evaluation grounded in prior surveys. A comprehensive comparison shows that SurveyWeave outperforms Codex by 8 points and the strongest AutoSurvey baseline by 6 points.

AI.tldr: SurveyWeave is a multi-agent framework for automated survey generation that coordinates four tasks across three reviewing agents, outperforming Codex and prior AutoSurvey baselines on the proposed WeaveEval benchmark.
AI.motivation: Writing academic surveys manually takes weeks to months, while automated survey generation struggles to synthesize hundreds to thousands of scoped papers, select valid structures, and remain faithful to sources.
AI.method: SurveyWeave decomposes survey generation into four tasks coordinated by three agents that review each other's work and revise based on feedback, evaluated using WeaveEval, a five-dimension evaluation grounded in prior surveys.
AI.result: SurveyWeave outperforms Codex by 8 points and the strongest AutoSurvey baseline by 6 points on WeaveEval.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent task decomposition with iterative peer review improves the quality and faithfulness of automated survey generation.

title: Beyond Controllability: Speaker Diversity in Instruction-Guided Text-to-Speech
summary: Instruction-guided text-to-speech (ITTS) lets users specify voice properties in natural language. Applications from conversational AI character voices to synthetic training data for downstream speech models depend on the system producing many distinct voices when the same broad category is requested repeatedly. No prior work audits whether ITTS outputs are in fact diverse, either compared to real speech or across attribute values. We evaluate seven open-source ITTS systems using speaker embeddings whose representational capacity we independently validate. Every system produces speaker distributions markedly narrower than real speech. Furthermore, female prompts produce less diverse voice pools than male prompts across most systems. In contrast, accent and emotion prompts barely alter speaker diversity in most systems, but reveal a strong controllability bias toward North American English and neutral speech. These results show that diversity and controllability capture complementary weaknesses, neither of which alone is sufficient to evaluate ITTS. Our code and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: An audit of seven open-source instruction-guided text-to-speech (ITTS) systems reveals that all produce much narrower speaker diversity than real speech and exhibit demographic and controllability biases.
AI.motivation: Applications such as character voices and synthetic speech training data require ITTS systems to generate diverse speakers from broad natural-language prompts, yet no prior work has audited speaker diversity in ITTS outputs.
AI.method: The authors evaluate seven open-source ITTS systems using independently validated speaker embeddings to measure speaker diversity across repeated prompts and attribute values.
AI.result: Every system produces markedly narrower speaker distributions than real speech, female prompts yield less diverse voice pools than male prompts in most systems, and accent and emotion prompts barely alter diversity while revealing strong bias toward North American English and neutral speech.
AI.conclusion: Diversity and controllability capture complementary weaknesses in ITTS systems, and neither metric alone is sufficient for evaluation.

title: The Geometry of Conceptors in Neural-Activation Spaces
summary: Conceptors represent concepts as graded collections of directions in neural-activation space rather than as single vectors. We develop a geometric account of how these representations depend on the contrast used to define a concept: opposing values in bipolar fitting, or presence and absence in unipolar fitting. We derive an exact decomposition of a centered pooled conceptor into an average pole filter, a mean-separation update, and a covariance-shape update. Experiments across five language models on sentiment, political leaning and stance, and depression expression show that both updates improve reconstruction of held-out contrasts. Additional directions preserve variation beyond the mean-difference line, and changing the comparator changes the benefit of these directions. Shape, size, and overlap each show up downstream: in amplification experiments, bipolar fits raise evidence for both poles more consistently than unipolar fits; conceptor size (the quota) correlates positively with layerwise probe performance; and cross-concept overlap quantifies interference under subspace removal, linking shared directions to Boolean composition. In an additional generation evaluation, conceptor filters achieve higher target-expression win rates against an unsteered reference than three mean-based controls. Together, these findings explain how fitting choices shape conceptor geometry and support bipolar fitting when the objective is to amplify both opposing poles.

AI.tldr: This paper derives an exact geometric decomposition of conceptors in neural-activation space and shows across five language models that bipolar fitting outperforms unipolar fitting when amplifying both opposing poles of a concept.
AI.motivation: Conceptors represent concepts as graded collections of directions rather than single vectors, but how contrast choices (bipolar vs. unipolar fitting) shape their geometry and downstream behavior has lacked a formal account.
AI.method: The authors decompose a centered pooled conceptor into an average pole filter, a mean-separation update, and a covariance-shape update, and evaluate them across five language models on sentiment, political leaning and stance, and depression expression.
AI.result: Both mean-separation and covariance-shape updates improve held-out contrast reconstruction, bipolar fits raise evidence for both poles more consistently than unipolar fits, conceptor quota correlates with layerwise probe performance, cross-concept overlap tracks interference, and conceptor filters beat three mean-based controls in generation win rates.
AI.conclusion: Fitting choices directly govern conceptor geometry, and bipolar fitting is preferable when steering or amplifying both opposing poles of a concept.

title: What Transfers Across Cuneiform? Script-Level Substrate and Language-Specific Regularities via Segmentation and Representation
summary: Cuneiform recorded typologically unrelated languages for more than three millennia, raising a natural question: which of its statistical regularities are properties of the shared writing system, and which belong to individual languages? We answer this with two probe pairs targeting the same script-versus-language decomposition. The first compares two unsupervised, dictionary-free segmentation methods: transitional probability (TP), grounded in infant statistical-learning research, and Morfessor. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic evaluation of dictionary-free segmentation on cuneiform; the only prior published baseline relies on a hand-built dictionary (Max-Match, F1 = 0.74). Both our methods reach F1 > 0.97 within language (Morfessor reaches F1 > 0.99 on Akkadian and Sumerian), exceeding MaxMatch by more than 23 F1 points, but diverge sharply in cross-language transfer: TP holds F1 > 0.95 across all six language pairs, while Morfessor collapses to F1 = 0.27 from the 13K-token Elamite source. A learning curve and a Hittite stress test (34.7% foreign-script logograms, where TP drops 35 points and Morfessor only 8) further isolate the two underlying mechanisms. The second probe pair extends the same decomposition to representations: concatenating Unicode and Latin features improves classification in 11 of 12 morphosyntactic tasks (p < 0.01). We release CUNEI-TOOLS and a three-language benchmark.

AI.tldr: Using dictionary-free segmentation and representation probes on cuneiform, this paper separates script-level substrate regularities from language-specific structure and releases CUNEI-TOOLS and a three-language benchmark.
AI.motivation: Cuneiform recorded typologically unrelated languages for over three millennia, making it unclear which statistical regularities belong to the shared writing system versus individual languages.
AI.method: The authors compare two unsupervised dictionary-free segmentation methods, transitional probability (TP) and Morfessor, across within-language and cross-language transfer, and test combined Unicode and Latin feature representations on 12 morphosyntactic classification tasks.
AI.result: Both methods exceed F1 = 0.97 within language (Morfessor > 0.99 on Akkadian and Sumerian, beating the Max-Match baseline of 0.74 by over 23 points), but TP holds F1 > 0.95 across all six transfer pairs while Morfessor drops to 0.27 from Elamite; concatenating Unicode and Latin features improves 11 of 12 morphosyntactic tasks (p < 0.01).
AI.conclusion: Unsupervised segmentation and dual-script representations effectively disentangle shared cuneiform script properties from language-specific regularities.

title: EEGHyena2: Fixation-Inspired Joint Lexical-Grammatical Conditional Random Field for Interpretable EEG-to-Text Decoding
summary: A sentence is built from words that carry lexical meaning and grammatical roles, and brain activity during reading reflects both. Current EEG-to-text decoders, however, let a large language model (LLM) propose and order the words, so fluent output can reflect the LLM's prior more than the recorded EEG. In this study, we asked whether fixation-linked EEG carries lexical and grammatical evidence during natural reading and how a decoder can use such evidence. Fixation-related potential analyses showed that content and function words differ reliably in group-averaged EEG but only weakly in single words. We therefore propose EEGHyena2, a structured decoder in which a bidirectional encoder inspired by StripedHyena 2 feeds a semantic head that ranks a fixed lexicon and a part-of-speech (POS) head that predicts grammatical categories; a joint word-POS conditional random field (CRF) scores a restricted candidate lattice, and a frozen Llama-2 scores the candidates in context. On two natural-reading corpora, ZuCo and ROAMM, it matched the state-of-the-art method on BLEU-1 (21.4 vs 21.3), exceeded it on ROUGE-1 F1 (23.3 vs 20.3), lowered the character error rate on ROAMM (75.3% vs 84.7%) and decoded each recording about 3-10 times faster than LLM candidate search. The CRF learned transitions that mirror English syntax, and the encoder drew local context from its convolutions and distant context from attention. Decoders can thus pool weak word-level EEG evidence across the sentence through explicit lexical and grammatical structure, with the language model adjudicating among candidates rather than generating them, which lowers decoding cost and keeps decisions inspectable.

AI.tldr: EEGHyena2 is a structured EEG-to-text decoder that combines a StripedHyena-2-inspired encoder, lexical and part-of-speech heads, a joint word-POS CRF, and frozen Llama-2 rescoring to match or exceed state-of-the-art accuracy at 3 to 10x faster decoding.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG-to-text decoders let an LLM propose and order words, causing fluent outputs to reflect the LLM's language prior rather than weak word-level EEG evidence.
AI.method: EEGHyena2 uses a bidirectional encoder inspired by StripedHyena 2 feeding a semantic lexicon-ranking head and a POS head, followed by a joint word-POS conditional random field over a restricted lattice and contextual scoring by a frozen Llama-2 model.
AI.result: On ZuCo and ROAMM, EEGHyena2 matches state-of-the-art BLEU-1 (21.4 vs. 21.3), improves ROUGE-1 F1 (23.3 vs. 20.3), lowers ROAMM character error rate (75.3% vs. 84.7%), and decodes 3 to 10 times faster than LLM candidate search.
AI.conclusion: Pooling weak word-level EEG evidence through explicit lexical-grammatical structure while restricting the LLM to candidate adjudication lowers decoding cost and improves inspectability.

title: Latency, Speech Recognition and Turn-Taking in Voice Agents for Spanish Phone Negotiation: An Externally Measured Comparison of Pipecat, LiveKit and GPT-Live
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables. Code and data: this https URL (archived at this https URL)
summary: A voice agent that negotiates by phone must answer quickly, understand spoken amounts and cope with a caller who talks over it. We compared three architectures for such an agent, negotiating freight rates in Spanish: two cascades (speech recognition, language model and speech synthesis) orchestrated by Pipecat and by LiveKit Agents, and GPT-Live, an OpenAI speech model that listens and speaks without separate stages. A program played the carrier with the same 47 recordings of one speaker for all agents, without the telephone network, in 77 calls per architecture over five negotiation scenarios, and measured latency on the listener's side with a validated instrument. Median latency to the content response was 2,616.0 ms (Pipecat), 3,090.0 ms (LiveKit) and 2,444.8 ms (GPT-Live); the confidence interval of GPT-Live's 171.2 ms advantage over Pipecat includes zero. According to its own timestamps, GPT-Live began to answer 800 ms after the end of the line, close to the 0.8 s published by OpenAI; most of the remaining wait, about 1,367 ms and nearly constant, is the audio's round trip through OpenAI's service. A tool call added 0.9-1.1 s in every architecture, more than any difference between them, and the frameworks' self-reported latency fell short of the listener's wait by 9% (Pipecat) and 22% (LiveKit). Word error rates were low (6.03, 4.93 and 1.47%), but the error on amounts was 13.01% and 12.61% in the cascades, against 2.86% in GPT-Live. With default settings, Pipecat and LiveKit stopped at almost every backchannel and often took it as the carrier's answer: an "ok" spoken over the agent ended in a registered agreement in 3 of 15 Pipecat calls, 2 of 15 LiveKit calls and no GPT-Live call (descriptive counts, not tested). Latency should therefore be measured on the listener's side, and a cascade needs safeguards for spoken amounts and backchannels.

AI.tldr: An externally measured comparison of Pipecat, LiveKit Agents, and GPT-Live on Spanish phone negotiation shows similar listener-side latency across systems, but much lower error rates on spoken amounts and fewer backchannel interruptions in GPT-Live.
AI.motivation: Voice agents for phone negotiation must respond quickly, accurately recognize spoken monetary amounts, and handle overlapping caller speech, yet frameworks' self-reported latencies and real-world cascade failure modes are poorly characterized.
AI.method: The authors run 77 simulated calls per architecture across five Spanish freight-negotiation scenarios using 47 recordings of one speaker, measuring listener-side latency, word and amount error rates, and backchannel handling.
AI.result: Median listener-side latency is 2,616.0 ms (Pipecat), 3,090.0 ms (LiveKit), and 2,444.8 ms (GPT-Live), with self-reported latency underestimating wait by 9% (Pipecat) and 22% (LiveKit); amount error rates are 13.01% and 12.61% for cascades vs. 2.86% for GPT-Live, and cascades falsely registered agreements on overlapping "ok" backchannels in 5 of 30 calls vs. 0 of 15 for GPT-Live.
AI.conclusion: Voice-agent latency should be measured on the listener's side, and cascade architectures require explicit safeguards for spoken amounts and backchannel speech.

title: Low-Latency LLM-Based Streaming Multi-Talker ASR with Verifiable Rewards
summary: LLM-based architectures offer strong generalization and instruction-following capabilities for streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR), but multi-talker use introduces coupled transcription, attribution, and latency challenges. Our wearable setting requires real-time transcription of a conversation between a near-field device wearer and a far-field partner. Because partial hypotheses are rendered on persistent sides of a dialogue UI, speaker roles cannot be permuted and each speaker tag must precede its turn. These sparse tags are weakly optimized by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while committing to a leading tag can delay the text that follows. We therefore post-train a streaming LLM-based ASR model with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), combining a fixed-role Speaker-Attributed WER (SA-WER) grader with a turn-level onset-delay reward. On an eight-direction multi-talker cohort, SA-WER RL reduces SA-WER from $20.51\%$ for SFT to $13.14\%$. Adding the delay objective reduces onset $p50$ by $65\%$ (from $0.918\,\text{s}$ to $0.320\,\text{s}$) and $p90$ by $44\%$ (from $1.389\,\text{s}$ to $0.780\,\text{s}$) relative to SA-WER-only RL, while achieving $12.70\%$ SA-WER. These results demonstrate that fixed-role recognition quality and streaming responsiveness can be improved jointly.

AI.tldr: Post-training a streaming LLM-based multi-talker ASR model with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) using Speaker-Attributed WER and onset-delay rewards jointly improves attribution accuracy and reduces latency.
AI.motivation: In wearable streaming multi-talker ASR, supervised fine-tuning weakly optimizes fixed-role leading speaker tags, and committing to a tag can delay subsequent transcription.
AI.method: The authors post-train a streaming LLM-based ASR model with RLVR combining a fixed-role Speaker-Attributed WER (SA-WER) grader and a turn-level onset-delay reward.
AI.result: On an eight-direction multi-talker cohort, SA-WER RL reduces SA-WER from 20.51% (SFT) to 13.14%, and adding the delay objective reduces onset p50 by 65% (0.918 s to 0.320 s) and p90 by 44% (1.389 s to 0.780 s) while reaching 12.70% SA-WER.
AI.conclusion: Verifiable speaker-attribution and onset-delay rewards can jointly optimize transcription quality and streaming responsiveness in fixed-role multi-talker ASR.

title: A Systematic Study of Cross-Token Transfer for Data-Efficient Non-Verbal Text-to-Speech
summary: Non-verbal vocalizations (NVs), such as laughter and breath, carry affective cues that words alone do not convey. Yet NV data remains scarce because speech annotation pipelines often omit or normalize these events. Existing work has improved NV text-to-speech through model design and data curation, but whether one NV token can help a model learn another has received little systematic study. We investigate this cross-token transferability in a controlled CosyVoice 2 setup. We first trace a laughter-only scaling curve, then hold laughter at 200 or 1,600 examples while adding breath, sigh, cough, lip-smack, or neutral speech. With only 200 laughter examples, adding 3,200 cough examples raises end-to-end laughter F1 from 0.170 to 0.529, surpassing the 0.495 obtained from 1,600 laughter examples alone. At the 1,600-example anchor, cough reaches 0.695, nearly matching 6,400 laughter examples (0.697). Waveform-level Whisper-D scoring and a semantic-token transcriber show consistent trends. Cross-token transfer therefore offers a complementary route to low-resource NV generation.

AI.tldr: A controlled study in CosyVoice 2 shows that cross-token transfer from other non-verbal vocalizations, especially coughs, substantially improves low-resource laughter generation.
AI.motivation: Non-verbal vocalizations (NVs) like laughter and breath are scarce in speech datasets, and it has been unclear whether training on one NV token helps a text-to-speech model learn another.
AI.method: Using CosyVoice 2, the authors trace a laughter-only scaling curve and then hold laughter at 200 or 1,600 examples while adding breath, sigh, cough, lip-smack, or neutral speech, evaluating with end-to-end laughter F1, Whisper-D, and a semantic-token transcriber.
AI.result: With 200 laughter examples, adding 3,200 cough examples raises laughter F1 from 0.170 to 0.529, surpassing 1,600 laughter examples alone (0.495); at 1,600 laughter examples, adding cough reaches 0.695, nearly matching 6,400 laughter examples (0.697).
AI.conclusion: Cross-token transfer offers an effective, data-efficient complement to target-token collection for low-resource non-verbal TTS.

title: MarineSparkLM-4B: A Lightweight Language Model for Marine and Offshore Engineering Built by Parameter-Efficient Adaptation
summary: Marine and offshore engineering text is spread across preprints, open-access journals, encyclopedias and institutional documents, and the amount of it is small by pretraining standards. We ask how far a lightweight language model for marine and offshore engineering can be taken with parameter-efficient adaptation on a single workstation-class device. Starting from the 4-billion-parameter OceanGPT-basic-4B-Instruct, we train two independent LoRA adapters, each updating 33.0 million of 4.06 billion parameters (0.81%). Training took 4 hours 40 minutes for the first adapter and 10 minutes for the second on one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The first adapter is trained by next-token prediction on a 61.6-million-token corpus covering ten engineering themes. The corpus was built from 13,879 source documents, of which 7,069 were retained after deduplication and a two-tier keyword filter that removes cross-domain lexical collisions. Its validation loss falls from 2.082 to 1.976 over 1,500 steps. Direct testing showed that this adapter could still drift off topic on a retrieval-grounded ballast-water prompt, so we trained a second adapter on 2,295 question-answer pairs (114 hand-written and 2,181 generated by the base model from corpus passages) with the loss restricted to answer tokens. On 20 held-out prompts scored by hand for accuracy, topicality and specificity (maximum 120), the plain base model, the continuation adapter, the instruction adapter and the instruction adapter with retrieval scored 42, 56, 84 and 88. Absolute accuracy stays low (14 of 40 without retrieval and 20 of 40 with it). We report the full pipeline, two negative results (a reverted keyword fix and an instruction run that overfit within 100 steps), and the limits of the evaluation, which uses one small prompt set, no inter-rater agreement measure and model-generated reference answers.

AI.tldr: MarineSparkLM-4B adapts OceanGPT-basic-4B-Instruct to marine and offshore engineering using two lightweight LoRA adapters trained on a single workstation, improving topicality and specificity on held-out prompts though absolute accuracy remains low.
AI.motivation: Marine and offshore engineering text is scattered and small by pretraining standards, raising the question of how far a 4B-parameter model can be adapted with parameter-efficient fine-tuning on a single workstation-class device.
AI.method: Starting from OceanGPT-basic-4B-Instruct on one NVIDIA DGX Spark, the authors train two independent 33.0M-parameter (0.81%) LoRA adapters: one for domain continuation on 61.6M tokens (7,069 filtered documents) and one for instruction tuning on 2,295 QA pairs.
AI.result: On 20 held-out prompts scored out of 120, scores rise from 42 (base) to 56 (continuation), 84 (instruction), and 88 (instruction with retrieval), while absolute accuracy stays low (14/40 without retrieval, 20/40 with retrieval); the paper also documents two negative results and evaluation limits.
AI.conclusion: Workstation-scale LoRA adaptation improves domain topicality and specificity for marine engineering, though factual accuracy remains limited without stronger retrieval and evaluation.

title: Personalized Language Models for One-to-Many Private Communications
summary: We study relationship-specific continual reply prediction for one-to-many private communication: a system predicts an author's reply to a recurring contact and updates its personalization state when the actual reply becomes available. We propose TRACE (Temporal Relationship-Aware Communication Evolution), which uses author-level lexical habits, contact-specific wording, and temporal expression estimates to guide a frozen language model, with a feedback-driven policy controlling revision. On 216 test emails from eight Enron users, all four main TRACE configurations achieve higher mean BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore and lower mean Reply Style MSE than Base LLM and Base RAG. Component ablations show mixed effects and do not establish statistically reliable improvements in Reply Style MSE after multiple-comparison correction. More accurate state forecasts and larger revision budgets do not consistently improve reply-level metrics. These exploratory findings expose the challenge of turning evolving relationship-specific expression estimates into useful generation guidance.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a continual reply-prediction framework that conditions a frozen LLM on evolving author- and contact-specific lexical and temporal estimates, outperforming Base LLM and Base RAG on Enron emails while revealing limits in component ablations.
AI.motivation: Predicting an author's reply to a recurring contact in one-to-many private communication requires adapting to relationship-specific and temporally evolving expression habits.
AI.method: TRACE combines author-level lexical habits, contact-specific wording, and temporal expression estimates to guide a frozen LLM, with a feedback-driven policy controlling reply revision.
AI.result: On 216 test emails from eight Enron users, all four main TRACE configurations achieve higher mean BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore and lower mean Reply Style MSE than Base LLM and Base RAG, though component ablations show mixed effects without statistically reliable MSE gains after multiple-comparison correction.
AI.conclusion: While relationship-aware conditioning improves overall reply metrics over baselines, turning evolving expression estimates into reliable generation guidance remains challenging.

title: A Bag of Concepts? Testing Role-Filler Binding in the Verbalizable Workspace
comment: Accepted at Interpretability as a Science Workshop, NeurIPS 2026
summary: Runtime alignment monitors built on a verbalizable workspace have been proposed as a way to surface a model's silent cognition before it produces output. Their value rests on the workspace carrying enough structure to distinguish safety-relevant propositions, most of which are relational: "the model plans to deceive the user" and "the user plans to deceive the model" share a concept set and differ only in role assignment. We ask whether the workspace carries the role-filler bindings (which entity fills which role) such a monitor would need, on three frontier language models (Qwen3.6-27B, Gemma-3-12B, Gemma-3-27B-IT), under two lens families (J-lens and R-lens), and with two methods for fitting the role direction (difference-of-means and LRE-gradient). We find a clean dissociation: the workspace carries directions that steer what the model outputs about roles but not the representations the model uses to compute them. Linear probes recover role at near-ceiling from the residual stream but score below a rank-matched random control when reading the workspace, and steering the model along the fitted role direction changes which entity it binds to no more than strength-matched control edits do. Ablating the workspace (zeroing the residual stream's projection onto its ten most active lens directions) damages binding on one of the three models (Gemma-3-27B-IT, holding across three lens variants) and shows no binding-specific damage on the other two, with a rank-matched random subspace as the control; this confirms our design detects binding when present, though scale and instruction tuning are confounded there. A workspace-lens monitor built on these directions would therefore miss a role assignment the model itself represents.

AI.tldr: Probing and steering experiments on three frontier language models show that verbalizable workspace lenses capture directions that steer role outputs but do not represent the role-filler bindings the models actually use internally.
AI.motivation: Runtime alignment monitors built on verbalizable workspaces assume the workspace encodes relational propositions such as who is deceiving whom, which requires representing role-filler bindings rather than just a bag of concepts.
AI.method: The authors test Qwen3.6-27B, Gemma-3-12B, and Gemma-3-27B-IT using J-lens and R-lens families with difference-of-means and LRE-gradient role directions, comparing linear probes, steering, and workspace ablation against rank-matched random controls.
AI.result: Linear probes recover role at near-ceiling from the residual stream but score below a rank-matched random control on the workspace, steering along the fitted role direction changes binding no more than control edits, and workspace ablation damages binding only on Gemma-3-27B-IT.
AI.conclusion: Workspace-lens monitors built on these directions would miss internal role-filler assignments that the model itself represents in the residual stream.

title: Isolating Perception for Multi-View Planning under Occlusion-Induced Partial Observability
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are beginning to saturate visual planning benchmarks, yet they fail to resolve depth ambiguity and degrade sharply with problem size under occlusion-induced partial observability (PO). We introduce BW-PO based on the Blocksworld domain, a controlled benchmark that reduces existing VLM planners and formalizers to near-zero performance, and propose VLM-as-perceiver, a paradigm that narrows the VLM's role to local perception while delegating cross-view evidence reconciliation and plan generation to external solvers. Across model-specific challenging subsets of BW-PO, this raises plan success from 1% to 97% for Gemma-4-31B, 0% to 95% for Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 3% to 84% for Gemini-3.1-Pro. Isolating perception in this way separates two bottlenecks that are otherwise entangled: reconciliation under depth ambiguity, and completeness of visual extraction under scene density.

AI.tldr: VLM-as-perceiver narrows vision-language models to local visual extraction while delegating cross-view reconciliation and planning to external solvers, boosting plan success on the new occlusion-heavy BW-PO benchmark from 0-3% to 84-97%.
AI.motivation: Existing VLMs fail to resolve depth ambiguity and degrade sharply with problem size under occlusion-induced partial observability in multi-view visual planning.
AI.method: The authors introduce BW-PO, a Blocksworld-based partial-observability benchmark, and propose VLM-as-perceiver, which restricts the VLM to per-view local perception and delegates cross-view evidence reconciliation and plan generation to external solvers.
AI.result: Across challenging BW-PO subsets, VLM-as-perceiver raises plan success from 1% to 97% for Gemma-4-31B, 0% to 95% for Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 3% to 84% for Gemini-3.1-Pro.
AI.conclusion: Isolating local perception from cross-view reconciliation and planning resolves depth-ambiguity bottlenecks and exposes visual extraction completeness as a separate challenge.

title: Omni-Workspace: Benchmarking Omni-Modal AI Assistants on Multimodal Workspace Tasks
summary: Omni-modal agents are expected to move beyond multimodal understanding toward completing complex tasks in realistic multimodal environments. In these settings, information is distributed across heterogeneous files and modalities, with cross-file and cross-modal dependencies requiring agents to continually coordinate perception, reasoning, and tool use as newly gathered evidence informs subsequent actions. However, existing omni-modal benchmarks primarily focus on multimodal perception and understanding, leaving complex task completion through sustained interaction with multimodal workspaces underexplored. We introduce Omni-Workspace, a benchmark comprising 380 deep-research-style tasks across four multimodal workspace types and two difficulty levels. These tasks require agents to inspect and process workspace files, retrieve external information when needed, integrate evidence across files and modalities, and produce artifacts satisfying explicit requirements. Evaluating 18 representative models reveals limitations in long-horizon multimodal workspace execution, with the best model scoring only 65.93 on average. Further analysis identifies multimodal context inflation and task-state drift as recurring challenges. Motivated by these findings, we further propose OmniFocus, a lightweight approach combining multimodal working-memory management with explicit task-state tracking to improve performance and efficiency. Omni-Workspace advances the evaluation and development of omni-modal agents toward autonomous completion of complex tasks in multimodal workspaces.

AI.tldr: Omni-Workspace benchmarks omni-modal agents on 380 long-horizon, cross-file multimodal workspace tasks, showing the best of 18 models scores only 65.93 and motivating OmniFocus for working-memory and task-state management.
AI.motivation: Existing omni-modal benchmarks focus on perception and understanding rather than sustained interaction across heterogeneous workspace files with cross-file and cross-modal dependencies.
AI.method: The authors introduce Omni-Workspace (380 deep-research-style tasks across four workspace types and two difficulty levels) and propose OmniFocus, a lightweight approach combining multimodal working-memory management with explicit task-state tracking.
AI.result: Evaluating 18 representative models reveals a top average score of 65.93, with multimodal context inflation and task-state drift identified as recurring failure modes.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon multimodal workspace execution remains challenging for current omni-modal agents and benefits from explicit working-memory and task-state management.

title: Speaking-Clock Mamba: Phoneme-Conditioned State-Space Modeling for Visual Forced Alignment
summary: Visual forced alignment (VFA) locates phoneme and word boundaries in a silent talking-face video given its transcript. Existing methods mainly enforce transcript order at the decoding stage, leaving the encoder without an explicit mechanism to anchor its temporally evolving representation to transcript progress. As a result, phoneme-specific evidence is blurred and alignment drift accumulates over long sequences. In this paper, we propose Speaking-Clock Mamba, which makes transcript progress part of the temporal recurrence. A selective state-space (Mamba) backbone is inserted between the visual frontend and the Conformer cross-attention encoder, and a Phoneme-Conditioned Selective Scan (PCSS) conditions its input-dependent step size on a supervised, structurally monotone speaking clock that estimates progress through the transcript. Since causal and bidirectional variants of this backbone make complementary errors, a training-free selector picks the more confident alignment per utterance. Experiments on LRS2 and LRS3 show consistent gains over protocol-matched baselines, and the supervised clock provides an explicit estimate of alignment progress.

AI.tldr: Speaking-Clock Mamba inserts a phoneme-conditioned selective state-space backbone into visual forced alignment to track transcript progress in the encoder, improving alignment over baselines on LRS2 and LRS3.
AI.motivation: Existing visual forced alignment methods enforce transcript order mainly during decoding, leaving the encoder without an explicit mechanism to anchor temporal representations to transcript progress, which causes alignment drift over long sequences.
AI.method: The authors insert a Mamba backbone between the visual frontend and Conformer cross-attention encoder, using Phoneme-Conditioned Selective Scan (PCSS) to condition step sizes on a supervised monotone speaking clock, plus a training-free selector between causal and bidirectional variants.
AI.result: Experiments on LRS2 and LRS3 show consistent gains over protocol-matched baselines, while the supervised clock provides an explicit estimate of alignment progress.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning state-space recurrence on estimated transcript progress reduces alignment drift in visual forced alignment.

title: UMM-JEPA: Generative Pretraining via Masked Next-Scale Representation Prediction for Unified Multimodal Models
summary: Unified multimodal models can support both visual understanding and generation, yet generative training does not necessarily improve understanding. We argue that this limitation may arise from a mismatch between the representation targeted by generation and the perceptual representation used for understanding. Conventional generation objectives primarily optimize synthesis-oriented spaces such as discrete visual codes or generative latents. We therefore introduce UMM-JEPA, which reformulates generation as progressive prediction of continuous visual-understanding representations. The model constructs a multi-scale representation hierarchy from coarse to fine, while pixel rendering is decoupled from representation pretraining and attached only afterward. Controlled comparisons show that the representation-prediction objective accounts for most of the understanding improvement, while a data-matched control leaves the group means nearly unchanged. UMM-JEPA reaches a 16-benchmark visual mean of 51.71, against 46.36 for the understanding-only Qwen-VL baseline, and the text mean also rises. Compared with discrete-code and latent-flow generation objectives, perceptual representation prediction yields stronger and more consistent transfer to understanding. Linear probes and visual-evidence interventions further reveal richer object and spatial structure and stronger use of image-specific information. These results suggest that generation can benefit understanding when it directly supervises the perceptual representations that understanding consumes.

AI.tldr: UMM-JEPA reformulates generative pretraining for unified multimodal models as multi-scale prediction of continuous visual-understanding representations with decoupled pixel rendering, raising 16-benchmark visual mean from 46.36 to 51.71.
AI.motivation: Generative training in unified multimodal models often fails to improve visual understanding because conventional objectives target synthesis-oriented discrete codes or generative latents rather than perceptual representations.
AI.method: UMM-JEPA builds a coarse-to-fine multi-scale representation hierarchy and predicts continuous visual-understanding representations directly, decoupling pixel rendering to attach only afterward.
AI.result: UMM-JEPA achieves a 16-benchmark visual mean of 51.71 vs. 46.36 for the understanding-only Qwen-VL baseline, while also improving text performance and outperforming discrete-code and latent-flow objectives in controlled comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Supervising generative pretraining directly in the perceptual representation space enables generation to transfer effectively to visual understanding.

title: LogicEye: Agent Driven Multimodal Dataset for Interpretable Ophthalmic Diagnosis
summary: Clinical adoption of ophthalmic Artificial Intelligence remains limited by low interpretability and a lack of finely annotated multimodal data. Most existing datasets provide only coarse disease labels without the granular pathological findings required for differential diagnosis. We present LogicEye$^{Agent}$, a dual-pool inference and verification agent that emulates clinical reasoning by jointly verifying positive inclusion signs and negative exclusion criteria. Using LogicEye$^{Agent}$, we curate LogicEye$^{Data}$, a large-scale multimodal dataset of 804,461 fundus and OCT images paired with structured pathological reports spanning 38 diseases and 29 subtypes, with quality assured through joint verification by multimodal large language models and clinical experts. Building on this dataset, we further develop LogicEye$^{Bench}$, which incorporates a category-constrained loss for hierarchical disease recognition and report generation. Grounding coarse labels into verified visual findings effectively curtails diagnostic hallucinations and establishes a solid foundation for interpretable vision-language modeling in ophthalmology. The code is available at:this https URL.

AI.tldr: LogicEye introduces an agentic verification pipeline (LogicEye^Agent), a 804,461-image multimodal ophthalmic dataset (LogicEye^Data), and a hierarchical benchmark (LogicEye^Bench) to ground ophthalmic diagnosis in verified pathological findings.
AI.motivation: Clinical adoption of ophthalmic AI is hindered by low interpretability and a lack of large-scale datasets pairing images with granular pathological findings rather than coarse disease labels.
AI.method: LogicEye^Agent emulates clinical reasoning by jointly verifying positive inclusion signs and negative exclusion criteria to curate LogicEye^Data (804,461 fundus and OCT images across 38 diseases and 29 subtypes), alongside LogicEye^Bench with a category-constrained loss.
AI.result: Grounding coarse labels into verified visual findings curtails diagnostic hallucinations and supports hierarchical disease recognition and report generation.
AI.conclusion: Agent-curated, finding-grounded multimodal data provides a foundation for interpretable vision-language modeling in ophthalmology.

title: Evidence-Calibrated Selective Decoding for Reliable Visual Question Answering
summary: Visual question answering systems can produce confident responses that are weakly supported by their input images. Contrastive decoding can reduce this dependence on language priors, but a fixed correction may also overturn a correct answer, while selective answering can conceal errors by reducing coverage. We develop evidence-calibrated selective decoding, a framework that separates three decisions: whether local visual evidence supports a candidate, how strongly to correct the original distribution, and whether the resulting answer should be released under a verification budget. Evidence Verification across Crops (EVC) measures visual support and disagreement; Adaptive Contrast Correction (ACC) applies a bounded modification within the backbone's plausible candidate set; Budgeted Selective Answering (BSA) calibrates an answer-admission threshold on held-out images. We provide a complete mathematical specification, bounded-perturbation analysis, and an evaluation protocol that distinguishes forced answering from selective risk. Our quantitative analysis re-examines published baselines on POPE instantiated over MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA, together with four MME subtasks. These public measurements reveal variation across backbones, tasks, and correction settings that motivates adaptive control. The proposed framework has not yet undergone model-level evaluation; its effectiveness remains a falsifiable hypothesis rather than an established empirical result.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a mathematical specification and analysis of evidence-calibrated selective decoding for VQA, separating visual evidence verification, adaptive contrast correction, and budgeted selective answering, though model-level evaluation remains future work.
AI.motivation: Fixed contrastive decoding can overturn correct VQA answers and selective answering can hide errors by reducing coverage, requiring a principled way to calibrate both.
AI.method: The framework combines Evidence Verification across Crops (EVC), Adaptive Contrast Correction (ACC) within plausible candidates, and Budgeted Selective Answering (BSA) on held-out images, alongside a bounded-perturbation analysis and an evaluation protocol separating forced answering from selective risk.
AI.result: Re-examining published baselines on POPE (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and four MME subtasks shows substantial variation across backbones, tasks, and correction settings; the framework itself has not yet undergone model-level evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Variation across backbones and tasks motivates adaptive, evidence-calibrated control, leaving empirical validation of the proposed framework as a falsifiable hypothesis.

title: Thinking from Another Side of the Box: Spacetime Images for Computer Vision
summary: Computer vision methods for video understanding, such as object detection and tracking, inherit the way videos are captured and displayed: as successive frames processed sequentially. However, a video is an inhomogeneous 2D+time volume of pixels, named voxels, and frames are only one family of cuts through it. In this frame-based representation, static backgrounds introduce computational redundancy, and motion can only be understood across several frames. In this position paper, we study another family of cuts: spacetime images (STIs), obtained by sampling any set of pixels other than frames, for instance a line of pixels followed over time. Such images are familiar in narrow forms, from line-scan inspection and kymographs to spatiotemporal slices for motion analysis, but have received little attention as a general input representation for computer vision and are often limited to (x,t) or (y,t) cuts. We define new cuts leading to STIs in their general form, explain how to read their content, and show that a family of cuts tiles the video so that existing dense annotations transfer at no cost. We also detail how motion appears in an STI, spatially and in the frequency domain, and discuss applications such as walking pedestrians, deposited objects, and dynamic scenes. Two pilot experiments illustrate the representation. The first trains a segmentation network entirely in the spacetime domain, on transferred annotations, and performs background subtraction on CDnet 2014 close to supervised frame-based methods, without explicit temporal modeling. The second recovers the pan speed of a camera as a moving cut, identified by a simple criterion on the frequency spectrum of the resulting image, turning a temporal estimation problem into the choice of a cut. Our position is not that STIs should replace frames, but that slicing the video volume is a design variable worth studying in its own right.

AI.tldr: This position paper advocates spacetime images (STIs)—general pixel cuts through a 2D+time video volume—as a complementary representation to frames, demonstrating zero-cost annotation transfer and competitive background subtraction and pan-speed estimation.
AI.motivation: Standard frame-by-frame video processing incurs static-background redundancy and requires multi-frame modeling for motion, whereas general cuts through the video volume remain underexplored.
AI.method: The authors formalize general spacetime image cuts, show how families of cuts tile the video for free dense-annotation transfer, and run two pilot experiments: spacetime-domain segmentation on CDnet 2014 and frequency-based camera pan-speed recovery.
AI.result: A segmentation network trained purely on STIs achieves background subtraction on CDnet 2014 close to supervised frame-based methods without explicit temporal modeling, and pan speed is recovered via a simple frequency-spectrum criterion.
AI.conclusion: Slicing the video volume into spacetime images is a useful design variable that complements frame-based representations for motion and efficiency.

title: Exists, Valid: Calibrated Validity of Stored 3D Geometry Across Long Observation Gaps
summary: Repeated airborne LiDAR surveys are costly, while stored 3D geometry can become outdated between observations. Existing change-detection methods compare observed epochs. However, they do not quantify the validity of geometry that has not been revisited. We distinguish observation, existence and geometric validity using a probabilistic filter over five geometric transitions: persistence, modification, growth, removal and replacement. The framework learns class-specific continuous-time transition priors from interval-censored observations and combines shape residuals with LiDAR free-space evidence. Functional anchors enable prior sharing across sites with different survey frequencies. In controlled experiments with misspecified dynamics and 60% visibility, our method reduces combined error from 36.9% to 16.5% and expected calibration error (ECE) from 0.19-0.32 to 0.017. Cross-site sharing reduces ECE at two-survey sites from 0.156 to 0.029. On Urb3DCD-v2, the method achieves 9.8% combined error and 0.016 ECE, outperforming baselines at 12.6% and at least 0.070, respectively. Re-survey prioritisation improves only modestly over random selection with two observations. Code and an evaluation protocol are released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: A continuous-time probabilistic filter over five geometric transitions quantifies the validity of unvisited 3D geometry between airborne LiDAR surveys, cutting combined error and calibration error substantially on controlled and Urb3DCD-v2 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Repeated airborne LiDAR surveys are expensive, and existing change-detection methods only compare observed epochs without quantifying whether unvisited stored 3D geometry remains valid.
AI.method: The framework learns class-specific continuous-time transition priors (persistence, modification, growth, removal, replacement) from interval-censored observations, combines shape residuals with LiDAR free-space evidence, and uses functional anchors for cross-site prior sharing.
