It therefore reports objects that only one capture shows and misses most removed and moved objects. We propose STILL, which reformulates change detection as object verification at a registered place. 3D geometry registers the place of each change hypothesis in the other capture, and one VLM answers, from a scene view and a local place view, whether the object is still at that place, trained with supervision of the same form. Under the official SceneDiff protocol, STILL raises the main metric obj/sc AP from 24.0 to 37.8, and from 11.6 to 20.6 on the egocentric kitchen subset without any kitchen training data. It improves F1 by more than 21 points over a VLM fine-tuned on the same annotations and adds only about 11% to the runtime.

AI.tldr: STILL reformulates scene-change detection as place-registered object verification using 3D geometry and a VLM, raising SceneDiff obj/sc AP from 24.0 to 37.8.
AI.motivation: Multi-image VLMs fail at detecting added, removed, or moved objects across robot visits because they cannot locate where an object was in the other capture under differing viewpoints and lighting.
AI.method: STILL uses 3D geometry to register the place of each change hypothesis in the other capture, and queries a VLM (trained with matching supervision) on a scene view and a local place view to verify whether the object is still there.
AI.result: Under the SceneDiff protocol, STILL improves obj/sc AP from 24.0 to 37.8 overall and from 11.6 to 20.6 on the egocentric kitchen subset without kitchen training data, while boosting F1 by over 21 points over a fine-tuned VLM with ~11% runtime overhead.
AI.conclusion: Grounding VLM queries via 3D place registration makes cross-visit scene-change detection substantially more reliable for embodied agents.

title: AITHER: Authority-Informed Evidence Routing for Mixed-Authority Vision-Language Reasoning
summary: Reliable vision-language reasoning requires a control decision that conventional grounding methods leave implicit: which input is entitled to determine the answer? Auxiliary text may be a defeasible claim about an image, a binding task instruction, or compatible context. Correcting every image-text conflict toward the image therefore repairs false claims but overwrites valid task rules. We formalize this setting as mixed-authority vision-language reasoning and introduce AITHER, an Authority-Informed Text-Image Hierarchy for Evidence Routing. Its final policy, the Semantic-Frame Router, is a training-free black-box control layer that (i) compiles explicit task directives, (ii) recovers standardized spatial frames from metadata-scrubbed pixels, (iii) resolves the semantic polarity of remaining notes, and (iv) routes among frozen observable candidates with fail-closed semantics. This ordered decomposition converts authority arbitration from an unconstrained prompt preference into a reproducible inference program. Across 1,620 MATRIX predictions, AITHER reaches 95.1% accuracy, exceeding the strongest task-and-frame baseline by 9.1 points with a 95% record-cluster interval of 6.8-11.5 points and no harmed records. It further reaches 100.0% on 1,800 controlled FRAME predictions and 93.3% on GQA-MATRIX. The results show that explicit authority routing can simultaneously improve false-claim correction, preserve task-defined answers, and eliminate clean-context overcorrection.

AI.tldr: AITHER is a training-free black-box control layer for mixed-authority vision-language reasoning that arbitrates between task instructions and image evidence, reaching 95.1% accuracy on MATRIX and 100.0% on FRAME.
AI.motivation: Conventional vision-language grounding resolves all image-text conflicts in favor of the image, which repairs false claims but erroneously overwrites binding task rules.
AI.method: AITHER's Semantic-Frame Router compiles explicit task directives, recovers standardized spatial frames from metadata-scrubbed pixels, resolves semantic polarity of remaining notes, and routes among frozen observable candidates with fail-closed semantics.
AI.result: Across 1,620 MATRIX predictions, AITHER achieves 95.1% accuracy (+9.1 points over the strongest baseline, 95% CI 6.8-11.5, zero harmed records), 100.0% on 1,800 FRAME predictions, and 93.3% on GQA-MATRIX.
AI.conclusion: Explicit authority-informed routing simultaneously improves false-claim correction, preserves task-defined answers, and prevents clean-context overcorrection.

title: TyphoonWorld: A Residual Token World Model for Probabilistic Forecasting of Typhoon Imagery
summary: A satellite forecast of a typhoon should give a low-error picture of the next two days, together with an ensemble whose members are coherent fields and whose spread responds to the storm at hand. A small direct regression network already gives the lowest squared error on held-out storms, so a generative model has to earn its cost through the part of the future that the regression smooths away. We present TyphoonWorld, a discrete-token world model that generates only that part. Conditioned on tokens of the regression forecast, the latest frames and the best-track state at forecast time, it samples residual fields lead by lead, and members add these residuals to the regression center. We compare it under one protocol with per-pixel Gaussian networks, a diffusion model of the same residuals, residuals from other storms and an unconditional token world model, on 276 forecast windows from 46 held-out storms of Digital Typhoon. TyphoonWorld matches the squared error of the regression, lowers the CRPS of the area colder than 220 K, a direct measure of deep convection, by 14 to 39% against every other ensemble, and ties its spread to forecast error as closely as the Gaussian network, with a correlation of 0.78 across windows. It uses 56% of the parameters of the unconditional world model.

AI.tldr: TyphoonWorld is a discrete-token world model that generates residual fields on top of a direct regression forecast, matching regression MSE while cutting deep-convection CRPS by 14-39% on Digital Typhoon.
AI.motivation: Direct regression networks already minimize squared error for two-day satellite typhoon forecasts, so generative world models must add value by capturing coherent ensemble spread in the details regression smooths away.
AI.method: Conditioned on tokens of the regression forecast, recent frames, and best-track state, TyphoonWorld samples discrete-token residual fields lead by lead and adds them to the regression center.
AI.result: Across 276 forecast windows from 46 held-out Digital Typhoon storms, TyphoonWorld matches regression MSE, lowers CRPS for areas colder than 220 K by 14-39% against all other ensembles, achieves 0.78 spread-error correlation, and uses 56% of the parameters of an unconditional token world model.
AI.conclusion: Modeling only the residuals around a regression center yields calibrated, parameter-efficient probabilistic typhoon forecasts.

title: Target-Free Autocalibration of Stereo PIV Camera Systems via Persistent-State Motion Representations
summary: Stereo Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) recovers three-component velocity fields by triangulating tracer particles observed by synchronized cameras. It requires an accurate extrinsic calibration, which is still obtained by inserting a physical target into the flow and must be repeated whenever the rig is moved. We present a target-free method that calibrates a stereo PIV rig directly from particle image sequences. Because tracer particles are visually indistinguishable, we match motion rather than appearance: building on CUT3R, each camera stream is processed by a recurrent transformer whose persistent state accumulates particle motion over time. The state is decoded into per-camera optical flow and queried by a cross-view decoder that regresses bidirectional point correspondences, from which the relative pose is recovered with a five-point RANSAC solver. We train on a new synthetic stereo PIV dataset with ground-truth poses and evaluate on standard PIV optical flow benchmarks and on 200 real rig placements. Our model achieves lower flow error than existing PIV networks, more accurate cross-view correspondences than COTR, and higher pose accuracy than the strongest detector-matcher pipelines on both synthetic and real data, without any calibration target.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a target-free extrinsic autocalibration method for stereo PIV cameras using recurrent persistent-state motion representations, outperforming existing flow and pose baselines on synthetic and 200 real rig placements.
AI.motivation: Stereo Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) requires frequent extrinsic calibration with a physical target whenever the camera rig moves, and standard appearance matching fails because tracer particles are visually indistinguishable.
AI.method: Building on CUT3R, each camera stream is processed by a recurrent transformer whose persistent state accumulates particle motion over time; the state is decoded into per-camera optical flow and queried by a cross-view decoder to regress bidirectional correspondences for a five-point RANSAC pose solver.
AI.result: Trained on a new synthetic stereo PIV dataset, the method achieves lower flow error than existing PIV networks, better cross-view correspondences than COTR, and higher pose accuracy than detector-matcher pipelines on both synthetic benchmarks and 200 real rig placements.
AI.conclusion: Matching accumulated particle motion rather than appearance enables accurate, target-free stereo PIV autocalibration.

title: Recognizing Events Is Not Enough: Why Streaming VLMs Struggle in Compositional Instruction Triggering
summary: Recognizing individual events does not guarantee correct execution of compositional instructions in streaming video. For example, given the request "Notify me when the pot boils after someone turns on the stove and leaves the kitchen", existing models may recognize the individual events yet notify too early or miss the intended moment, failing to track how their temporal conditions are satisfied over time. To evaluate this gap, we introduce CoTriggerBench, which composes annotated video events into temporally constrained instructions and verifies notification timing and silence through executable event plans and source-event replay. To address this challenge, we propose a real-time VLM agent, TEMPI. TEMPI decomposes instructions into atomic event queries and temporal constraints, and uses Scenario Memory to continuously maintain task progress as event evidence arrives, allowing earlier observations to support subsequent decisions beyond the detector's visual window. Even when no notification is required, relevant events continue to update the scenario state. On CoTriggerBench, TEMPI achieves 44.4% instruction-level success, outperforming the strongest closed-source and fine-tuned open-source VLM baselines by 15.6 (Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash-Realtime) and 18.1 (MOSS-VL-Realtime) percentage points, respectively. To support efficient on-device streaming inference, we further optimize the streaming inference pipeline by overlapping partial visual encoding and LLM prefix prefill with frame arrival. On an 8 GB RTX 5060, our optimized detector implementation achieves a 4.90$\times$ speedup.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce CoTriggerBench for temporally constrained streaming video instructions and propose TEMPI, a real-time VLM agent with Scenario Memory that reaches 44.4% instruction-level success and 4.90x detector speedup.
AI.motivation: Recognizing individual events in streaming video is insufficient for compositional instructions with temporal constraints, as existing VLMs trigger too early or miss events outside their visual window.
AI.method: TEMPI decomposes instructions into atomic event queries and temporal constraints, maintains task progress in Scenario Memory across arriving events, and overlaps partial visual encoding with LLM prefix prefill during frame arrival.
AI.result: On CoTriggerBench, TEMPI achieves 44.4% instruction-level success, outperforming Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash-Realtime by 15.6 points and MOSS-VL-Realtime by 18.1 points, while the optimized detector runs 4.90x faster on an 8 GB RTX 5060.
AI.conclusion: Explicit temporal decomposition, persistent scenario state, and overlapped encoding-prefill execution are key to reliable real-time compositional instruction triggering.

title: Neural Latent Gaussian Process for 3D reconstruction of Mouse Brain Lipids
summary: We address the problem of reconstructing continuous three-dimensional lipid profiles of the mouse brain from lipid measurements acquired only on a sparse set of two-dimensional tissue sections. Using MALDI-MSI measurements from coronal sections of two densely sampled and six sparsely sampled mouse brains, registered to the Allen Mouse Brain Common Coordinate Framework (CCF), we seek to interpolate the measured hundreds of lipid profiles across the unobserved voxels of the reference brain. We introduce a Neural Latent-Space Gaussian Process (LGP) architecture for this task and critically evaluate its ability to reconstruct spatial lipid distributions, using held-out mouse brain sections to assess generalization. We propose a Gaussian Process prior for the distribution of low-dimensional lipid profiles across the mouse brain (with Matérn or a Riemann manifold kernel). This allows us to encode 3D coordinates in a small number of latent 3D volumes that are then mapped to particular lipids using a multilayer perceptron (MLP). We performed an exhaustive analysis over a range of algorithms from simple linear regression, XGBoost, MLP to state of the art models such as Neural Transcriptomic Field, graph-based SPA3D for spatial omics reconstruction and DEEPSPATIAL. We additionally evaluate GPLFR as an alternative Gaussian-process-based approach. Across 173 measured lipids, LGP outperforms all evaluated baselines, including recent spatial-omics models and GPLFR, achieving a mean correlation of 0.613 and demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach for sparse 3D lipid interpolation.

AI.tldr: Neural Latent Gaussian Process (LGP) reconstructs continuous 3D mouse brain lipid distributions from sparse 2D MALDI-MSI sections, outperforming spatial-omics and regression baselines with a 0.613 mean correlation across 173 lipids.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing continuous 3D brain lipid profiles from sparse 2D tissue sections registered to the Allen Mouse Brain CCF requires interpolating hundreds of lipid species across unobserved voxels.
AI.method: LGP places a Gaussian Process prior (with Matérn or Riemann manifold kernel) over low-dimensional latent 3D volumes encoding 3D coordinates, and maps these latent volumes to individual lipids via an MLP.
AI.result: Evaluated on held-out sections from two densely sampled and six sparsely sampled mouse brains across 173 lipids, LGP outperforms linear regression, XGBoost, MLP, Neural Transcriptomic Field, SPA3D, DEEPSPATIAL, and GPLFR, achieving a mean correlation of 0.613.
AI.conclusion: Combining a spatial Gaussian Process prior in latent space with an MLP decoder provides accurate 3D interpolation of sparse spatial lipidomics data.

title: VTG-RAG: Long-Video Reasoning via Query-Adaptive Coarse-to-Fine Sampling and Temporal Graph Retrieval
summary: Long-video reasoning requires a system to localize sparse evidence over extended temporal sequences, preserve temporal structure, and generate answers despite substantial multimodal distractors. Existing video retrieval-augmented generation methods typically build indexes from uniformly sampled video segments. In long-video settings, this design readily introduces irrelevant context and is unreliable for questions with explicit temporal constraints. We propose VTG-RAG, a framework for long-video question answering that combines query-adaptive coarse-to-fine sampling with temporal graph retrieval. First, a two-stage sampling strategy selects core segments with high mean query relevance or high intra-segment relevance variance. The framework then integrates subtitles, speech transcripts, visual descriptions, entities, and relations from these segments into a temporally ordered multimodal graph. Finally, it performs temporally filtered, two-pass retrieval and reasoning across frame, text, and graph evidence spaces. A lot of experiments have proven the effectiveness of the VTG-RAG. Specifically, we evaluate the framework on Video-MME and LongVideoBench. On LongVideoBench, the reported Qwen2.5-VL-32B and 72B results improve from 48.16% to 50.56% and from 52.13% to 53.32%, respectively, with 24 answer-input frames. These correspond to gains of 2.40 and 1.19 percentage points. The ablation experiments of VTG-RAG further support that the contributions of each component are very important.

AI.tldr: VTG-RAG combines query-adaptive coarse-to-fine sampling with a temporally ordered multimodal graph for long-video QA, improving Qwen2.5-VL-32B and 72B on LongVideoBench by 2.40 and 1.19 points.
AI.motivation: Uniformly sampled video RAG indexes introduce irrelevant distractors in long videos and fail on questions with explicit temporal constraints.
AI.method: VTG-RAG selects core segments with high mean query relevance or high intra-segment variance, builds a temporally ordered multimodal graph from subtitles, transcripts, visual descriptions, entities, and relations, and runs temporally filtered two-pass retrieval and reasoning.
AI.result: On LongVideoBench with 24 input frames, VTG-RAG improves Qwen2.5-VL-32B from 48.16% to 50.56% (+2.40) and 72B from 52.13% to 53.32% (+1.19), with ablations on Video-MME and LongVideoBench confirming each component's contribution.
AI.conclusion: Query-adaptive sampling paired with temporally structured multimodal graph retrieval strengthens long-video reasoning under temporal constraints.

title: Feature-Space Latent Forecasting for Endoscopic Surgical Video Understanding
summary: Surgical workflow assistance is inherently anticipatory: systems must reason about how procedures evolve, not just recognize the current frame. However, many prior approaches perform prediction in pixel space by synthesizing future frames, which primarily focuses on appearance fidelity rather than the semantic representations required for downstream reasoning. To address this limitation, we propose a feature-space semantic forecasting framework that models temporal dynamics directly within the representations of a frozen Vision Foundation Model (VFM). Specifically, we build a hierarchical target representation from multi-layer VFM features, replace future-frame feature tokens with learnable \texttt{[MASK]} tokens, and train a masked transformer to forecast the corresponding future latent features from observed context, thereby formulating procedural evolution as masked future feature prediction. Experiments on public laparoscopic benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in phase anticipation, multi-label tool presence prediction, and remaining-time estimation over RGB-based forecasting baselines, while enabling a plug-and-play representation interface for lightweight downstream heads.

AI.tldr: This work formulates surgical workflow anticipation as masked future feature prediction in the latent space of a frozen Vision Foundation Model, outperforming RGB-based forecasting baselines.
AI.motivation: Prior surgical anticipation methods predict future RGB frames in pixel space, prioritizing appearance fidelity over the semantic representations needed for downstream workflow reasoning.
AI.method: The framework constructs a hierarchical target from multi-layer features of a frozen VFM, replaces future-frame tokens with learnable [MASK] tokens, and trains a masked transformer to forecast future latent features from observed context.
AI.result: On public laparoscopic benchmarks, the approach consistently outperforms RGB-based forecasting baselines on phase anticipation, multi-label tool presence prediction, and remaining-time estimation.
AI.conclusion: Forecasting directly in frozen VFM feature space provides a more effective, plug-and-play representation for anticipatory surgical video understanding.

title: From Hosted Service to Field-Owned Infrastructure: Open, Self-Hosted Real-Time Camera-Trap Alerting with Regional Open-Weight Models
summary: Cellular camera traps can alert field teams within minutes, supporting anti-poaching, threatened-species protection and human-wildlife conflict mitigation. Most systems use central servers, sending images of people and sensitive species locations outside the collecting organisation and often across national borders. We ask whether this capability can run on infrastructure owned by field organisations. Trap Tracker RT is an open-source, self-hosted application that receives images by email or locally via FTP/SFTP, classifies them with a project-specific model and sends alerts through a mail server chosen by the organisation. We evaluated DeepFaune-SSA v1.2, pairing MegaDetector v6 with a DINOv3-based classifier for 33 sub-Saharan taxa, against three open alternatives on 31,131 out-of-distribution images from Kenya, Namibia and Malawi, independent of its training data. DeepFaune-SSA achieved image-level species accuracy of 0.901 (95% CI 0.894-0.908), versus 0.530 for the global SpeciesNet classifier and 0.556 and 0.547 for YOLOv10x and YOLO26x detectors trained on the same regional data. DeepFaune-SSA had the highest recall for all 26 species evaluated. The single-stage detectors missed animals in about a quarter of images; SpeciesNet assigned species labels in only 57%, usually falling back to coarser labels otherwise. In bench tests of the fully local path, alerts were issued about 6 s after upload completion, including with slowed and interrupted uploads. The two-stage pipeline processed 19 images per minute on eight CPU threads without a graphics processor. Trap Tracker RT is used by five organisations in the United Kingdom and Kenya, including for human-elephant conflict mitigation. We discuss how data paths, rather than inference location, determine data sovereignty, the responsibilities of self-hosting and the ethics of real-time monitoring.

AI.tldr: Trap Tracker RT is an open-source, self-hosted camera-trap alerting system that pairs MegaDetector v6 with DeepFaune-SSA v1.2, achieving 0.901 species accuracy on 31,131 out-of-distribution images and ~6 s local alerts.
AI.motivation: Central cloud camera-trap alerting services send sensitive wildlife and human imagery across borders, creating data-sovereignty, privacy, and compliance risks for field organizations.
AI.method: Trap Tracker RT receives images via email or FTP/SFTP on field-owned infrastructure, runs a two-stage pipeline (MegaDetector v6 + DINOv3-based DeepFaune-SSA v1.2 for 33 sub-Saharan taxa), and dispatches alerts through the organization's mail server.
AI.result: On 31,131 out-of-distribution images from Kenya, Namibia, and Malawi, DeepFaune-SSA reaches 0.901 species accuracy (95% CI 0.894-0.908) versus 0.530 for SpeciesNet, 0.556 for YOLOv10x, and 0.547 for YOLO26x; locally it processes 19 images/min on 8 CPU threads and issues alerts in ~6 s.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight regional models running on self-hosted infrastructure can deliver high-accuracy, real-time wildlife alerting while preserving local data sovereignty.

title: Conv-Reluplex: A Verification Framework For Convolution Neural Networks
comment: 6 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables. Published in SEKE 2021
summary: In recent years, machine learning has demonstrated impressive performance in many real-world tasks, especially in computer vision and natural language processing. However, to apply them in safety-critical systems one needs formal guarantees on the neural network outputs. The Reluplex tool is proposed to verify the safety of deep neural networks (DNNs), and in case the DNN fails to give a correct output, can generate adversarial examples. Since the tool can only handle DNNs, it is necessary to extend the tool to process image data. Therefore, in this paper, we propose the Conv-Reluplex framework, which is designed to verify the convolutional layer and pooling layer in convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and generate adversarial examples when classification is misguided. We conduct several experiments on MNIST to evaluate our approaches. The results show that the original CNN is improved using the adversarial examples generated by our tool, and the precision of classification can be increased significantly.

AI.tldr: Conv-Reluplex extends the Reluplex DNN verification tool to handle convolutional and pooling layers in CNNs, enabling formal safety verification and adversarial example generation on MNIST.
AI.motivation: Reluplex provides formal verification and counterexample generation for fully connected DNNs, but cannot directly process image data through convolutional and pooling layers.
AI.method: The authors propose Conv-Reluplex, extending Reluplex to model convolutional and pooling layers for verifying CNNs and generating adversarial examples when classifications fail.
AI.result: Experiments on MNIST show that retraining or augmenting the original CNN with adversarial examples generated by Conv-Reluplex significantly improves classification precision.
AI.conclusion: Extending Reluplex to convolutional and pooling operations enables formal verification and adversarial robustness improvement for CNNs.

title: Frame First, Decode Once: Object-Centric Coordinates and Single-Pass Decoding for System-1 World Models
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Code, frozen configurations and per-seed results will be released
summary: Single-pass primitive decoders such as LocateAnything and VFlash predict all quantized coordinate tokens of a geometric primitive in one forward pass, enabling fast, System-1 visual planning. We study what matters when such a decoder serves as a System-1 world model: a fast action-conditioned predictor that ranks candidate pushes by their predicted outcome. On ManiSkill3 PushT-v1 (512 held-out test families, 8,192 rollouts) and on human demonstrations from lerobot/pusht (2,384 test windows), we compare decoders, training losses, rigid-body projections and coordinate frames, using matched checkpoints, hierarchical bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm correction. Two factors of similar size dominate. First, expressing inputs and outputs in the SE(2) frame of the object's initial pose lowers decision regret by 1.9-2.2x for each of five decoders, and the object-frame model trained on 128 families matches the world-frame model trained on 512. Second, single-pass decoding outperforms iterative decoding: in the object frame, single-pass heads reach 0.020-0.021 regret at 1.6-1.8 ms per decision, against 0.046 for 10-step DDIM diffusion and 0.059 for KV-cached autoregression at 10.3 and 12.9 ms. The choice among single-pass heads has no measurable effect on regret, and our registered hypothesis that the frame effect exceeds the decoder spread is not supported. Soft-token expectation with an end-to-end 2D Kabsch projection gives the lowest trajectory error (11.35 px on ManiSkill3, 3.78 px on lerobot/pusht), exact rigid-body consistency, and lower regret than diffusion at every budget from 4 to 50 DDIM steps, at 3-29x lower latency.

AI.tldr: Expressing inputs and outputs in the object's initial SE(2) frame and using single-pass primitive decoders cuts System-1 planning regret by ~2x and achieves 0.020-0.021 regret at 1.6-1.8 ms per decision.
AI.motivation: Fast System-1 visual planning requires action-conditioned world models that rank candidate pushes accurately at millisecond latency, but the relative impact of coordinate frames versus iterative vs. single-pass decoding was unclear.
AI.method: On ManiSkill3 PushT-v1 (8,192 rollouts) and lerobot/pusht human demonstrations (2,384 windows), the authors systematically compare decoders, losses, 2D Kabsch rigid-body projections, and world vs. object-centric SE(2) frames.
AI.result: Object-frame coordinates cut regret by 1.9-2.2x across five decoders; single-pass heads reach 0.020-0.021 regret at 1.6-1.8 ms versus 0.046 for 10-step DDIM (10.3 ms) and 0.059 for KV-cached autoregression (12.9 ms), while soft-token expectation with 2D Kabsch projection yields 11.35 px / 3.78 px trajectory error.
AI.conclusion: Object-centric SE(2) framing and single-pass decoding with rigid-body projection dominate System-1 world-model performance, beating diffusion at 3-29x lower latency.

title: AerialOcc: Unified 3D Aerial Perception without Task-Specific Head
summary: Aerial perception systems are increasingly expected to support diverse tasks, yet existing solutions remain fundamentally tied to task-specific outputs. Detection, segmentation, and other perception objectives are usually learned either by separate models or by sharing a backbone with multiple task heads, leaving the model itself unaware of the common structure underlying these tasks. We are interested in asking: can a single perception representation support different levels of understanding without being designed for any specific task? We notice that occupancy is a promising task-agnostic representation for drone perception. By modeling the spatial existence and semantics of the environment, it naturally bridges different perception granularities, from coarse scene understanding to fine-grained object localization. Therefore, we introduce AerialOcc, a unified occupancy-based perception model that enables multiple drone perception tasks from a single inference process, without maintaining task-specific prediction heads. To facilitate this direction, we construct AerialOcc-20K, a large-scale multi-class occupancy dataset for aerial environments. Extensive experiments show that AerialOcc achieves competitive performance across diverse perception tasks while preserving a unified architecture. Our findings demonstrate that occupancy can serve as a universal perception interface, offering a new perspective toward flexible and scalable visual intelligence for autonomous drones from a common 3D scene representation. Models and data are publicly available at this https URL

AI.tldr: AerialOcc is a unified 3D occupancy-based perception model for drones that supports multiple perception tasks in a single inference pass without task-specific heads, trained on the new AerialOcc-20K dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing aerial perception systems rely on separate models or multiple task-specific heads for detection and segmentation, failing to exploit a shared 3D scene representation.
AI.method: The authors adopt 3D semantic occupancy as a universal task-agnostic representation, build AerialOcc to perform multiple drone perception tasks in one pass, and construct AerialOcc-20K, a large-scale multi-class aerial occupancy dataset.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that AerialOcc achieves competitive performance across diverse aerial perception tasks while maintaining a single unified architecture without task-specific heads.
AI.conclusion: 3D occupancy serves as an effective, scalable universal perception interface for autonomous drones.

title: Agri-MRAG: Parameter-Enhanced Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Agricultural Visual Question Answering
summary: Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (MRAG) has shown promise for Agricultural Visual Question Answering (Agri-VQA), but existing methods still face challenges in retrieving relevant knowledge while avoiding redundancy and in integrating retrieved evidence beyond simple prompt concatenation. To address these issues, we propose Agri-MRAG, a multimodal retrieval-augmented framework for agricultural VQA. Specifically, we first introduce a semantic-consistency-guided clustering mechanism that combines multimodal clustering and weighted relevance scoring to select high-confidence knowledge subsets and adaptively determine the retrieval size $k$. We then design a parameterized knowledge injection strategy, where retrieved agricultural knowledge is encoded into LoRA adapters and merged into the feed-forward network (FFN) layers of the MLLM, allowing external knowledge to influence generation through parameter-level adaptation. In addition, a perplexity-guided (PPL-guided) routing mechanism is employed to switch between implicit parametric reasoning and explicit retrieval-assisted generation according to model uncertainty, balancing inference efficiency and answer reliability. For evaluation, we use PlantVillageVQA as a broad agricultural benchmark and construct PlantVQA, a region-specific forestry and fruit crop VQA dataset containing 7,514 images and 15,028 expert-verified question-answer pairs. Experiments show that Agri-MRAG achieves ROUGE-L scores of 41.21 and 46.58 on the two datasets, outperforming mRAG by 11.70 and 4.51 points, and VisRAG by 8.80 and 3.39 points, respectively.

AI.tldr: Agri-MRAG combines semantic-consistency clustering, LoRA-based FFN knowledge injection, and perplexity-guided routing for agricultural VQA, outperforming mRAG and VisRAG on PlantVillageVQA and PlantVQA.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal RAG methods for agricultural VQA suffer from redundant retrieval and rely on simple prompt concatenation that underutilizes retrieved evidence.
AI.method: Agri-MRAG uses multimodal clustering and weighted relevance scoring to adaptively select retrieval size k, encodes retrieved knowledge into LoRA adapters merged into MLLM FFN layers, and routes between parametric and retrieval-assisted reasoning via perplexity.
AI.result: On PlantVillageVQA and the newly constructed PlantVQA (7,514 images, 15,028 expert-verified QA pairs), Agri-MRAG achieves 41.21 and 46.58 ROUGE-L, beating mRAG by 11.70 and 4.51 points and VisRAG by 8.80 and 3.39 points.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-level LoRA knowledge injection and uncertainty-based routing significantly improve retrieval-augmented agricultural VQA.

title: Quantum-inspired orthogonal adapters for certifiably robust medical image classification
summary: Medical image classifiers require not only high accuracy but also reliable predictions under small input perturbations. Certified robustness provides mathematical guarantees of prediction stability, but preserving these guarantees when adapting pretrained models to new tasks remains challenging. We propose a fine-tuning approach based on quantum-inspired orthogonal butterfly layers that preserves the Lipschitz bounds of pretrained certified networks. Inspired by quantum circuits of reconfigurable beam splitters, these layers preserve orthogonality by construction using only $\mathcal{O}(n\log n)$ trainable parameters. Their structured design enables efficient classical implementation and offers a path toward future quantum implementations with logarithmic circuit depth under suitable connectivity assumptions. Controlled experiments on MNIST and MedMNIST demonstrate improved certified robustness compared with conventional alternatives and, in the DermaMNIST transfer, greater resistance to the tested attacks than low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We then apply it to trichoscopic image classification for alopecia diagnosis and alopecia areata activity assessment. By adapting a certified ImageNet-pretrained network, butterfly fine-tuning achieves approximately twice the certified accuracy of conventional fine-tuning and LoRA, with comparable classification accuracy on the same backbone and data split and similar empirical resistance to the tested adversarial attacks. Larger robustness guarantees, including certificates covering certain image-processing transformations, can be obtained at the cost of reduced accuracy. These results highlight the potential of quantum-inspired butterfly layers for parameter-efficient adaptation of medical image classifiers while preserving the mathematical guarantees underlying certified robustness.

AI.tldr: Quantum-inspired orthogonal butterfly adapters preserve Lipschitz bounds of certified pretrained networks using O(n log n) parameters, doubling certified accuracy over conventional fine-tuning and LoRA on alopecia imaging.
AI.motivation: Adapting certified-robust pretrained medical image classifiers to new tasks typically breaks their mathematical Lipschitz guarantees or requires excessive parameters.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune certified networks using quantum-inspired orthogonal butterfly layers (modeled after reconfigurable beam-splitter circuits) that preserve orthogonality by construction with O(n log n) trainable parameters.
AI.result: On MNIST, MedMNIST (including DermaMNIST), and trichoscopic alopecia diagnosis/activity assessment, butterfly fine-tuning achieves ~2x the certified accuracy of conventional fine-tuning and LoRA at comparable clean accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonal butterfly adapters offer a parameter-efficient way to transfer certified robustness guarantees to specialized medical imaging tasks.

title: Third-Place Solution for the UCF UrbanTwin V2X-Real Track at ECCV 2026: Synthetic Point Cloud Generation and Sim-to-Real 3D Object Detection
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. 3rd place, Track 7 (V2X-Real), UCF UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, 6th DriveX Workshop at ECCV 2026
summary: This report presents a complete technical solution for the UrbanTwin V2X-Real Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, covering both synthetic point cloud generation and 3D object detection. For data generation, we adopt per-axis quantile calibration. Public V2X-Real training data are used to construct the real reference distribution, and independent one-dimensional quantile mappings are estimated for the x, y, and z axes of the base synthetic point clouds. The calibrated point clouds are then resampled using a fixed random seed and clipped to the valid spatial range, producing 50 frames with 2,000 float32 XYZ points per frame. For detection, we use a two-stage Voxel R-CNN (VoxelRCNN) detector trained with RangeLDM-enhanced synthetic point-cloud data, point clouds downsampled to 50k points per frame, and reconstructed pedestrian data. Training is performed on four NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPUs with a global batch size of 16 for 40 epochs. Final testing uses direct single-model inference with the original VoxelRCNN model. On the official evaluation server, the normalized Realism score is 0.7905 and the normalized Detection score is 0.5583, with mAP@0.5 of 0.3908, BEV mAP@0.5 of 0.4219, and mAP@0.7 of 0.1047. According to the official weighting rule, the final combined score is 0.6 x 0.5583 + 0.4 x 0.7905 = 0.6512. This report documents the complete implementation details of data construction, model training, inference, submission formatting, and official evaluation.

AI.tldr: This report details the third-place solution for the ECCV 2026 UrbanTwin V2X-Real Track, combining per-axis quantile calibration for synthetic LiDAR generation with a RangeLDM-augmented VoxelRCNN detector to score 0.6512 overall.
AI.motivation: Bridging the sim-to-real gap in V2X-Real LiDAR perception requires generating realistic synthetic point clouds and training 3D object detectors that generalize to real-world evaluation.
AI.method: For generation, independent 1D quantile mappings per x/y/z axis calibrate synthetic point clouds to the V2X-Real reference distribution (50 frames, 2,000 points/frame); for detection, a two-stage VoxelRCNN is trained on RangeLDM-enhanced synthetic data, 50k-point downsampled clouds, and reconstructed pedestrians across 4 RTX 4090s.
AI.result: On the official evaluation server, the solution achieves 0.7905 normalized Realism, 0.5583 normalized Detection (0.3908 mAP@0.5, 0.4219 BEV mAP@0.5, 0.1047 mAP@0.7), and a combined weighted score of 0.6512.
AI.conclusion: Per-axis quantile calibration paired with RangeLDM-augmented VoxelRCNN training provides a competitive sim-to-real V2X LiDAR pipeline.

title: Same Evidence, Different Verdicts: Delivery of CT Images and DICOM Metadata Changes VLM Quality-Control Decisions
comment: 4 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are being proposed as automated checks on clinical imaging inputs, where a scan and its DICOM metadata can disagree; a truncated CT series wrongly admitted to volumetric follow-up, such as lung-nodule growth assessment in screening, biases the measurement. A natural safeguard is to let the model judge the image before it sees the metadata. We find this backfires. On 60 NLST chest CT pairs with coverage defects whose ground truth is computed from scan geometry, a false header that Claude Haiku 5.5 resisted when shown with the image (2% of its detections overruled) overturned 91% of them when it arrived after the model's answer (Nemotron-3.5-VL 43% to 100%). With the order reversed, the image overturned 98-100% of the header's errors (Claude models): whichever source came second won. This is not generic sycophancy: a neutral "please confirm" reversed 0 of 1,072 correct refusals, and the effect persisted when the header arrived as a tool result, as in agentic pipelines. One warning sentence cut sequential reversal to at most 9%, and the pattern held on 24 real mismatched pairs. Contributions: (i) evidence that VLM input-check decisions on identical evidence depend on delivery; (ii) a testbed with exact geometric ground truth; (iii) a validation protocol for clinical VLM input checks. Code, prompts and all call logs: this https URL

AI.tldr: Sequential delivery of CT images and DICOM metadata causes VLMs to overturn 91-100% of prior detections in favor of whichever source arrives second, a bias reduced to <=9% by a single warning sentence.
AI.motivation: Clinical VLM quality-control pipelines often show the image before the DICOM metadata to prevent header bias, but it is unknown whether sequential delivery actually protects judgment.
AI.method: Using 60 NLST chest CT pairs with geometrically verified coverage defects and 24 real mismatched pairs, the authors test simultaneous vs. sequential delivery (including tool-result delivery) across Claude Haiku 5.5 and Nemotron-3.5-VL.
AI.result: While Claude Haiku 5.5 resisted a false header shown with the image (2% overruled), delivering the header afterward overturned 91% of detections (43-100% for Nemotron-3.5-VL), and reversing the order overturned 98-100% of header errors; a neutral confirmation prompt reversed 0/1,072 refusals, and a single warning sentence cut sequential reversal to <=9%.
AI.conclusion: VLM clinical input checks are highly sensitive to evidence delivery order rather than generic sycophancy, requiring simultaneous presentation or explicit conflict warnings.

title: From Retouched Images to Paired Videos: A Synthetic Benchmark for Face Video Retouching
summary: Paired unretouched/retouched face videos are costly to produce because professional editing must remain consistent over time, while releasing identifiable face footage raises privacy, consent, and governance concerns. We present DeepVFR, an initial controlled synthetic benchmark-not a new retouching architecture-for paired face video retouching. Starting from paired synthetic DeepFRR images, Wan2.2 generates mild-motion source clips, and backend-specific face transfer constructs synchronized proxy retouching targets, followed by automatic validity screening and manual visual inspection. DeepVFR contains 1,024 pairs of 150-frame clips at 30 fps, evaluated under an identity-disjoint protocol with explicit frame correspondence; release metadata will record the construction route. Within-benchmark baselines, external checkpoints applied to DeepVFR, qualitative analysis, and a 17-participant ranking study establish reference behavior in the controlled domain. The constructed targets exhibit a substantial low-preference tail in the human study. Because both streams inherit synthetic content and the targets additionally inherit commercial-API or face-transfer artifacts, the benchmark neither replaces artist-retouched captured video nor establishes synthetic-to-real generalization. DeepVFR provides a starting point for paired supervision and controlled evaluation. Data, individual study rankings, and training logs will be made publicly available upon acceptance. Broader motion coverage and real-video validation remain future work.

AI.tldr: DeepVFR is an initial controlled synthetic benchmark of 1,024 paired 150-frame face retouching video clips at 30 fps, accompanied by baseline evaluations and a 17-participant human ranking study.
AI.motivation: Paired unretouched/retouched face videos are expensive to produce with temporal consistency and raise privacy and consent barriers for public release.
AI.method: Starting from paired synthetic DeepFRR images, Wan2.2 generates mild-motion source clips and backend-specific face transfer creates synchronized proxy retouching targets, followed by automatic screening, manual inspection, and an identity-disjoint evaluation protocol.
AI.result: DeepVFR provides 1,024 clip pairs (150 frames, 30 fps); baseline evaluations and a 17-participant ranking study establish reference behavior while revealing a substantial low-preference tail in the proxy targets due to synthetic and transfer artifacts.
AI.conclusion: DeepVFR offers a privacy-safe starting point for paired face video retouching research, though artist-retouched real-video validation remains future work.

title: CARET: Clinical Assertion-Aware Residual Calibration for Medical Image-Text Alignment
summary: Medical vision--language models align radiographs with free-text reports, but radiology language distinguishes explicit findings, negation, uncertainty, and omission. Treating these report states as interchangeable during feature adaptation can change image predictions without supporting visual evidence. We introduce CARET, a parameter-efficient image-side adaptation method that retains pretrained image and text encoders and uses paired positive and negative clinical statements to define a low-dimensional semantic correction space. A bounded residual adjusts image features along these directions, while assertion-aware supervision distinguishes explicitly present and absent findings from uncertain or unmentioned ones. At inference, the adapter requires only an image; textual references remain fixed. In zero-shot classification, CARET achieves 67.80\% accuracy on CheXpert 5$\times$200 and 65.20\% on RSNA. These scores exceed the published CLEFT-LoRA results by 1.06 and 0.27 percentage points, respectively. Comparisons to literature baselines are informative but not controlled for differences in pretraining and evaluation protocols. Ablations across eight components identify the four-state distinction and assertion objective as major contributors, with task-dependent effects for nonmention preservation and pair alignment.

AI.tldr: CARET is a parameter-efficient image-side adapter for medical VLMs that calibrates image features along paired positive/negative clinical assertion directions, reaching 67.80% on CheXpert 5x200 and 65.20% on RSNA.
AI.motivation: Radiology reports distinguish explicit findings, negation, uncertainty, and omission, and treating these states interchangeably during adaptation alters image predictions without visual support.
AI.method: Keeping pretrained encoders frozen, CARET defines a low-dimensional semantic correction space from paired positive/negative clinical statements and applies a bounded residual to image features under assertion-aware supervision, requiring only images at inference.
AI.result: In zero-shot classification, CARET achieves 67.80% accuracy on CheXpert 5x200 (+1.06 points over published CLEFT-LoRA) and 65.20% on RSNA (+0.27 points), with ablations confirming the four-state distinction and assertion objective as key drivers.
AI.conclusion: Assertion-aware residual calibration on the image side improves medical image-text alignment without modifying pretrained encoders or needing text at inference.

title: RescueVLM: Model-Agnostic Vision-Language Framework for Rescue Drone Imagery
summary: A single unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) mission over an incident site produces hundreds of images, far more than a rescue commander can review under time pressure, and human screening of destruction imagery carries a documented psychological cost. The two obvious remedies both fail in search and rescue (SAR) practice: cloud vision-language model (VLM) services are excluded because the imagery must not leave the incident network under GDPR and German civil-protection (BOS) rules, and fine-tuned specialist detectors age quickly while retraining and re-certifying them exceeds most SAR organizations resources. We present RescueVLM, an open-source, training-free and model-agnostic triage tool built on SketchVLM: a general-purpose open-weight VLM runs fully on-premise and is swapped for a newer model through a simple dropdown selection, so triage quality grows with the underlying models because all task knowledge lives in prompts and an output contract rather than in trained weights. One natural-language query over a mission folder returns a ranked shortlist with per-image justifications, editable SVG overlay annotations, and a GPS map of the hits. In a qualitative evaluation on German fire-brigade field data from three real deployments and a live fire exercise, a single query condenses an entire survey mission into a handful of annotated frames that a commander can review at a glance.

AI.tldr: RescueVLM is an open-source, training-free, model-agnostic on-premise VLM triage tool for rescue drone imagery, validated on German fire-brigade deployments and a live fire exercise.
AI.motivation: UAV search-and-rescue missions generate hundreds of images that overwhelm commanders and cause psychological strain, while cloud VLMs violate GDPR/BOS data rules and fine-tuned detectors are too costly to retrain.
AI.method: Built on SketchVLM, RescueVLM runs general-purpose open-weight VLMs locally with all task knowledge encoded in prompts and an output contract, returning a ranked shortlist, justifications, editable SVG overlays, and a GPS map from a single natural-language query.
AI.result: In a qualitative evaluation on German fire-brigade data from three real deployments and one live fire exercise, a single query condenses an entire survey mission into a handful of annotated frames for rapid commander review.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-driven, swappable on-premise VLMs provide a compliant, zero-training triage solution for time-critical search-and-rescue drone operations.

title: LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 Technical Report
summary: Recent advances in audio-driven avatar video generation have enabled increasingly realistic synthesis, yet achieving precise lip-audio synchronization, natural, human-like motion, and visual consistency over long sequences remains challenging. We present LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6, which builds on LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.5 to improve expressive naturalness and reduce error accumulation during extended generation, e.g., exaggerated lip movements and overly red, temporally unstable lip coloration, enhance the naturalness of facial expressions and coordinated head and body movements. These improvements are driven by a refined post-training pipeline that integrates reinforcement learning, improved classifier-free guidance strategies for DMD-based few-step distillation, long-video rollouts, and on-policy distillation. Together, these refinements improve expressive realism and enable the generation of videos exceeding 10 minutes while maintaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Arena evaluations show that LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 outperforms its predecessor and competing commercial audio-driven avatar models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the improved post-training pipeline.

AI.tldr: LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 upgrades audio-driven avatar video generation via an RL- and distillation-based post-training pipeline, enabling >10-minute videos with improved lip-sync and naturalness over version 1.5 and commercial rivals.
AI.motivation: Audio-driven avatar models struggle with error accumulation over long sequences, causing exaggerated lip motion, unstable lip coloration, and unnatural head/body coordination.
AI.method: Building on LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.5, version 1.6 introduces a post-training pipeline combining reinforcement learning, improved CFG strategies for DMD-based few-step distillation, long-video rollouts, and on-policy distillation.
AI.result: Arena evaluations show LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 outperforms its predecessor and competing commercial audio-driven avatar models while sustaining visual quality and temporal consistency beyond 10 minutes.
AI.conclusion: Combining RL, on-policy distillation, and long-video rollouts effectively mitigates long-horizon error accumulation in audio-driven avatar synthesis.

title: Scaling Channel-Adaptive Self-Supervised Learning
summary: Recent advances in self-supervised pre-training of foundation models for natural images have made them a popular choice for various visual systems and applications. Self-supervised strategies are also promising in non-RGB scientific imaging domains such as in biology, medical and satellite imagery, but their broader application is hampered by heterogeneity in channel composition and semantics between relevant datasets: two datasets may contain different numbers of channels, and these may reveal distinct aspects of an object or scene. Recent works on channel adaptive strategies report substantial advantages for those that account for variable channel compositions without sacrificing the ability to jointly encode channels; yet, how these strategies behave at scale remains unclear. We here show that, surprisingly, trained across large-scale datasets, independent-encoding of channels outperforms joint-encoding methods by a substantial margin. We validate this result along an extensive set of experiments on various datasets from cell microscopy to geospatial imagery. Our DINO BoC approach sets a new state-of-the-art across challenging benchmarks, including generalization to out-of-distribution tasks and unseen channel combinations. We open-source code and model weights for a new general-purpose feature extractor for fluorescent microscopy.

AI.tldr: Contrary to prior small-scale findings, independent channel encoding (DINO BoC) outperforms joint channel encoding at scale across cell microscopy and geospatial benchmarks, with code and weights released.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous channel compositions across scientific imaging datasets hinder self-supervised foundation models, and it was unknown how channel-adaptive strategies scale to large datasets.
AI.method: The authors train and evaluate channel-adaptive self-supervised models at scale, comparing independent channel encoding (DINO BoC) against joint-encoding methods across cell microscopy and geospatial imagery.
AI.result: Across extensive experiments, independent channel encoding outperforms joint encoding by a substantial margin, setting a new state of the art including on out-of-distribution tasks and unseen channel combinations.
AI.conclusion: Scaling independent channel encoding provides a strong, general-purpose feature extractor for multi-channel scientific imaging.

title: Guided Group Featurizers (GGF): Improving Block-Sparse Featurizers with Object-Guided Learning
summary: Block-sparse featurizers (BSFs) use groups of learned directions to capture the multidimensional structure of visual concepts. However, grouping alone does not ensure that information about a concept is consolidated within a single group. We introduce Guided Group Featurizers (GGF), a novel object-guided extension that uses object annotations for initialization and training while preserving the BSF architecture. We assess whether each group's strongest response regions share an object type, part or material across images. Blinded reviews give GGF groups an average semantic coherence score of $94.1\pm0.9$%, versus $83.0\pm1.9$% for SLiCS and $65.3\pm2.2$% for supervised Vanilla BSF. GGF's consolidation advantage extends to unguided categories: one selected group per category covers $65.6\pm2.4$% of target-containing crops, versus $58.2\pm2.2$% for supervised Vanilla BSF, at approximately 5% false-positive rates for both. Across COCO and VOC, GGF also improves single-group object Capture and localization over Vanilla BSFs, SLiCS and Concept-SAE. Its groups produce more focused and reproducible object responses while supporting recognition and retaining associations under rotation, scale and brightness changes. GGF also uses fewer learned parameters than Concept-SAE and shorter recorded VOC training loops than both supervised alternatives. These findings support object guidance for organizing more interpretable BSF groups and show that response concentration extends to categories excluded from guidance.

AI.tldr: Guided Group Featurizers (GGF) add object-guided initialization and training to block-sparse featurizers, raising semantic coherence to 94.1% and improving object capture and localization on COCO and VOC.
AI.motivation: Standard block-sparse featurizers (BSFs) group learned directions but do not guarantee that information about a single visual concept consolidates within one group.
AI.method: GGF uses object annotations for initialization and training while preserving the BSF architecture, concentrating concept responses into single groups.
AI.result: Blinded reviews give GGF 94.1+/-0.9% semantic coherence versus 83.0+/-1.9% for SLiCS and 65.3+/-2.2% for supervised Vanilla BSF; on unguided categories, one group covers 65.6+/-2.4% of target crops (vs. 58.2+/-2.2%) at ~5% FPR, and GGF beats Vanilla BSF, SLiCS, and Concept-SAE on COCO/VOC with fewer parameters than Concept-SAE.
AI.conclusion: Object-guided learning organizes BSF groups into more interpretable, concentrated, and transformation-robust concept representations that generalize to unguided categories.

title: FiReIQ: Field-Level Confidence Estimation with Reasoning and Image Quality in Document Extraction
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in structured document extraction, yet their deployment in high-stakes applications requires reliable confidence estimates for individual fields. Existing uncertainty estimators often aggregate signals across an entire generation, obscuring field-specific reasoning uncertainty while overlooking visual degradations that may lead to confident extraction errors. To address these limitations, we introduce FiReIQ, a field-level confidence estimation framework that combines field-aligned reasoning signals from a single VLM generation with local and global image-quality features through quality-conditioned visual fusion. To facilitate systematic evaluation, we further introduce FiReIQ-Bench, a benchmark spanning financial receipts and legal contracts. Experiments with two reasoning VLMs show that FiReIQ consistently improves confidence discrimination, selective prediction, and probabilistic accuracy over existing estimators. These gains extend to private financial service data, where FiReIQ improves AUROC by 6.8% and coverage at 95% precision by 10.6% over an existing baseline. Together, these results highlight the potential of FiReIQ to reduce manual review while enabling more reliable document automation.

AI.tldr: FiReIQ estimates field-level VLM extraction confidence by fusing field-aligned reasoning signals with local/global image-quality features, improving AUROC by 6.8% on private financial data.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM uncertainty estimators aggregate signals across an entire generation, obscuring field-specific reasoning uncertainty and ignoring visual degradations that cause confident extraction errors.
AI.method: FiReIQ combines field-aligned reasoning signals from a single VLM pass with local and global image-quality features via quality-conditioned visual fusion, evaluated on a new FiReIQ-Bench (receipts and legal contracts) and private financial data.
AI.result: Across two reasoning VLMs, FiReIQ consistently outperforms existing estimators in confidence discrimination, selective prediction, and probabilistic accuracy, improving AUROC by 6.8% and coverage at 95% precision by 10.6% on private financial data.
AI.conclusion: Combining field-aligned reasoning uncertainty with image-quality fusion enables more reliable document automation and reduces manual review.

title: UnSPAD: Uncertainty-aware Single Photon Burst Photography
comment: Accepted at The Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027
summary: We introduce UnSPAD, an uncertainty-aware burst photography framework capable of fusing and denoising arbitrarily long sequences of binary single photon avalanche diode (SPAD) measurements. Unlike prior methods that require fixed burst lengths or rely on powerful generative priors, UnSPAD combines learned motion estimation with uncertainty-informed measurement fusion and denoising to produce temporally consistent, hallucination-free reconstructions. UnSPAD first forms an initial scene estimate by averaging flow-aligned binary frames. UnSPAD then uses per-pixel uncertainty maps to perform uncertainty-aware denoising; the denoiser is informed about which regions accumulated the fewest observations (and thus contain the most relative shot noise) due to motion, occlusion, or alignment errors. This two-step reconstruction pipeline helps mitigate hallucinations---outside of the structure implicitly introduced by the flow estimates, the initial scenes estimates are entirely prior-free. Experiments on real and simulated SPAD and quantum image sensor (QIS) benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art reconstruction quality, improved temporal consistency, and superior color fidelity relative to the state of the art.

AI.tldr: UnSPAD reconstructs arbitrarily long binary SPAD burst sequences by combining learned motion estimation with uncertainty-aware denoising, achieving state-of-the-art quality without generative hallucinations.
AI.motivation: Existing single-photon (SPAD) burst reconstruction methods are limited to fixed burst lengths or rely on generative priors that can hallucinate scene details.
AI.method: UnSPAD averages flow-aligned binary frames into a prior-free initial estimate, then applies an uncertainty-aware denoiser guided by per-pixel uncertainty maps reflecting shot noise from motion, occlusion, or alignment errors.
AI.result: On real and simulated SPAD and QIS benchmarks, UnSPAD achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction quality, improved temporal consistency, and superior color fidelity without generative hallucinations.
AI.conclusion: Explicit per-pixel observation uncertainty enables prior-free, temporally consistent burst photography for arbitrarily long single-photon sequences.

title: RAVEN-Bench: A Paired EO-IR Video QA Benchmark for Aerial Multimodal Understanding
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Datasets and Benchmarks Track)
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have advanced rapidly in image and video understanding, yet their ability to reason over paired aerial electro-optical and infrared (EO-IR) videos remains poorly understood. Such video poses a harder test than standard RGB video QA: targets are often small, evidence may appear only briefly, viewpoints change with the platform, and useful cues may appear in only one stream. We introduce RAVEN-Bench (Reasoning over Aerial Videos with EO-IR aligNment), a paired EO-IR video QA benchmark for low-altitude aerial multimodal understanding. RAVEN-Bench contains 100 temporally aligned EO-IR video pairs and 1,200 human-authored four-way multiple-choice questions, each independently audited for answer keys, modality requirements, evidence intervals, and group validity. It supports EO-only, IR-only, and paired EO+IR evaluation, and uses hierarchical capability levels and structured question groups to diagnose paired-input gain beyond the stronger unimodal condition, unimodal reliance, target consistency, and evidence-chain coherence. We evaluate frontier, open-weight, and remote-sensing MLLMs, showing that aggregate accuracy can overstate evidence-supported EO-IR reasoning. RAVEN-Bench provides controlled modality conditions and group-level diagnostics for auditing whether progress on RGB video benchmarks transfers to aerial cross-spectral understanding. Code and data are available at this https URL and this https URL.

AI.tldr: RAVEN-Bench is a paired aerial EO-IR video QA benchmark (100 video pairs, 1,200 questions) designed to diagnose cross-spectral reasoning, revealing that aggregate accuracy overstates true EO-IR fusion.
AI.motivation: Existing RGB video benchmarks do not test whether MLLMs can reason over paired aerial electro-optical and infrared (EO-IR) videos with small targets, brief evidence, and modality-specific cues.
AI.method: RAVEN-Bench pairs 100 temporally aligned EO-IR aerial videos with 1,200 audited four-way multiple-choice questions supporting EO-only, IR-only, and EO+IR evaluation across hierarchical capability levels and diagnostic question groups.
AI.result: Evaluating frontier, open-weight, and remote-sensing MLLMs shows that aggregate accuracy overstates evidence-supported EO-IR reasoning and exposes gaps in paired-input gain over the stronger unimodal stream.
AI.conclusion: Controlled unimodal-vs-paired diagnostics in RAVEN-Bench provide a rigorous audit of whether RGB video progress transfers to aerial cross-spectral understanding.

title: CISyn: Human Mesh Recovery in Close Interactions with Physics-Simulated Synthetic Data
summary: 3D human mesh recovery (HMR) in close-interaction scenarios is hindered by the lack of large-scale, accurately annotated training data: real capture is expensive, and existing synthetic datasets rarely include physical contact. We introduce CISyn, a large-scale synthetic dataset purpose-built for close human-human interactions, generated via physics simulation and Blender-based rendering. By simulating collision dynamics between SMPL-X-rigged humanoids, CISyn naturally produces the contact, mutual occlusion, and pose entanglement that characterize close-interaction scenes, with no manual annotation effort. The released set provides 25,000 sequences with accurate 3D annotations. We further propose an uncertainty-aware loss that allows models to learn more effectively from the heavily occluded examples in our data. Augmenting state-of-the-art HMR training with CISyn and replacing the regression loss with our uncertainty-aware variant yields consistent improvements on close-interaction benchmarks, validating CISyn as a scalable complement to real-world data. The dataset, generation pipeline, and code are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CISyn is a physics-simulated synthetic dataset of 25,000 close human-human interaction sequences with 3D SMPL-X annotations, which paired with an uncertainty-aware loss improves 3D human mesh recovery.
AI.motivation: 3D human mesh recovery in close interactions lacks large-scale, accurately annotated training data because real capture is costly and existing synthetic sets rarely model physical contact.
AI.method: Using physics simulation of collision dynamics between SMPL-X humanoids and Blender rendering, CISyn generates 25,000 sequences with natural contact, occlusion, and pose entanglement, alongside an uncertainty-aware loss for heavily occluded samples.
AI.result: Augmenting state-of-the-art HMR training with CISyn and replacing the regression loss with the uncertainty-aware variant yields consistent improvements on close-interaction benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Physics-simulated contact data and occlusion-aware loss functions provide a scalable complement to real-world data for close-interaction HMR.

title: Effects of Conventional, Adaptive, and AI-Powered Upscaling on the Legibility of License Plates
summary: Small details in digital images -- a face, a street sign, a license plate -- are routinely upscaled in hopes of making them interpretable. Upscaling options now range from conventional interpolation, whose operations are spatially invariant and fully explainable, to AI-powered methods that synthesize detail potentially absent from the source. Here, we ask which of these techniques most reliably helps human readers. In two online experiments, we measured legibility of 255 US license plates ranging in resolution from 128 to 8 pixels tall, as well as their legibility after upscaling by eight different methods. Legibility of the un-upscaled plates collapsed from ceiling to floor across a narrow band of plate heights (32 to 10 pixels). Conventional upscaling techniques (bilinear, bicubic, and Lanczos interpolation) gave modest gains of about 5-9 percentage points within this range. Nearest-neighbor interpolation, however, was harmful, rendering unreadable many plates that were readable without any upscaling. Advanced methods diverged: SwinIR, an open-source AI enhancer, raised performance by up to 38 points relative to no upscaling, while an adaptive denoiser-based image prior and commercial AI upscaler tended to impair legibility. We found no strong evidence of consistent character hallucinations across methods. Decomposing the task, conventional interpolators mainly helped readers count characters, whereas SwinIR alone made the characters themselves more identifiable.

AI.tldr: In human legibility tests on 255 US license plates (8-128 px tall), SwinIR boosts legibility by up to 38 percentage points, conventional interpolators add 5-9 points, and nearest-neighbor or denoiser/commercial AI methods hurt legibility.
AI.motivation: Various upscaling methods are routinely applied to low-resolution details like license plates, but it is unclear which techniques genuinely improve human legibility versus introducing harmful artifacts.
AI.method: Two online human experiments measured legibility of 255 US license plates (8 to 128 pixels tall) un-upscaled and upscaled by eight conventional, adaptive, and AI-powered methods.
AI.result: Un-upscaled legibility collapsed between 32 and 10 pixels; bilinear, bicubic, and Lanczos gained 5-9 points (mainly helping character counting), nearest-neighbor hurt legibility, and SwinIR gained up to 38 points (making characters more identifiable) without consistent character hallucinations, whereas an adaptive denoiser and commercial AI upscaler impaired legibility.
AI.conclusion: Only specific enhancers like SwinIR substantially improve human character identification on low-resolution plates, while nearest-neighbor and some AI upscalers can degrade readability.

title: Probing Where Surprise Happens: Localized Violation-of-Expectation Evaluation of Video World Models
summary: Violation-of-expectation (VOE) benchmarks evaluate intuitive physics in video world models by testing whether physically impossible events produce greater prediction errors than matched possible events. However, conventional VOE evaluations aggregate prediction errors across space and time, making it unclear whether successful discrimination reflects model's understanding of physical violations at the locations and time where they occur. To address this limitation, we introduce localized VOE evaluation, a framework that measures prediction error differences between possible and impossible events within spatial regions and temporal intervals associated with physical violations. We compare global, temporally localized, and spatiotemporally localized evaluations of V-JEPA models pretrained on developmental egocentric videos or large-scale natural video datasets. Our results reveal that global and localized judgments can diverge in both directions: global aggregation can either obscure correct localized discrimination or produce apparent discrimination without corresponding localized evidence. During continued pretraining on developmental egocentric videos, agreement between global and localized judgments changes non-monotonically, while confidence in localized judgments increases despite modest improvements in accuracy. Together, these findings establish localized VOE evaluation as a complementary diagnostic for assessing intuitive physics in video world models and demonstrate that global prediction errors do not necessarily reflect the spatiotemporal evidence of physical violations.

AI.tldr: Localized Violation-of-Expectation (VOE) evaluation measures prediction error differences specifically at the space-time locations of physical violations, revealing that global VOE scores on V-JEPA often diverge from localized evidence.
AI.motivation: Standard VOE benchmarks aggregate prediction error across the entire video, making it unclear whether a model's discrimination stems from understanding the physical violation at its actual location and time.
AI.method: The authors propose temporally and spatiotemporally localized VOE evaluation and compare global versus localized judgments on V-JEPA models pretrained on developmental egocentric or natural videos.
AI.result: Global and localized judgments diverge in both directions—global aggregation can hide localized discrimination or show discrimination without localized evidence—and during continued egocentric pretraining, global-localized agreement varies non-monotonically while localized confidence rises.
AI.conclusion: Spatiotemporally localized VOE evaluation is a necessary complementary diagnostic because global prediction errors do not reliably reflect localized physical understanding.

title: Role-Separated Diffusion Transformers: Global Rule Isolation and Deterministic Sampling Manifold Compression
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Github Repo: this https URL
summary: We present Role-Separated Diffusion Transformers (RoSeDiT), a new diffusion transformer architecture that isolates the global rule from the image tokens. RoSeViT showed in visual reasoning that a vanilla ViT spreads a shared rule over all $L$ tokens at an entropy of order $Ld$, whereas an enforced controller route reduces it to order $d$. In class-conditional DiT and SiT, the class and the noise level are explicitly conditioned by adaLN, so a RoSeViT-style controller channel on the ViT side is insufficient to establish the full role separation. By introducing the adaLN listening mechanism, which makes adaLN compute under the controller's command, RoSeDiT brings the entropy theorem and role separation into the latent diffusion domain. Under the same SiT training and evaluation protocol at the same level of parameter count, RoSeDiT surpasses SiT at all four model scales at 400K steps, and RoSeDiT-L/2 even surpasses SiT-XL/2's 17.2 FID with 15.34 and 32% fewer parameters. RoSeDiT-XL/2 surpasses SiT-XL/2's 7M-step FID of 8.3 at 1.4M steps with 7.98, using one-fifth as many training steps. We further observe that models with the same denoising loss can have a large FID gap, which indicates a misalignment between the denoising objective and the image manifold. We formalize this phenomenon into Deterministic Sampling Manifold Compression (DSMC), a two-stage training schedule with which RoSeDiT-XL/2 surpasses SiT + REPA's 4M-step FID of 5.9 at 2.4M steps with 5.84.

AI.tldr: RoSeDiT introduces an adaLN listening mechanism to isolate global rules into a controller channel, beating SiT across scales and achieving 5.84 FID at 2.4M steps with a two-stage DSMC schedule.
AI.motivation: Vanilla DiT/SiT models spread shared global conditioning across all tokens via adaLN, preventing the entropy reduction achieved by role separation in visual reasoning (RoSeViT).
AI.method: RoSeDiT adds an adaLN listening mechanism so adaLN computes under the controller's command, and introduces Deterministic Sampling Manifold Compression (DSMC), a two-stage training schedule addressing denoising-loss/FID misalignment.
AI.result: Under the SiT protocol, RoSeDiT outperforms SiT at all four scales at 400K steps; RoSeDiT-L/2 beats SiT-XL/2 (15.34 vs. 17.2 FID) with 32% fewer parameters, RoSeDiT-XL/2 beats SiT-XL/2's 7M-step 8.3 FID at 1.4M steps (7.98), and with DSMC beats SiT+REPA's 4M-step 5.9 FID at 2.4M steps (5.84).
AI.conclusion: Enforcing role separation via adaLN listening and two-stage manifold compression substantially improves diffusion transformer parameter and training efficiency.

title: Hard or Mislabeled? Failure Screens Enrich Vision Benchmarks for Label Errors
summary: Hard vision benchmarks often keep images that strong classifiers get wrong. Since a classifier is also marked wrong when the label is wrong, such failure screens may collect label errors. We measure this on ImageNet's twice-relabeled validation set with 103 classifiers. Among the 1,892 images that all 66 supervised classifiers get wrong, 61% have a wrong label, versus 11.1% overall. The fewer images a screen lets through, the more of them are mislabeled, along approximately one curve. Fit on one model family, this curve predicts the screens of two held-out model families with a mean error of 2.4 percentage points, and replays of ImageNet-D's and ImageNet-Hard's screens within 0.1 and 6.3 points. On new pools, ImageNet-V2 and CIFAR-10, enrichment at the strictest screens is stronger than the curve predicts: on ImageNet-V2, by human relabeling, 67% of the images that all 66 classifiers get wrong are mislabeled, against 46% predicted. Screens that let models choose among only some of the classes, as ImageNet-A's does (200 of 1,000), fall below the curve. By ReImageNet, 32% of ImageNet-Hard's ImageNet images have no correct label. ScreenAudit, which comprises an audit tool, a script that rebuilds corrected answer sets for the 5,464 decided ImageNet-Hard images (of 5,646) from ReImageNet's gated release, and per-image audits of 1,198 benchmark images, will be released later.

AI.tldr: Failure screens used to build hard vision benchmarks heavily enrich for label errors—61% of ImageNet images missed by all 66 classifiers are mislabeled—and a single curve predicts this enrichment across model families.
AI.motivation: Hard vision benchmarks retain images that strong classifiers misclassify, but because classifiers are also marked wrong on mislabeled images, failure screens may inadvertently collect label errors.
AI.method: Using 103 classifiers on ImageNet's twice-relabeled validation set, ImageNet-V2, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-D, ImageNet-Hard, and ImageNet-A, the authors measure label-error enrichment versus screen strictness and build the ScreenAudit tool.
AI.result: Among 1,892 ImageNet images missed by all 66 supervised classifiers, 61% have wrong labels (vs. 11.1% overall); a curve fit on one model family predicts two held-out families within 2.4 percentage points and replays ImageNet-D/Hard within 0.1/6.3 points, while on ImageNet-V2 all-wrong images are 67% mislabeled (vs. 46% predicted) and 32% of ImageNet-Hard's ImageNet images lack a correct label.
AI.conclusion: Strict failure screens systematically concentrate label errors rather than purely hard examples, underscoring the need for label auditing tools like ScreenAudit.

title: Quantize, Qualify, Rerank: A Recipe for Compressing LLMs Without Losing Quality
summary: Compressing large language models lowers serving cost, but a single automatic metric may miss quality loss. For the WMT26 Model Compression constrained track, we compress google/gemma-3-12b-it (24.4 GB in bf16) for three translation directions on one H100. Paired bootstrap analysis exposes metric disagreement on 4-bit quantization; guided by WMT24 human meta-evaluation, we use MetricX24-XXL as primary and CometKiwi-XXL as a cross-check.
