LEAP-LLM uses the clinical question to guide ECG feature extraction while preserving explicit lead and temporal structure. Task-trained instruction representations distill information from the question and guide two complementary branches. The Lead branch captures question-relevant temporal patterns within each ECG lead, while the Temporal branch summarizes relevant information across leads at each temporal position. Together, they provide the LLM with compact, question-relevant ECG information while preserving lead and temporal structure. LEAP-LLM reduces modality-token count by 89.0% and prefill FLOPs by 7.2x on average relative to other ECG-LLMs baselines. Across four ECG benchmarks, LEAP-LLM achieves better performance, including a 3.4-percentage-point improvement in G12EC over the strongest prior ECG-specific method. We further show that the model adaptively emphasizes the clinically relevant anatomical lead groups for different cardiac abnormalities, with lead importance patterns consistent with established diagnostic knowledge, providing interpretable evidence that the predictions are supported by clinically meaningful ECG structure.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces LEAP-LLM, a question-conditioned ECG-LLM architecture that preserves lead and temporal structure via dual Lead and Temporal branches, cutting modality tokens by 89.0% and improving G12EC accuracy by 3.4 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Existing ECG-language models encode ECGs independently of the clinical question and pool across leads, retaining irrelevant signal information while obscuring lead-specific details needed to answer a given question.
AI.method: LEAP-LLM distills task-trained instruction representations from the clinical question to guide two branches: a Lead branch capturing question-relevant temporal patterns per lead and a Temporal branch summarizing across leads at each time step.
AI.result: Compared to prior ECG-LLM baselines, LEAP-LLM reduces modality-token count by 89.0% and prefill FLOPs by 7.2x on average, achieves superior performance across four ECG benchmarks including a 3.4-percentage-point gain on G12EC, and adaptively highlights clinically relevant anatomical lead groups.
AI.conclusion: Question-conditioned dual-branch alignment produces compact, interpretable, and more accurate ECG representations for clinical LLM reasoning.

title: What to Practice Next? Latent Profile-Guided Task Selection for Skill-Evolving LLM Agents
summary: Task selection shapes the experiences available for skill evolution in LLM agents, yet fixed practice schedules overlook differences in skill requirements and evolving task value. Most existing methods, however, rely on fixed schedules or scalar measures of progress, leaving nonstationary skill demands unaddressed. We propose SPG-Select, a framework for allocating limited practice budget using a multidimensional profile inferred from binary outcomes via MIRT. The framework predicts surrogate progress, defined as the difference between consecutive profile estimates, and prioritizes progress in dimensions with larger estimated proficiency gaps. Our SPG-Select-R policy combines these predictions with uncertainty-based exploration and periodic restarting to accommodate nonstationarity. We evaluate SPG-Select on ALFWorld and WebShop with three skill-evolution backends. In the reported runs, SPG-Select-R achieves higher mean held-out terminal success than uniform sampling in all six backend-benchmark combinations, with gains of 1.49-13.18 percentage points on ALFWorld and 0.93-3.13 points on WebShop. Under a predictable linear surrogate model and boundedness assumptions, we establish a high-probability dynamic pseudo-regret bound for surrogate task allocation in terms of parameter path variation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SPG-Select, a latent-profile-guided task selection framework using MIRT and uncertainty exploration for skill-evolving LLM agents, outperforming uniform sampling across all six ALFWorld and WebShop setups.
AI.motivation: Fixed practice schedules and scalar progress measures fail to account for nonstationary, multidimensional skill requirements when training skill-evolving LLM agents under limited budgets.
AI.method: SPG-Select infers a multidimensional skill profile from binary outcomes via MIRT, predicts surrogate progress between consecutive estimates to prioritize dimensions with larger proficiency gaps, and combines this in SPG-Select-R with uncertainty exploration and periodic restarting.
AI.result: Across six backend-benchmark combinations on ALFWorld and WebShop, SPG-Select-R outperforms uniform sampling in mean held-out terminal success by 1.49-13.18 percentage points on ALFWorld and 0.93-3.13 points on WebShop, supported by a high-probability dynamic pseudo-regret bound.
AI.conclusion: Multidimensional latent-profile task allocation with nonstationary exploration substantially improves skill evolution in LLM agents under fixed practice budgets.

title: Identification and external validation of the sets of 4-, 6-, 8-, 12-, and 24-hour CGM motifs
summary: There is growing interest in using CGM for purposes other than those initially intended. Recent work of Lobo et al. identified $\Omega$: a set of motifs such that almost any daily CGM profile (the 24-hour CGM time series starting at midnight) can be classified - matched to a motif in $\Omega$. This work generalizes the prior work by identifying sets of motifs for 4-, 6-, 8-, 12-, and 24-hr CGM profiles where an $x$-hr CGM profile does not have to be 24 hours in length, and does not have to start at midnight. The prior work methods are modified to identify the five new sets of motifs using data from the same 6 studies in the original work. The newly identified sets were subjected to rigorous external validation using a data set comprised of data from 21 studies (3,455 subjects, 289,592 days of CGM data). The external validation data set has both temporal and geographic transportability and addresses limitations of the data set used to define the five new sets of motifs. The results of the external validation indicate that the prior work generalizes well: the performance of each $x$-hr set of motifs on the external validation set is almost identical to that obtained for $\Omega$. The generalization of the original work broadens the potential use cases of the framework to include short term predictions (e.g., impending hypoglycemia) and diagnostics which rely on detecting changes in CGM time series which are less than 24 hours in length.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes 24-hour midnight-aligned CGM motif sets to 4-, 6-, 8-, 12-, and 24-hour arbitrary-start CGM motifs and validates them externally across 21 studies (289,592 days), matching original performance.
AI.motivation: Prior CGM motif work (Omega) was restricted to 24-hour profiles starting at midnight, limiting its use for shorter-term predictions such as impending hypoglycemia.
AI.method: The authors adapt the original motif-identification methods on the same 6 studies to derive motif sets for 4-, 6-, 8-, 12-, and 24-hour profiles without a midnight start requirement, and externally validate them on 21 studies (3,455 subjects, 289,592 days).
AI.result: On the external validation dataset with temporal and geographic diversity, each x-hour motif set achieves performance almost identical to that of the original 24-hour Omega set.
AI.conclusion: Arbitrary-start, sub-daily CGM motif sets generalize reliably and broaden the framework's applicability to short-term clinical diagnostics and hypoglycemia prediction.

title: Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Harness optimization is often studied with a fixed policy model and benchmark. When either changes, the optimizer must decide which parts of an evolved harness to reuse or revise, but the harness alone may not explain why earlier edits were made or how they performed. In this work, we study Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI), a setting for continuing existing harness-optimization methods across compatible benchmarks or policy models. We propose Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) for the harness optimizer, rather than the task-solving policy. SIM groups edits by recurring harness problem and records their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context. New attempts extend this history as optimization continues. In our experiments across four domains, SIM achieves higher final scores than harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in cross-dataset and pairwise cross-model comparisons. Across ten independent source runs in coding, paired continuations with SIM improve final scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation ($p=0.003$).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI) and Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) for harness optimizers, improving final coding scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation.
AI.motivation: When continuing harness optimization across new benchmarks or policy models, the evolved harness alone does not explain why past edits were made or how they performed.
AI.method: SIM equips the harness optimizer with a memory that groups edits by recurring harness problems and records their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context, extending this history across optimization runs.
AI.result: Across four domains in cross-dataset and cross-model comparisons, SIM achieves higher final scores than harness-only and root-cause-only continuation, improving coding scores across ten source runs by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation (p=0.003).
AI.conclusion: Retaining structured optimization history in Self-Improvement Memory enables more effective continual recursive self-improvement across changing models and benchmarks.

title: SLICES: A Benchmark and Evaluation Framework for Self-Supervised Learning on Sparse ICU Time Series
comment: Accepted at the Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) Symposium 2026, Proceedings track (PMLR 346). 28 pages, 8 figures, 21 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) results for intensive care unit (ICU) time series are hard to compare when data processing, encoders, and adaptation vary together. We present SLICES, a benchmark and evaluation framework for comparing and extending SSL methods under a shared clinical setup. It fixes 24-hour value and observation-mask inputs, a Transformer encoder, patient-level splits, four endpoints, two adaptation protocols, and five matched seeds across MIMIC-IV, eICU-CRD, and their pooled union. Masked autoencoding (MAE), joint-embedding prediction (JEPA), and contrastive learning provide reference implementations. Among these objectives, MAE leads mean AUPRC in all nine frozen classification comparisons, also under converged probes, and in seven of nine fine-tuning comparisons. Fine-tuned MAE leads hospital mortality at full labels and scores higher than a supervised Transformer of the same architecture at every label fraction, and SSL fine-tuning gives the lowest length-of-stay error. Supervised baselines remain strong elsewhere: GRU-D leads 24-hour mortality and XGBoost leads acute kidney injury in all three regimes. Rankings depend on the adaptation protocol, the comparator set, and whether the probe loss matches the metric. A two-seed MIMIC-IV rerun with the maintained code stays within two across-seed SDs of the reference in all 48 downstream runs. The code repository supports new objectives, shared downstream evaluation, and regeneration of the reference results, so new SSL methods can be compared with these references under the same conditions. Generalization to unseen hospitals is not tested here and is the natural next extension.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SLICES, a standardized benchmark for self-supervised learning on sparse ICU time series across MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD, finding that masked autoencoding (MAE) leads SSL objectives while supervised baselines remain strongest on some tasks.
AI.motivation: Comparing self-supervised learning (SSL) methods on ICU time series is difficult because prior studies vary data processing, encoders, and adaptation protocols simultaneously.
AI.method: SLICES fixes 24-hour value and observation-mask inputs, a Transformer encoder, patient-level splits, four endpoints, two adaptation protocols, and five seeds across MIMIC-IV, eICU-CRD, and their pooled union, providing reference implementations for MAE, JEPA, and contrastive learning.
AI.result: MAE leads mean AUPRC in all nine frozen classification comparisons and seven of nine fine-tuning comparisons, outperforming a supervised Transformer on hospital mortality and achieving the lowest length-of-stay error via SSL fine-tuning, though GRU-D leads 24-hour mortality and XGBoost leads acute kidney injury; a two-seed rerun stays within two SDs across all 48 runs.
AI.conclusion: SLICES establishes a reproducible clinical SSL benchmark and shows that while MAE is the strongest tested SSL objective, method rankings depend on adaptation protocol and supervised baselines remain competitive.

title: Factorized Self-Supervised Speech Tokenization
comment: 26 pages, 6 figures, 16 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Speech tokenizers convert audio into discrete units, enabling language models to process and generate speech. The goal is to learn compact, text-like representations while preserving enough detail to reconstruct a speaker's voice and delivery. We propose Facto: a factorized tokenizer that disentangles time-varying information (content and prosody) from static components (speaker identity and recording conditions). We build on a recent linear factorization method for self-supervised features, extending it to handle unseen speakers. Then, we cluster the factorized space and train a lightweight decoder to reconstruct audio from the resulting tokens. By removing the static components before clustering, our tokens are more robust to small noise perturbations. We validate this by testing token stability under various noise conditions. Next, we theoretically analyze Facto's convergence and scaling properties, quantifying how the factorization improves with the number of training speakers. Finally, we evaluate Facto on a range of downstream tasks. We show that greater token stability translates into improved text-to-speech performance and competitive results in voice conversion and spoken language modeling. Code and checkpoints at this https URL and demo page at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Facto, a factorized self-supervised speech tokenizer that disentangles time-varying content/prosody from static speaker/recording components, improving token noise stability and downstream TTS performance.
AI.motivation: Speech tokenizers aim to produce compact, text-like discrete units while preserving vocal detail, but static speaker and recording variations degrade token stability under noise.
AI.method: Extending a linear factorization method for self-supervised features to unseen speakers, Facto removes static components before clustering the factorized space and trains a lightweight decoder for audio reconstruction, accompanied by a theoretical convergence and scaling analysis.
AI.result: Removing static components improves token stability under various noise conditions, which translates into improved text-to-speech performance and competitive results on voice conversion and spoken language modeling.
AI.conclusion: Factorizing out static speaker and recording attributes before clustering yields more noise-robust discrete speech tokens and stronger downstream synthesis.

title: How Much Do Foundation Models Add to Gradient Boosting on Financial Event Sequences?
comment: 49 pages, 5 figures, 24 tables. Code, synthetic data generator and per-seed predictions available at this https URL
summary: Foundation models pretrained on raw transaction sequences are proposed for credit, fraud and churn modeling, with reported gains over gradient boosting, but the data and baselines behind these gains are rarely public. We measure how much the pretraining and adaptation recipes of these models add to a baseline of point-in-time window aggregates and LightGBM, and we propose TBS (Temporal Boosting-Sequence ensemble), which averages the ranks of a boosting model enriched with label-free event-transition features and of a pretrained sequence network fine-tuned jointly with the aggregates. On a synthetic credit-card dataset, the public MBD-mini banking dataset and two proprietary datasets of trade credit and B2B churn, we compare 27 methods at three label budgets with five seeds and paired bootstrap intervals, using sequence models of about 0.4 million parameters pretrained per dataset. Frozen self-supervised embeddings rarely improve the baseline, and a fine-tuned sequence network alone clears it in 9 of 21 target-budget cells. TBS clears it in 19 of 21 cells (18 after FDR adjustment), with a median gain of +1.8 AUC points, and the controls suggest that combining boosting with the pretrained network is the main source of the observed gain. Gains shrink as labels grow and with rich tabular data: with both, the gain on the proprietary datasets is +0.7 and +0.8 points, the latter with an interval including zero. We also re-examine two benchmarks. On IBM TabFormer, the test follows a change in the fraud pattern and the published baseline has no history; with the training period the vendor states, our history-aware LightGBM and our own foundation model stay below the published scores of a commercial model. On IBM AML, a simulation artifact lets a date rule reach F1 0.482, and a point-in-time LightGBM reaches the F1 of graph neural networks whose test graph includes later transactions.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks foundation models against LightGBM on financial event sequences, proposing the TBS ensemble (+1.8 median AUC) while showing that gains shrink with larger label budgets and rich tabular features.
AI.motivation: Foundation models pretrained on transaction sequences claim gains over gradient boosting, but the underlying data and baselines are rarely public, and benchmark artifacts can inflate reported results.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 27 methods across four datasets (synthetic credit-card, MBD-mini, and two proprietary datasets) at three label budgets, propose TBS (rank-averaging a transition-feature-enriched boosting model with a fine-tuned pretrained sequence network), and re-examine IBM TabFormer and IBM AML.
AI.result: Frozen embeddings rarely beat LightGBM, fine-tuned sequence networks clear it in 9 of 21 cells, and TBS clears it in 19 of 21 cells (+1.8 median AUC, shrinking to +0.7 and +0.8 on rich-feature proprietary datasets); on IBM AML, a simulation artifact lets a date rule reach F1 0.482 and point-in-time LightGBM matches GNNs.
AI.conclusion: Combining pretrained sequence models with feature-enriched gradient boosting helps under low labels, but rich tabular features and proper leakage-free baselines narrow the gap substantially.

title: The Human Side of ML Engineering: Analyzing the Collaboration and Communication Skills in ML Job Postings
summary: Studies of Machine Learning (ML) practice highlight the importance of combining technical expertise with interpersonal capabilities, particularly collaboration and communication. However, evidence on how ML job postings express these skills is scarce, and prior work largely relies on keyword-based analyses that overlook implicit expression. We analyze demand for these skills in ML job postings across regions, industries, and seniority levels, and compare it with software engineering (SE) roles. We collected 1,000 postings (500 ML, 500 SE) from five continents via a semi-automated pipeline. For annotation, we synthesized a taxonomy of collaboration and communication sub-categories from prior work and used an LLM as a third annotator alongside two humans, enabling detection of context-dependent and implicit skill references. Collaboration appeared in 88.6% of ML postings and communication in 72.2%, far above prior keyword-based estimates for AI roles. Roughly one in five collaboration and one in four communication requirements were expressed only implicitly. Decomposing these requirements into the taxonomy's sub-categories reveals what aggregate figures conceal. Collaboration is demanded predominantly as integration across role boundaries rather than team membership. Communication is mostly required in generic terms, with fewer than half of the postings requiring it naming whom the candidate must communicate with. ML and SE postings demand interpersonal competence at statistically indistinguishable levels but orient it differently, SE toward team practices and ML toward presentation and audience-facing interaction. Within ML, the advertised role separates interpersonal profiles more sharply than any other dimension, including the contrast with SE.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 1,000 ML and SE job postings across five continents using human and LLM annotation, finding that 88.6% of ML postings require collaboration and 72.2% require communication, often implicitly.
AI.motivation: Evidence on how ML job postings express interpersonal skills is scarce, and prior keyword-based analyses miss context-dependent and implicit requirements.
AI.method: The authors collect 500 ML and 500 SE postings from five continents, synthesize a taxonomy of collaboration and communication sub-categories, and annotate them using two humans plus an LLM as a third annotator.
AI.result: Collaboration appears in 88.6% of ML postings and communication in 72.2% (roughly one in five and one in four expressed only implicitly); while overall levels match SE postings, ML orients communication toward presentation and audience-facing interaction rather than team practices, and advertised role differentiates interpersonal profiles more than ML vs. SE.
AI.conclusion: Implicit and role-specific interpersonal demands are pervasive in ML engineering postings and are underestimated by keyword-based analyses.

title: Simplify, Agree, Distill: Label-Free Self-Distillation with Stepping Stones
summary: Can a language model teach itself to reason without labels? On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the model as its own teacher, but strengthens that teacher with a ground-truth solution. The natural label-free substitute, voting over the model's attempts, fails precisely on hard problems: attempts disagree, and their most common answer is often wrong. We propose STONE, a label-free alternative that moves agreement to easier related problems. The model writes these stepping stones, keeps those it solves consistently, and shows the teacher their worked solutions, with final answers removed; the student sees only the original problem. No step reads a label, and inference needs no extra context or model calls. Across five math benchmarks, the proposed method achieves the highest average accuracy for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode. Without thinking mode, it gains 13.2 and 22.7 points, 2.5 and 2.7 times the gains of OPSD with ground-truth solutions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes STONE, a label-free self-distillation method that generates and solves easier stepping-stone problems to teach a model on harder ones, outperforming OPSD on five math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) relies on ground-truth solutions, while its natural label-free substitute—majority voting—fails on hard problems where attempts disagree and the mode is often wrong.
AI.method: STONE prompts the model to write easier related stepping-stone problems, filters for those it solves consistently, and shows the teacher their worked solutions (with final answers removed) while the student sees only the original problem.
AI.result: Across five math benchmarks, STONE achieves the highest average accuracy for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode, and without thinking mode it gains 13.2 and 22.7 points, 2.5 and 2.7 times the gains of OPSD using ground-truth solutions.
AI.conclusion: Shifting agreement to self-generated stepping-stone problems enables effective label-free self-distillation without extra inference context or ground-truth labels.

title: OverclusterDRG: a Deterministic, LP-Free Heuristic for Robust $k$-Center
summary: The $k$-center problem is a fundamental formulation for metric clustering. However, its min-max objective is highly sensitive to outliers, motivating the Robust $k$-Center (R$k$C) formulation which permits excluding up to $z$ points as outliers. Existing algorithms for R$k$C suffer from scalability issues: LP rounding relies on fractional relaxations that scale poorly, known combinatorial approximation algorithms are computationally expensive due to radius guessing, and scalable randomized heuristics require exponential trial multipliers to guarantee success. We present OverclusterDRG, a deterministic, LP-free heuristic for R$k$C. The algorithm leverages the theoretical insight of farthest-point oversampling -- adding exactly $z$ extra candidates to the center set to absorb outliers -- followed by a forward-greedy initialization and a $1$-swap local search. Evaluations across real-world datasets show that OverclusterDRG attains a mean approximation ratio of 1.147 against fractional LP lower bounds on the UCI Adult dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in both clustering quality and speed. By avoiding subset-guessing and exponential trial multipliers, it scales smoothly to $n=10^5$ points where LP solvers and theoretical algorithms become intractable.

AI.tldr: This paper presents OverclusterDRG, a deterministic, LP-free heuristic for Robust k-Center clustering that achieves a 1.147 mean approximation ratio on UCI Adult and scales to 10^5 points.
AI.motivation: Existing Robust k-Center (RkC) algorithms struggle to scale because LP rounding requires large fractional relaxations, combinatorial approximations use expensive radius guessing, and randomized heuristics need exponential trial multipliers.
AI.method: OverclusterDRG uses farthest-point oversampling to add exactly z extra candidate centers to absorb outliers, followed by forward-greedy initialization and a 1-swap local search.
AI.result: On real-world datasets, OverclusterDRG achieves a mean approximation ratio of 1.147 against fractional LP lower bounds on UCI Adult, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in both quality and speed while scaling smoothly to n=10^5 points.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic oversampling with greedy initialization and 1-swap local search provides a fast, scalable, and accurate alternative to LP-based Robust k-Center algorithms.

title: Geometrically Disentangling Concept Learning from the Language Modeling Loss
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code: this https URL . Pretrained probes and research artifacts: this https URL
summary: Language models acquire a vast array of concepts and abilities from next-token prediction alone. We introduce an interpretability framework that exposes how this single loss relates to the development of different concepts at different points during pretraining. We propose Concept Energy, a measure of the concept-specific alignment between a concept subspace and the average gradient outer product (AGOP) of the next-token-prediction loss. The concept subspace captures where the concept currently lives in the model's representation; AGOP captures the directions to which the loss is most sensitive. Across 19 checkpoints of Pythia-410M and -1B and 12 lexical, syntactic, and semantic concepts, we find that the first peak in Concept Energy generally occurs at or before the steepest increase in probe decodability. Furthermore, whereas probe performance usually increases monotonically throughout training, Concept Energy is not confined to a single peak; some concepts exhibit sustained or repeated engagement across pretraining, suggesting that concept learning may require continual reinforcement or occur at multiple points. Our results indicate that the loss contributes to concept learning in a myriad of ways that simple probe performance alone cannot reveal.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Concept Energy, measuring alignment between concept subspaces and the next-token-prediction loss's average gradient outer product (AGOP), revealing non-monotonic concept engagement during Pythia pretraining.
AI.motivation: Language models acquire diverse concepts from next-token prediction alone, but simple probe decodability does not show how the training loss drives different concepts at different pretraining stages.
AI.method: The authors define Concept Energy as the alignment between a concept subspace (where the concept lives in representations) and the AGOP of the next-token-prediction loss (directions to which the loss is most sensitive), evaluating 19 checkpoints of Pythia-410M and Pythia-1B across 12 concepts.
AI.result: The first peak in Concept Energy generally occurs at or before the steepest rise in probe decodability, and unlike monotonically increasing probe accuracy, Concept Energy exhibits sustained or repeated peaks across pretraining for some concepts.
AI.conclusion: Geometric alignment between concept subspaces and loss gradients uncovers multi-stage, non-monotonic concept learning dynamics invisible to standard probing.

title: Contextual Non-Convex Bandit Optimization with Two-Point Feedback
summary: We study a non-stochastic contextual bandit problem with Lipschitz losses. At every round, the learner observes the context then picks two actions, observes the difference between their losses, and incurs their mean. The aim is to minimize the regret against a generic non-parametric comparator class of policies mapping contexts to actions; for example, Lipschitz policies and Hölder-smooth policies. We show how relying on a hierarchical discretization technique allows us to improve upon the regret rates achievable under one-point feedback, and even recover the full-information rate in some cases; notably, for sufficiently smooth policy classes or low-dimensional instances. Additionally, for Lipschitz policies, we present an algorithm whose per-round computational complexity is only logarithmic in the time horizon.

AI.tldr: This paper studies non-stochastic contextual bandits with Lipschitz losses and two-point feedback, showing that hierarchical discretization improves regret rates over one-point feedback and achieves logarithmic per-round complexity for Lipschitz policies.
AI.motivation: Minimizing regret against generic non-parametric policy classes (such as Lipschitz or Holder-smooth policies) in non-stochastic contextual bandits is challenging under limited feedback.
AI.method: At each round, the learner observes the context, selects two actions, observes their loss difference while incurring their mean, and applies a hierarchical discretization technique to compete against non-parametric comparator policy classes.
AI.result: Hierarchical discretization improves regret rates over one-point feedback, recovers full-information rates for sufficiently smooth policy classes or low-dimensional instances, and yields an algorithm for Lipschitz policies with per-round computational complexity logarithmic in the time horizon.
AI.conclusion: Two-point feedback combined with hierarchical discretization enables near-full-information regret and fast per-round computation for non-parametric contextual bandits.

title: Bilateral Log-Linear Attention
summary: Sequence models represent past context at different resolutions, using token-level keys and values, fixed-size recurrent states, or hierarchies of compressed summaries. Full attention supports strong associative recall but requires quadratic work during training and prefill and a linearly growing key-value cache during inference. Linear attention and state-space models reduce these costs through fixed-size recurrent memory, but this compression can limit recall. Log-linear attention offers a middle ground by maintaining logarithmically many state matrices. However, its hierarchy favors finer resolution near the current query while compressing earlier context into coarser summaries. To complement this allocation of resolution, we introduce bilateral log-linear attention, which pairs the existing hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin. By combining their reads, the two branches provide finer access to both early and recent context while remaining causal. We derive recurrent and chunkwise parallel formulations for the added branch, preserving log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding work per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage at fixed feature dimensions and chunk size. In multi-query associative recall, this design raises mean overall test accuracy from 76.37% to 96.12% over forward log-linear attention across multiple training seeds. For pretrained language models under approximate parameter matching, it raises the mean score on six selected RULER needle-in-a-haystack tasks from 26.97% to 50.03% at a context length of 6144 tokens. In the same setting, bilateral attention also outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces bilateral log-linear attention, which pairs forward log-linear attention with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin to improve recall of both early and recent context.
AI.motivation: Forward log-linear attention allocates finer resolution near the current query while compressing earlier context into coarser summaries, which degrades long-range associative recall.
AI.method: The authors add a second causal log-linear hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin and derive recurrent and chunkwise parallel formulations that preserve log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic per-token decoding work, and logarithmic persistent state storage.
AI.result: On multi-query associative recall, bilateral log-linear attention raises mean overall test accuracy from 76.37% to 96.12% over forward log-linear attention; on six RULER needle-in-a-haystack tasks at 6144 tokens, it raises the mean score from 26.97% to 50.03% and outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks.
AI.conclusion: Bilateral log-linear attention provides finer access to both early and recent context while retaining the asymptotic efficiency of log-linear attention.

title: Large language models as oncology world models
comment: 63 pages (main text 35, Supplementary Information 28), 6 figures, 9 Extended Data figures. Code: this https URL. Data: this https URL
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can synthesize cancer patient cases, but their internal representation of oncology, or world model, has not been explored systematically. By only specifying tumor type, we show that LLMs tend to generate similar patients per cancer, with on average 81.0% to 93.2% of a cancer's patients sharing the most frequent value of each baseline feature. By systematically varying patient features in 12 clinical scenarios, we show that they follow biomarker and treatment logic in 29 of 36 model-scenario assessments, against 1 of 12 when previous treatment or frailty matters. Continuing real patient trajectories, an LLM predicted 89.9% 12-month survival, and 79.2% with similar patients as examples, against 72.2% observed. To represent these trajectories, we developed the Clinical State Space, a dynamic representation framework that we also applied to real patients. Despite the limits we show, improved world models may support digital twins, which our framework can evaluate.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates the internal oncology world models of large language models and introduces the Clinical State Space framework to represent patient trajectories.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs can synthesize cancer patient cases, their internal oncology representations and ability to reason over clinical trajectories have not been systematically evaluated.
AI.method: The authors test LLMs on tumor-type patient synthesis, 12 clinical scenarios with systematically varied patient features, and real patient trajectory continuation, while developing the Clinical State Space dynamic representation framework.
AI.result: When given only tumor type, LLMs generate repetitive patients with 81.0% to 93.2% sharing the most frequent baseline feature value; they follow biomarker and treatment logic in 29 of 36 assessments versus 1 of 12 when prior treatment or frailty matters, and predict 89.9% 12-month survival (79.2% with similar-patient examples) against 72.2% observed.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs exhibit clear gaps in clinical diversity and prior-treatment reasoning, but the Clinical State Space framework offers a structured way to evaluate future oncology digital twins.

title: Revealing the Biases of Large Language Models By Inferring Prior Distributions
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been known to exhibit a wide range of social biases including name-nationality associations, occupation-gender associations and racial stereotypes. Existing approaches to evaluating these biases typically involve measuring surface-level behavior where a model is fed a dataset of prompts and its outputs are scored relative to ground-truth answers. Inspired by prior elicitation in cognitive science, we propose a different perspective that reconstructs latent bias as a prior underlying the model's behavior. We formulate the problem as a Bayesian inverse problem where, given prompt-response observations on a bias benchmark dataset, we infer a low-dimensional latent distribution that summarizes the model's stereotyping tendencies. This paper develops the mathematical foundation, a practical reconstruction algorithm, and experiments using the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) benchmark to infer the prior distributions of LLMs over responses in ambiguous social contexts.

AI.tldr: This paper frames LLM social bias evaluation as a Bayesian inverse problem that infers a low-dimensional latent prior distribution underlying model responses.
AI.motivation: Existing bias evaluations measure surface-level prompt-response behavior against ground-truth answers rather than characterizing the latent stereotyping priors driving model outputs.
AI.method: Inspired by cognitive science prior elicitation, the authors formulate bias discovery as a Bayesian inverse problem and develop a practical reconstruction algorithm to infer latent prior distributions from prompt-response observations.
AI.result: The paper establishes the mathematical foundation, presents the reconstruction algorithm, and demonstrates its use on the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) dataset to infer LLM priors over responses in ambiguous social contexts.
AI.conclusion: Inferring latent prior distributions provides a principled, model-level view of LLM social biases beyond surface-level accuracy metrics.

title: AdaMenu: Query-Adaptive Menus for Decision Models over Large Label Spaces
summary: Decision models such as Jev return probabilities over caller-defined options and are increasingly used for classification. Large label spaces challenge both accuracy and scalability: larger menus can impair decisions, increase input costs, and exceed option limits. Hierarchical classification reduces menu size but introduces serial calls and error propagation. We propose AdaMenu, which builds a compact candidate menu from retrieved labeled examples and makes a single decision-model request. Its candidate labels adapt to the query, and its default setting also adjusts menu size using aggregated retrieval scores. We evaluate AdaMenu with open and closed decision models on four label sets containing up to 1,016 labels. It outperforms TypeSafe's beam-search baseline on all 16 model and label-set pairs where both methods run, improving accuracy by 16.6-34.3 percentage points. Relative to the full menu on the three smaller label sets, accuracy differences range from -0.5 to +7.2 percentage points, while input token usage falls by factors of 3.2-22.9. AdaMenu also runs when option limits exclude the full menu, including settings where the hierarchical baseline is unavailable.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes AdaMenu, a query-adaptive menu construction method for decision models over large label spaces that uses a single model request.
AI.motivation: Large label spaces degrade decision model accuracy, raise input token costs, and exceed option limits, while hierarchical classification introduces serial calls and error propagation.
AI.method: AdaMenu retrieves labeled examples to build a compact query-adaptive candidate menu, adjusts menu size using aggregated retrieval scores by default, and issues a single decision-model request.
AI.result: Evaluated on four label sets up to 1,016 labels, AdaMenu outperforms TypeSafe's beam-search baseline on all 16 runnable model-label pairs by 16.6 to 34.3 percentage points, and stays within -0.5 to +7.2 percentage points of the full menu on three smaller sets while reducing input tokens by 3.2x to 22.9x.
AI.conclusion: AdaMenu enables accurate, single-request decision-model classification in large label spaces where full menus or hierarchical baselines are costly or infeasible.

title: Advancing the Calibration-Compute Frontier of LLM Classifiers via Asymmetric Duos
summary: The importance of reliable uncertainty estimation in large language models (LLMs) has become increasingly pronounced, yet modern models remain poorly calibrated and frequently overconfident. In this study, we address this by proposing an efficient method for LLM classifier calibration using the Asymmetric Duos framework. Our approach combines a strong base model with a smaller sidekick model via logit-space fusion, utilizing global scaling parameters optimized on a validation set. Across diverse benchmarks, this Asymmetric LLM Duo consistently achieves best or second-best performance on expected calibration error and negative log-likelihood, without degrading predictive accuracy. More importantly, these gains are realized at a fraction of the computational cost of more complex baselines, placing our method on the calibration-compute Pareto frontier. We further demonstrate that our method acts orthogonal to various established calibration-aware techniques, meaning it can be easily combined with them to consistently boost their performance. Finally, our analysis of the logit-space behavior illustrates how asymmetric fusion successfully mitigates base model overconfidence. Overall, our findings demonstrate that the benefits of an asymmetric fusion successfully transfer to the language domain, providing a simple, highly cost-efficient approach to improving uncertainty estimation in LLM classifiers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Asymmetric Duos, a logit-space fusion framework pairing a strong base LLM with a smaller sidekick model to improve classifier calibration at low computational cost.
AI.motivation: Modern LLM classifiers are often poorly calibrated and overconfident, and existing calibration methods can be computationally expensive.
AI.method: Asymmetric Duos fuses the logits of a strong base model and a smaller sidekick model using global scaling parameters optimized on a validation set.
AI.result: Across diverse benchmarks, Asymmetric LLM Duos achieves best or second-best expected calibration error and negative log-likelihood without hurting accuracy, places on the calibration-compute Pareto frontier, and combines orthogonally with existing calibration-aware techniques.
AI.conclusion: Asymmetric logit-space fusion offers a simple, cost-efficient way to mitigate LLM overconfidence and improve uncertainty estimation.

title: The Critic Can Hurt: On the Safety of Critics in LLM-Guided AutoML Search
summary: LLM critics increasingly steer iterative search in agentic AutoML, prompt optimization, and self-refinement--evaluated for whether they help, but rarely for whether they can hurt. We isolate the critic's marginal effect through a four-arm audit and characterize the loop's tolerance through controlled fault injection. We show a naive 8B critic drives search below the no-critic random-search floor on 7 of 8 tabular datasets, losing up to 0.245 AUC in the worst case; the magnitude varies strongly with dataset, frontier, and budget. When: stronger critics attenuate the loss on the evaluated suite, without establishing a universal capability threshold. Why: controlled fault injection shows that non-directional errors are nearly costless under best-so-far search, whereas directional errors consume finite search opportunities; an idealized effective-sample calculation yields a necessary condition, $q(m-1) > \beta$, not a deployment certificate. How: a simple observable validation gate and a learned detector can reduce realized loss, but neither is guaranteed to preserve the full-budget no-critic baseline. We will release CRITFAULT, to our knowledge the first benchmark for detecting harmful critic feedback in AutoML. A critic is not a free addition: audit before trusting, and gate when capability or verification is insufficient.

AI.tldr: This paper audits LLM critics in iterative AutoML search and shows that weak or directionally biased critics can degrade performance below random search.
AI.motivation: LLM critics are widely used to steer iterative AutoML, prompt optimization, and self-refinement, but their potential to harm search has rarely been isolated or quantified.
AI.method: The authors conduct a four-arm audit to isolate marginal critic effects, perform controlled fault injection to characterize loop tolerance, derive an idealized necessary condition q(m-1) > beta, and release the CRITFAULT benchmark.
AI.result: A naive 8B critic performs worse than no-critic random search on 7 of 8 tabular datasets, losing up to 0.245 AUC; non-directional errors are nearly costless under best-so-far search whereas directional errors waste finite search opportunities, and neither a validation gate nor a learned detector guarantees preserving the no-critic baseline.
AI.conclusion: LLM critics are not a risk-free addition to AutoML loops and should be audited and gated before deployment.

title: Understanding the Role of Reasoning Data in Pretraining
summary: Reasoning data expose models to multi-step reasoning, but reasoning traces may cover only a subset of the available facts. How should pretraining balance atomic facts with reasoning traces? We study this question by constructing a setting in which every fact provides an atomic training signal, while only a subset appears in reasoning supervision, enabling us to measure generalization to transitions observed atomically but never used in training traces. For a linear transformer, we derive the weight assigned to atomic training signals that minimizes held-transition squared error and show that its leading-order optimum increases with reasoning-chain length and decreases with the fraction of facts held out from reasoning traces. These trends persist in a full transformer layer with an MLP, softmax attention, and cross-entropy loss. We further validate the role of reasoning complexity and data coverage in two natural-language settings: controlled multi-hop reasoning and mathematical pretraining. Together, our results provide a principled view of how reasoning-chain structure and data coverage should shape the allocation of training data during pretraining.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how pretraining should balance atomic facts and multi-step reasoning traces when only a subset of facts appears in reasoning supervision.
AI.motivation: Reasoning traces in pretraining data often cover only a fraction of available facts, leaving unclear how atomic fact supervision and reasoning data should be weighted.
AI.method: The authors construct a controlled setting measuring generalization to held-out transitions, derive the optimal atomic-signal weight minimizing held-transition squared error in a linear transformer, and test these trends in a full transformer layer as well as multi-hop reasoning and mathematical pretraining.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows the leading-order optimal atomic weight increases with reasoning-chain length and decreases with the fraction of facts held out from reasoning traces, and these trends persist in full transformer layers and natural-language experiments.
AI.conclusion: Optimal pretraining data allocation depends systematically on reasoning-chain complexity and fact coverage across reasoning traces.

title: A Fast Algorithm for the Familywise Loss
summary: The familywise (FW) loss for multiclass classification, introduced by Duchi, Ruan, and Khosravi, achieves universal equivalence to the 0-1 loss, and thus has stronger theoretical properties than cross entropy (CE). Prior work, however, left open whether FW is as computationally efficient as CE. First, on the theoretical side, we prove that the FW gradient can be computed in $O(K)$ time, where $K$ is the number of classes. Second, on the practical side, we develop optimized kernels for computing the forward and backward passes of FW which outperform CE in terms of speed on both CPU and GPU.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that the familywise (FW) loss gradient for multiclass classification can be computed in O(K) time and provides CPU/GPU kernels faster than cross entropy.
AI.motivation: Although the familywise loss achieves universal equivalence to 0-1 loss, prior work left open whether it could match the computational efficiency of cross entropy.
AI.method: The authors derive an O(K)-time algorithm for computing the FW gradient across K classes and implement optimized forward and backward kernels for both CPU and GPU.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis establishes O(K) gradient complexity, and empirical benchmarks show the optimized FW kernels outperform cross entropy in speed on both CPU and GPU.
AI.conclusion: The familywise loss can be computed faster than cross entropy in practice, removing its computational barrier to adoption.

title: Nahual: A Sequence Model for Language and Atoms
summary: Generative models play a rapidly growing role in the design and simulation of molecules. The most widely used applications of generative models are in large language models (LLMs), owing to the natural flexibility of language for specifying and answering queries. However, generalist LLMs do not effectively handle large sets of 3D coordinates, whereas specialist generative models of 3D molecules cannot reach the controllability afforded by language. To bridge these capabilities, we propose Nahual, a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for any sequence of text and 3D molecules. To enable expressive autoregression on continuous coordinates, we propose next-token diffusion, whereby a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to the clean tokens before it, without increasing context size. We train Nahual on a curated set of twelve 3D chemistry tasks ranging from microsolvation to molecular conformer search to adsorption on metal surfaces, with associated evaluation metrics and baselines. The result is a single set of end-to-end-trained weights that simultaneously performs all tasks and surpasses state-of-the-art models specialized for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation. Our results demonstrate the viability of scaling generalist decoder-only models for native multimodal understanding and generation across language and chemistry. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Nahual, a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model that unifies text and 3D molecular coordinates in a single sequence model.
AI.motivation: Generalist LLMs struggle with large sets of continuous 3D coordinates, while specialist 3D molecular generative models lack the natural-language controllability of LLMs.
AI.method: Nahual introduces next-token diffusion, where a causal transformer denoises each continuous coordinate token while attending to clean preceding tokens without expanding context length, trained end-to-end on twelve 3D chemistry tasks.
AI.result: A single set of Nahual weights performs all twelve tasks simultaneously and surpasses specialized state-of-the-art models on crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation.
AI.conclusion: Next-token diffusion enables generalist decoder-only models to natively understand and generate across both language and 3D chemistry.

title: DynaDFlash: Dynamic Feature Projection for Block Diffusion Speculators
comment: Code and trained models available at this https URL
summary: DFlash trains a parallel draft model on hidden features from its target model. Inspired by the previous work of DFlare that introduced per layer combinations of target hidden states, we test whether context dependent weighting of these states helps improve acceptance length of block diffusion speculators. We trained both a DFlash baseline for the Qwen 3 of block size 16, and a dynamic model that computes gates for each layer to affect the magnitude of hidden features before projection. While mean acceptance length between the dynamic model and the DFlash baseline didn't significantly differ, we notice that the dynamic model excels for drafting in the context of math. In an evaluation of 700 prompts from the MetaMathQA and Orca-Math datasets, the mean accepted length improves by 5%. We also found this lead to a 4.1% higher throughput for a subset of the same dataset in the context of speculative decoding.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DynaDFlash, which adds context-dependent gating to layer-wise target hidden features in block diffusion speculators, improving math speculative decoding.
AI.motivation: DFlash trains parallel draft models on target hidden features, but it is unclear whether context-dependent weighting of per-layer hidden states improves acceptance length.
AI.method: The authors train a DFlash baseline for Qwen 3 (block size 16) and a dynamic variant that computes per-layer gates to scale hidden features before projection.
AI.result: While overall mean acceptance length does not differ significantly, on 700 prompts from MetaMathQA and Orca-Math the dynamic model improves mean accepted length by 5% and increases throughput by 4.1% on a evaluated subset.
AI.conclusion: Context-dependent layer gating offers targeted gains for block diffusion speculators in mathematical reasoning tasks.

title: Knowledge-Guided Local-to-Global Anomaly Learning for Longitudinal Medication Trajectories
summary: Detecting suspicious deviations in longitudinal medication trajectories requires distinguishing knowledge-consistent treatment variations from anomalous changes and linking local deviations to account-level decisions. We propose a knowledge-guided local-to-global (L2G) anomaly learning framework that addresses both challenges. It constructs proxy supervision at three granularities: medication occurrences, treatment episodes, and contiguous visit segments. Knowledge-consistent medication and episode replacements provide plausible negatives, while cross-category and cross-account perturbations provide suspicious proxies. A medication-multiset encoder and causal visit-sequence encoder feed a shared scoring head that produces visit-level anomaly logits. Top-\(\alpha\) aggregation derives account-level scores from these logits, while account-level classification and class-balanced visit-localization objectives jointly optimize the same visit-level evidence. Experiments on two city cohorts compare L2G with native and proxy-adapted anomaly methods. On City-A, L2G outperforms the strongest comparators. Cross-city results show more consistent gains in localization than in account-level detection.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a knowledge-guided local-to-global (L2G) anomaly learning framework for detecting suspicious deviations in longitudinal medication trajectories.
AI.motivation: Detecting medication anomalies requires separating knowledge-consistent treatment variations from genuine anomalies and linking visit-level deviations to account-level decisions.
AI.method: L2G constructs multi-granularity proxy supervision using knowledge-consistent replacements as negatives and cross-category or cross-account perturbations as suspicious proxies, feeding a medication-multiset encoder, causal visit-sequence encoder, and top-alpha aggregation head trained jointly on account classification and visit localization.
AI.result: Across two city cohorts, L2G outperforms strong native and proxy-adapted baselines on City-A, while cross-city evaluations show more consistent gains in visit-level localization than in account-level detection.
AI.conclusion: Combining knowledge-guided proxy supervision with joint local-to-global optimization improves anomaly localization in longitudinal medication data.

title: Empowering Masked Diffusion Models to Self-Correct with Leave-One-Out Transformers
summary: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for language modeling, enabling parallel token generation with competitive performance. Yet standard MDMs suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) inability to revise tokens, and (2) sparse training signal. We revisit hollow transformers, which address both limitations by predicting each token from its surrounding context, independently of the input at that position. We introduce the Leave-One-Out Transformer (LOOT), a more efficient and expressive architecture that advances hollow transformers through two complementary advances. First, we redesign the merging mechanism to enable frequent interaction between left and right contexts, substantially improving predictive performance over prior hollow transformers. Second, we derive a lower-variance estimator of the MDM NELBO that supervises all tokens and improves validation perplexity. Together, these advances yield a competitive standalone diffusion language model capable of effective self-correction during inference. On LM1B, LOOT matches the strongest dense-supervision MDM baseline in validation perplexity. On OpenWebText, LOOT achieves higher MAUVE and better generation quality-diversity tradeoffs than prior remasking methods, using $8\times$ fewer forward evaluations and $3.5\times$ fewer inference FLOPs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Leave-One-Out Transformer (LOOT), an architecture and lower-variance training objective that enables masked diffusion language models to self-correct during inference.
AI.motivation: Standard masked diffusion models cannot revise already-generated tokens and suffer from sparse training signals.
AI.method: LOOT advances hollow transformers by redesigning the left-right context merging mechanism for frequent interaction and deriving a lower-variance MDM NELBO estimator that supervises all tokens.
AI.result: On LM1B, LOOT matches the strongest dense-supervision MDM baseline in validation perplexity; on OpenWebText, it achieves higher MAUVE and better quality-diversity tradeoffs than prior remasking methods using 8x fewer forward evaluations and 3.5x fewer inference FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: LOOT makes masked diffusion language models capable of efficient, standalone self-correction at reduced inference cost.

title: How Much Determinism Can Fine-Tuning Buy? Margin Regularisation Against Batch-Induced Token Flips
summary: Greedy decoding at zero temperature is widely assumed to be deterministic, although the exact same prompt may yield different tokens depending on the number of other prompts sharing the batch for inference. The currently available solutions operate during inference, trading determinism for throughput. Can we train a model in such a way that fewer decoding steps would be susceptible? We characterize the perturbation empirically across six model families and three numerical precisions and observe two empirical facts about the measurement: the perturbation depends exactly on the representable precision (8.00x for bfloat16 vs float16, 8192.0x for float16 vs float32, in line with predictions based on mantissa bits) and the batch invariance happens accidentally at certain tensor shapes, allowing a practitioner to achieve zero nondeterminism merely by setting the sequence length. Then we apply hinge penalization of the model's top-1 / top-2 logit gap, scaled to twice the measured noise quantile. On GSM8K dataset it leads to a 35% reduction in token flips and divergence from 53.8% to 38.1%, at the cost of 1.3 - 2.9 accuracy points, increasing monotonically with the margin size. It does not affect the gap threshold sufficient for determinism: the logit gaps of surviving flips are unchanged (median 0.125 for all arms), as the hinge is a soft penalty and the largest hardware perturbation remains the same. We reject seven hypotheses, including a per-model viability diagnosis, holding on six models and falsified on the seventh.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes batch-induced nondeterminism in greedy LLM decoding and evaluates hinge margin regularization during fine-tuning as a mitigation.
AI.motivation: Greedy decoding at zero temperature can still produce different tokens depending on batch size, and existing inference-time fixes trade throughput for determinism.
AI.method: The authors measure floating-point perturbations across six model families and three precisions, then fine-tune with a hinge penalty on the top-1/top-2 logit gap scaled to twice the measured noise quantile.
AI.result: Perturbations scale with mantissa precision (8.00x for bfloat16 vs float16, 8192.0x for float16 vs float32); on GSM8K, margin regularization cuts token flips by 35% and divergence from 53.8% to 38.1% at a cost of 1.3 to 2.9 accuracy points, without altering the median logit gap of surviving flips (0.125).
AI.conclusion: Margin regularization reduces batch-induced token flips at a modest accuracy cost, though it cannot eliminate rare large hardware perturbations.

title: LogT: Logically Think with Images for Visual Search
summary: Thinking with images empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to use an external Zoom-in tool for fine-grained visual search. Recent works employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) with tool-specific designs to enable such capabilities. However, achieving logical reasoning alongside accurate and efficient tool use remains a significant challenge. To address this, we shift the focus away from increasing RL complexity and instead identify SFT data quality as a key bottleneck. We then propose LogT (short for Logically Think with Images), a fully automated SFT data engine that explicitly enforces logic-chain-guided reasoning. LogT generates an SFT dataset featuring challenging, visually grounded questions and structured tool-use traces with human-like logic. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two base models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B, on the dataset and evaluating them across seven benchmark test sets. We show that LogT-SFT based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforms the state-of-the-art trained with both SFT and RL, despite using 3.1$\times$ less data and $>120\times$ fewer GPU hours. Furthermore, applying a simple RL recipe without tool-specific design on LogT-SFT yields a model that surpasses prior methods with complex RL setups by a substantial 9.59-point margin. In addition to strong performance gains, our model exhibits higher tool-use accuracy and efficiency, as well as more structured and logically consistent reasoning traces, directly validating the effectiveness of our approach.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LogT, an automated SFT data engine that generates logic-chain-guided visual search traces to improve VLM tool use without complex RL.
AI.motivation: Enabling vision-language models to use external Zoom-in tools for logical visual search remains challenging, with recent work relying heavily on complex RL designs.
AI.method: LogT automatically constructs an SFT dataset of visually grounded questions paired with structured, human-like logic-chain tool-use traces, used to fine-tune Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks, LogT-SFT on Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforms prior SFT+RL state-of-the-art using 3.1x less data and over 120x fewer GPU hours, and adding a simple RL recipe yields a further 9.59-point gain over complex RL baselines.
AI.conclusion: High-quality logic-guided SFT data is a primary bottleneck for visual search tool use, outperforming complex RL setups at a fraction of the compute.

title: On-policy distillation as a Backdoor Propagation Channel
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for the post training of large language models, improving student models by leveraging supervision generated online by teacher models. However, whether this process also transfers latent security risks from teacher models to student models remains insufficiently studied. In this work, we reveal a new security risk in which an attacker first implants a conditional backdoor into the teacher model through supervised fine tuning (SFT), after which OPD can transfer the backdoor to the student model with only an extremely small proportion of trigger prompt exposure. More concerningly, we find that such backdoor transfer is substantially stronger under OPD than under conventional distillation methods, suggesting that OPD may provide an efficient channel for propagating backdoors across models. Our mechanistic analysis shows that the backdoor signal is primarily transmitted through anomalous differences in the conditional probabilities produced by the teacher model for triggered and clean inputs, and is gradually internalized into the internal representations of the student model during training. Furthermore, we investigate how to suppress such anomalous conditional probability signals at the source of distillation supervision and, based on this analysis, propose an OPD training method tailored to this conditional backdoor propagation setting to mitigate the risk of backdoor transfer induced by untrusted teacher supervision.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that on-policy distillation (OPD) efficiently propagates conditional backdoors from teacher LLMs to students and proposes a mitigation method.
AI.motivation: While OPD improves student models via online teacher supervision, its potential to transfer latent security backdoors from untrusted teachers has not been adequately studied.
AI.method: The authors implant a conditional backdoor into a teacher via SFT, analyze how OPD transfers it through anomalous conditional probability differences between triggered and clean inputs, and propose an OPD training method that suppresses these anomalous signals at the supervision source.
AI.result: OPD transfers conditional backdoors to student models with only minimal trigger prompt exposure and substantially more strongly than conventional distillation, while the proposed suppression-based OPD method mitigates this transfer.
AI.conclusion: On-policy distillation poses a heightened backdoor propagation risk from untrusted teachers, requiring source-level supervision defenses.

title: Neural Dual Bounds: Valid-by-Construction JGLP Warm-Starts for MAP and Constrained MAP
summary: We present Neural Dual Bounds, a calibration-free framework that produces deterministic upper bounds for MAP inference in probabilistic graphical models using a single neural-network forward pass. The framework trains a network to output the edge messages of a mini-bucket style upper bound on a given join-graph decomposition in a self-supervised manner by directly minimizing a smooth dual objective. The output of this network can be used at test time to warm-start a standard JGLP optimizer. Across diverse benchmarks, this warm start yields dual gaps that are orders of magnitude tighter than those from zero initialization, with the largest gains in the early-iteration regime. We also apply our framework for the constrained MAP (CMPE) task, where neural warm starts with test-time adaptation are comparable to the adaptive baseline on Bayesian networks and achieve the tightest dual gaps, by one to two orders of magnitude, on the grid and segmentation families.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Neural Dual Bounds, a self-supervised framework that predicts valid mini-bucket edge messages in a single forward pass to warm-start JGLP for MAP and constrained MAP inference.
AI.motivation: Obtaining tight upper bounds for MAP inference in probabilistic graphical models typically requires many iterative message-passing steps from zero initialization.
AI.method: A neural network is trained self-supervisedly to minimize a smooth dual objective and output edge messages for a join-graph decomposition, providing deterministic upper bounds and warm-starts for a standard JGLP optimizer.
AI.result: Across diverse benchmarks, neural warm-starts yield dual gaps orders of magnitude tighter than zero initialization in early iterations, and on constrained MAP (CMPE) they match adaptive baselines on Bayesian networks while achieving 1 to 2 orders of magnitude tighter gaps on grids and segmentation.
AI.conclusion: Single-pass neural dual predictions provide calibration-free, valid-by-construction warm-starts that substantially accelerate graphical model MAP inference.

title: Learning Graph-Conditioned Predictors in Weight Space
summary: The same node attributes can imply different labels in different structural contexts. Yet fast graphless models typically treat topology as additional evidence supplied to a globally shared predictor. This assumes that structure augments the available information, rather than determining how node attributes should be interpreted. We introduce SCOPE (Structure-COnditioned PrEdictor), in which a small generator maps each node's cached structural fingerprint to coefficients over a shared low-rank basis, producing a context-specific update to a global weight matrix. The base predictor, basis, and generator remain shared across all nodes, while the resulting transformation adapts how attributes are processed in each relational environment. Once fingerprints are cached, inference requires only a forward pass and no online message passing. This design combines context-specific specialization with global parameter sharing, compact low-rank adaptation, and message-passing-free inference. On two large OGB node-classification graphs, conditioning the weights with raw positional signals yields clear gains over supplying the same signals through input concatenation. Further results under a structure-transductive held-out-node protocol and in teacher-free graph classification show that the mechanism extends beyond a particular distillation setting. These findings establish graph structure not only as predictive evidence, but as context that determines the predictor used to interpret that evidence.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SCOPE, a graphless predictor that maps each node's cached structural fingerprint to low-rank weight updates on a shared base predictor.
AI.motivation: Fast graphless models usually concatenate topology features to node inputs, treating structure as extra evidence rather than context that determines how attributes should be interpreted.
AI.method: SCOPE uses a shared generator to map cached structural fingerprints into coefficients over a shared low-rank basis, producing context-specific weight updates to a global weight matrix with message-passing-free inference.
AI.result: On two large OGB node-classification graphs, conditioning weights with raw positional signals outperforms input concatenation, and gains generalize to a structure-transductive held-out-node protocol and teacher-free graph classification.
AI.conclusion: Graph structure is more effective when used to condition predictor weights rather than merely appended as input features.

title: ReCALM: A Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism for Distributed Continual Service Construction
summary: Crowdsourcing has emerged as a promising paradigm for constructing AI services by harnessing the collective capabilities of distributed workers. As consumers' demands continually evolve, service models must acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned information. However, due to the inherited reliance on gradients for backpropagation, existing approaches typically suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual model updates on heterogeneous data. Recent studies have introduced analytic learning, a gradient-free paradigm that achieves invariance through recursive closed-form solutions. Nevertheless, existing analytic methods are typically constrained by single-layer linear networks, which tend to suffer from underfitting due to their inability to perform deep representation learning. To address this issue, we propose ReCALM, a Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism that achieves deep nonlinear invariance for distributed continual service construction. Inspired by the success of ResNet, we develop gradient-free residual blocks for ReCALM with closed-form solutions. To implement distributed continual training for ReCALM, we further devise a cross-recursive strategy via least squares. Both theoretical and experimental analyses verify ReCALM's dual superiority in heterogeneity invariance and deep representation. With 20 residual layers, ReCALM improves accuracy by 8.85%-9.83% over the single-layer analytic baseline, while reducing computational costs by over 94% compared with gradient-based baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ReCALM, a gradient-free residual analytic learning mechanism for distributed continual service construction that avoids catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: Gradient-based continual learning suffers from catastrophic forgetting on heterogeneous data, while existing single-layer analytic learning methods underfit due to limited representation capacity.
AI.method: ReCALM introduces gradient-free residual blocks with closed-form solutions inspired by ResNet, paired with a cross-recursive least-squares strategy for distributed continual training.
AI.result: With 20 residual layers, ReCALM improves accuracy by 8.85% to 9.83% over the single-layer analytic baseline while cutting computational costs by over 94% compared to gradient-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: ReCALM combines deep nonlinear representation with gradient-free heterogeneity invariance for efficient distributed continual learning.

title: Where Mixture Recognition Fails: An Ingredient-Level Audit of Unseen Combinations in SmellNet
summary: An electronic nose must name every ingredient of a mixture, including combinations it has never measured. SmellNet, a public benchmark for this task, scores ingredients with a hit rate that is told how many each sample contains. We audit what this protocol hides. We hold out ingredient combinations from the SmellNet training data, evaluate four architectures (MLP, CNN, LSTM and a Transformer encoder) without revealing the ingredient count, and repeat the evaluation once on the official unseen split. Under the count-informed protocol, 90-96% of mixtures receive an ingredient that is absent, on our folds and on the official split alike. On our folds, every model identifies one ingredient reliably but the second rarely, and it completes the pair with a familiar training partner about twice as often as chance. On the official split, even the first-ranked ingredient is correct in only 29-46% of binary mixtures, often because a frequent training ingredient that is absent from every test pair is ranked first, and on its combinations that are truly absent from training no model names both ingredients in more than 1.2% of them. The failures fall on the same ingredients for every architecture, and a frequency correction only moves errors between ingredients. Mixture recognition is therefore limited by ingredients the models cannot separate and by a preference for frequent ingredients, not by the architecture, and it should be evaluated with set-level errors and without oracle cardinality.

AI.tldr: This paper audits electronic-nose mixture recognition on SmellNet without oracle ingredient counts and shows that models fail on unseen combinations due to ingredient inseparability and frequency bias.
AI.motivation: SmellNet's default evaluation reveals the number of ingredients in each mixture, potentially masking severe generalization failures on unseen ingredient combinations.
AI.method: The authors hold out ingredient combinations from SmellNet training data, evaluate MLP, CNN, LSTM, and Transformer models without oracle cardinality, and repeat the evaluation on the official unseen split.
AI.result: Under the count-informed protocol, 90% to 96% of mixtures receive an absent ingredient; without counts, models name both ingredients in at most 1.2% of truly unseen combinations on the official split, and first-ranked accuracy is only 29% to 46% on binary mixtures due to frequent training ingredients dominating predictions.
AI.conclusion: Mixture recognition is bottlenecked by inseparable ingredients and frequency bias rather than architecture, and should be evaluated with set-level metrics without oracle cardinality.

title: NetBreaker: Benchmarking Network Dismantling across Objectives, Scales, and Toplogoies
summary: Network dismantling seeks to fragment a network with as few node removals as possible, which is widely applied in vulnerability analysis, epidemic containment, and infrastructure protection. Although learning-based methods have become increasingly prominent, their progress remains difficult to assess because existing studies differ in method coverage, datasets, evaluation criteria, and experimental protocols. Thus, we introduce NetBreaker, a comprehensive benchmark designed for the learning era of network dismantling. NetBreaker organizes 30 methods (18 non-learning and 12 learning-based) under a common taxonomy and evaluates them on 185 networks from eight unified domains, ranging from 14 to 1.69 million nodes. To enable fair comparison, heterogeneous method outputs are converted into node removal sequences and assessed under a unified execution protocol. The evaluation covers four complementary dimensions: target-based effectiveness, trajectory-based effectiveness, structural diagnostics, and applicability & computational efficiency. Extensive experiments show that current learningbased methods do not consistently outperform strong non-learning approaches, while exposing substantial differences in effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency across network conditions and evaluation perspectives. NetBreaker provides a reproducible basis for measuring progress and developing reliable, scalable, and computationally efficient network dismantling methods.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces NetBreaker, a unified benchmark evaluating 30 network dismantling methods across 185 networks and four evaluation dimensions.
AI.motivation: Progress in learning-based network dismantling is hard to measure because prior studies use inconsistent datasets, method sets, evaluation criteria, and protocols.
AI.method: NetBreaker standardizes 18 non-learning and 12 learning-based methods into node removal sequences and evaluates them across 185 networks (14 to 1.69M nodes) on target-based effectiveness, trajectory-based effectiveness, structural diagnostics, and efficiency.
