AI.result: Extensive experiments reveal that current learning-based methods do not consistently outperform strong non-learning approaches and expose large differences in scalability and efficiency across network conditions.
AI.conclusion: NetBreaker provides a reproducible benchmark for developing scalable and genuinely superior network dismantling algorithms.

title: Does Lifestyle Information Improve Hypertension Prediction? A Leakage-Controlled Evaluation on NHANES
comment: Accepted to the Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026 Symposium, Findings Track. Code: this https URL
summary: Does readily available lifestyle information improve machine-learning prediction of hypertension beyond routine demographic and anthropometric data? On NHANES 2017-March 2020, five model families (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Bagged Decision Trees, and XGBoost) were evaluated with fold-local preprocessing and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. Adding physical activity, alcohol use, smoking, and sleep information showed no consistent detectable improvement in held-out discrimination: every paired ROC-AUC confidence interval included zero, including under a stricter measured-blood-pressure phenotype and without synthetic oversampling. Mean cross-model SHAP rank agreement fell from 0.873 to 0.806 over all encoded columns, but this decline was largely attenuated over the 19 baseline columns shared by both arms (0.873 vs. 0.863), and likewise under both robustness checks; attribution-agreement comparisons across feature sets of different sizes therefore require a matched comparison space. In exploratory analysis of untreated adults (measured-blood-pressure outcome), all five models showed small positive differences, two with unadjusted intervals excluding zero, meriting confirmation. These results do not imply that lifestyle factors are clinically unimportant; within this cohort, the evaluated lifestyle block added little incremental discrimination beyond an already-informative baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a leakage-controlled evaluation on NHANES and finds that adding lifestyle features yields no consistent improvement in hypertension prediction over demographic and anthropometric baselines.
AI.motivation: It remains unclear whether self-reported lifestyle data improves machine-learning hypertension prediction beyond routine demographic and anthropometric measurements when data leakage is strictly controlled.
AI.method: On NHANES 2017-March 2020, five model families (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Bagged Decision Trees, XGBoost) are evaluated with fold-local preprocessing, paired bootstrap confidence intervals, and matched-column SHAP rank agreement.
AI.result: Every paired ROC-AUC confidence interval for adding physical activity, alcohol, smoking, and sleep included zero; cross-model SHAP rank agreement dropped from 0.873 to 0.806 across all columns but remained similar (0.873 vs. 0.863) over the 19 shared baseline columns.
AI.conclusion: Within this cohort, the evaluated lifestyle features add little incremental discrimination beyond baseline features, and feature-attribution comparisons across differently sized feature sets require matched comparison spaces.

title: A Backdoor Trigger Is Legible in Fine-Tune Weights
summary: A backdoored language model behaves normally until a trigger phrase appears in its input. Every published method for recovering such a trigger runs the model. We show the trigger is legible in the weights alone: a static statistic reads a fine-tuned checkpoint with no forward pass of the suspect, no data, no labelled population of poisoned models and no prior knowledge that a backdoor exists, and names one of the tokens of the trigger phrase as the single highest-ranked candidate in the vocabulary.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that a backdoor trigger in a fine-tuned language model can be recovered directly from the weights using a static statistic without running the model.
AI.motivation: All prior methods for recovering backdoor triggers in language models require executing forward passes on the suspect model.
AI.method: The authors compute a static statistic directly from a fine-tuned checkpoint with no forward passes, no data, no population of poisoned models, and no prior knowledge of a backdoor.
AI.result: The static weight-based statistic identifies one of the trigger phrase tokens as the single highest-ranked candidate in the vocabulary.
AI.conclusion: Backdoor triggers leave legible signatures in fine-tuned model weights that can be detected purely statically.

title: Gradient-Based Co-Design of Systems and Reinforcement Learning Policies with Differentiable Simulators
summary: Co-design is the problem of jointly optimizing the design of a system and the policy that operates it. Neither can be chosen independently: a system design is only as good as the policy trained for it, and the optimal policy changes with the design. When that policy is learned by reinforcement learning (RL), evaluating a candidate design requires a full policy training run, and the design is usually optimized by black-box search such as Bayesian optimization (BO) or evolution strategies (ES). These methods scale poorly with the design dimension and ignore the differentiable structure of modern simulators and, in particular, the sensitivity of the optimal policy with respect to the design. We instead derive a gradient-based co-design method, where the design gradient decomposes into a direct effect of changing the design at a fixed policy and an indirect effect through the design-dependent optimal policy. The indirect effect requires the sensitivity of the converged policy to the design, which we obtain by applying the implicit function theorem to the stationarity condition of the policy gradient. Based on this sensitivity, we develop a proof-of-concept co-design algorithm with stochastic value gradient (SVG)-style policy optimization, prove that it converges to an approximately stationary design, and demonstrate on a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional design spaces that it consistently outperforms BO and ES.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a gradient-based co-design method for jointly optimizing physical systems and RL policies using differentiable simulators and the implicit function theorem.
AI.motivation: Black-box co-design methods like Bayesian optimization and evolution strategies scale poorly with design dimension and ignore simulator differentiability and policy sensitivity.
AI.method: The authors decompose the design gradient into a direct effect and an indirect effect via optimal-policy sensitivity obtained from the implicit function theorem on policy-gradient stationarity, implemented in an SVG-style co-design algorithm.
AI.result: The paper proves convergence to an approximately stationary design and shows on a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional design spaces that the method consistently outperforms BO and ES.
AI.conclusion: Differentiable co-design with implicit policy gradients enables scalable joint optimization of high-dimensional systems and RL controllers.

title: Benchmarking the State of AI for Crop Yield Forecasting: A Global Assessment Across Modeling Paradigms
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in Proceedings of the 33rd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD '27), August 2027, San Jose, CA, USA. Code is available at this https URL and an interactive results dashboard is available at this https URL
summary: Accurate crop yield forecasting is essential for food security, agricultural policy, and commodity markets. Although statistical, process-based, and machine learning approaches have all been proposed, their relative strengths remain poorly understood due to the lack of large-scale, standardized comparisons. We address this gap through a comprehensive benchmark of five modeling paradigms -- statistical baselines, process-based models, conventional feature-engineered machine learning, deep sequence models, and tabular foundation models -- using the CY-Bench benchmark spanning 63 country-crop datasets (>12,000 administrative regions) across six continents. Beyond conventional pooled accuracy metrics, we introduce a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that separately quantifies overall, spatial, temporal, and anomaly prediction skill. Across multiple crops and countries, feature-engineered machine learning and tabular foundation models achieve the strongest overall predictive performance. Data-driven models reduce NRMSE in 72% of countries growing maize and 78% of countries growing wheat, with median reductions of 8.8% and 11.9%, respectively. Across all modeling paradigms, spatial prediction is substantially easier than temporal and anomaly prediction. While data-driven models markedly improve temporal and anomaly prediction over statistical baselines, accurately forecasting year-to-year yield variability remains challenging. These findings suggest that future progress in large-scale crop yield forecasting will depend on the improved characterization of the environmental and management factors driving inter-annual yield variability, founded on effective representations for crop yield forecasting systems that support agricultural decision-making, early-warning applications, and food security planning

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks five crop yield forecasting paradigms across 63 country-crop datasets in CY-Bench and finds that feature-engineered ML and tabular foundation models perform best overall.
AI.motivation: The relative strengths of statistical, process-based, and machine learning models for crop yield forecasting remain unclear due to a lack of standardized global comparisons.
AI.method: Using CY-Bench (>12,000 administrative regions across six continents), the authors evaluate statistical baselines, process-based models, feature-engineered ML, deep sequence models, and tabular foundation models across overall, spatial, temporal, and anomaly skill.
AI.result: Feature-engineered ML and tabular foundation models achieve the strongest overall skill, reducing NRMSE in 72% of maize-growing countries (median 8.8%) and 78% of wheat-growing countries (median 11.9%), though temporal and anomaly prediction remain much harder than spatial prediction.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven tabular models lead current crop yield forecasting, but improving inter-annual variability prediction requires better representations of environmental and management drivers.

title: SMELL: Sparsity-aware Memory Efficient Federated Fine-tuning for Long-context LLMs
summary: Federated fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to collaboratively adapt to distributed private data. However, long-context fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices faces substantial challenges arising from excessive activation memory, heterogeneous token-importance patterns across clients, and communication overhead. To address these challenges, we propose SMELL, a Sparsity-aware and Memory-Efficient federated fine-tuning framework for Long-context LLMs. SMELL integrates three complementary mechanisms: Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation (LSFA), Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination (CASC), and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery (CPUR). These mechanisms jointly enable memory-efficient local adaptation, heterogeneity-aware sparsity coordination, and lightweight model-update transmission. Experiments on OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B demonstrate that SMELL reduces peak memory consumption by up to 88.35% compared with conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% compared with forward-only LoRA fine-tuning at a 16K context length. Furthermore, SMELL improves fine-tuning performance under certain non-IID settings and supports compact update transmission with progressive reconstruction, demonstrating its potential for resource-efficient federated long-context LLM adaptation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SMELL, a sparsity-aware federated fine-tuning framework that cuts activation memory and communication overhead for long-context LLMs.
AI.motivation: Federated fine-tuning of long-context LLMs on resource-constrained devices is bottlenecked by activation memory, heterogeneous client token-importance patterns, and communication costs.
AI.method: SMELL combines Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation (LSFA), Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination (CASC), and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery (CPUR).
AI.result: On OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B at 16K context length, SMELL reduces peak memory by up to 88.35% over conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% over forward-only LoRA, while improving performance under certain non-IID settings.
AI.conclusion: Sparsity-aware coordination and progressive update recovery make long-context federated LLM fine-tuning feasible on memory-limited devices.

title: $β$-number and Its Applications to Data Science
summary: In this paper, we introduce a novel metric, $\beta$-number, designed to measure the "$p$-th order $d$-dimensional oscillation degree" of a set. For a given set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, $\beta$-number is computed by identifying an optimal $d$-dimensional plane $L$ that minimizes the average $p$-th order distance of all points in $K$ to $L$. This metric serves as a versatile tool in data science, functioning both as a dimensionality reduction technique to find the optimal $p$-th order $d$-dimensional subspace and as a measure to characterize data oscillation for classification. We conduct a thorough exploration of $\beta$-number through theoretical analysis and numerical experiments. Initially, we establish the upper and lower bounds of $\beta$-number for any set $K$, along with its scaling law. We then elucidate the relationships between $\beta$-number and its related parameters. A key finding of this study is that in discrete settings, when $p=2$, the $d$-dimensional plane determined by $\beta$-number coincides with that obtained via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), positioning $\beta$-number as a generalization of PCA. Furthermore, we propose two algorithms for calculating $\beta$-number in both continuous and discrete settings. We validate our theoretical results through a series of numerical experiments in low-dimensional cases. Finally, we demonstrate the potential of $\beta$-number in practical data analysis through a dimensionality reduction task and an image classification task.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the beta-number metric to quantify the p-th order d-dimensional oscillation degree of a set and connects it to PCA as a generalization.
AI.motivation: Data science tasks need versatile geometric metrics that both find optimal lower-dimensional subspaces and characterize data oscillation for classification.
AI.method: The authors define the beta-number via the optimal d-dimensional plane minimizing average p-th order distance, establish theoretical bounds and scaling laws, and propose continuous and discrete computation algorithms.
AI.result: In discrete settings with p=2, the optimal plane coincides with Principal Component Analysis (PCA); numerical experiments validate the theory and demonstrate utility on dimensionality reduction and image classification.
AI.conclusion: The beta-number generalizes PCA to arbitrary p-th order norms and provides a unified tool for subspace estimation and oscillation-based classification.

title: Test-Time Constraint-Aware Diffusion Predictive Control
summary: Diffusion models can learn multimodal distributions over finite-horizon state-input sequences, providing a way to generate candidates for predictive control. However, sequences generated by a pretrained model may violate safety constraints introduced at deployment, for example when obstacles are added or repositioned. Retraining whenever these constraints change limits the usefulness of learned predictive controllers. In this paper, we propose Test-Time Constraint-Aware Diffusion Predictive Control (TCA-DPC), an algorithm for adapting the sampling distribution of a pretrained diffusion controller to newly introduced safety constraints without retraining. We treat the pretrained model as a prior over finite-horizon sequences and define an adapted distribution through exponential tilting based on a constraint-violation penalty. The tilt strength is adjusted online using the fraction of generated sequences that fail constraint verification. We approximately sample the adapted distribution using the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm in the Gaussian noise space of the pretrained diffusion sampler.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Test-Time Constraint-Aware Diffusion Predictive Control (TCA-DPC) to adapt pretrained diffusion controllers to new safety constraints without retraining.
AI.motivation: Pretrained diffusion predictive controllers can violate newly introduced deployment-time safety constraints such as moved obstacles, and retraining for every constraint change is impractical.
AI.method: TCA-DPC treats the pretrained diffusion model as a prior, defines an exponentially tilted target distribution using a constraint-violation penalty with online-adjusted tilt strength, and samples via MALA in the Gaussian noise space.
AI.result: The algorithm adapts the sampling distribution of a pretrained diffusion controller to new safety constraints at test time without any model retraining.
AI.conclusion: Noise-space MALA sampling over an exponentially tilted prior enables flexible, retraining-free constraint adaptation for diffusion predictive control.

title: Revisiting What Makes a Good Context Subset: A Sparse Latent Basis Perspective
comment: 17 pages, 2 figures. The format of ACL rolling review
summary: Selecting context subsets is increasingly important in modern LLM inference, yet what makes a subset effective remains unclear. We study this question in the controlled setting of few-shot demonstration selection. We examine a hypothesis that demonstrations should collectively provide task-relevant information needed by a target query. Assuming that the query representation provides a useful proxy for these requirements, we formulate selection as sparse reconstruction and instantiate it with Residual Explanation Search (RES), a Matching-Pursuit-style diagnostic procedure. Across seven benchmarks and eight open-weight LLMs, no retrieval objective is universally best. RES outperforms MMR in 34 of 56 model--dataset pairs, with its clearest advantage on sentiment tasks, suggesting that query-conditioned collective reconstruction may capture useful complementarity that pairwise dissimilarity misses. Relevance-based retrieval remains strong on template-heavy reasoning benchmarks, while all retrieval methods underperform zero-shot prediction on average on StrategyQA, where a solution-reconstruction analysis is consistent with the query not exposing the required external knowledge. Target-model hidden states further show that retrieval objectives interact differently with representation spaces: middle-layer representations generally favor similarity retrieval, whereas last-layer representations are often stronger for residual- and diversity-based selection. These findings support a conditional, representation-dependent account of context subset quality rather than a universally superior selector.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates what makes a good few-shot context subset by framing selection as sparse reconstruction via Residual Explanation Search (RES) across seven benchmarks and eight LLMs.
AI.motivation: Despite the importance of context subset selection in LLM inference, the underlying properties that make a subset effective remain poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors formulate demonstration selection as sparse reconstruction of the query representation using Residual Explanation Search (RES), a Matching-Pursuit-style diagnostic, and compare retrieval objectives across model hidden-state layers.
AI.result: No single objective is universally best: RES beats MMR in 34 of 56 model-dataset pairs (especially on sentiment), relevance retrieval excels on template-heavy reasoning, all methods underperform zero-shot on StrategyQA, and middle layers favor similarity while last layers favor residual/diversity selection.
AI.conclusion: Context subset quality is conditional and representation-dependent rather than governed by a single universal retrieval objective.

title: B-OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs
summary: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) has recently attracted interest because it provides dense teacher guidance without a separate, often larger teacher model. However, OPSD conditions its teacher on ground-truth solutions, which limits its use when such solutions are unavailable. We propose On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs (B-OPSD). Using a prompt template, the initial model or a saved student checkpoint generates a problem brief from the question alone. The prompt asks for relevant principles, applicability conditions, and likely pitfalls, but not a final answer or a complete solution. A frozen teacher uses the brief as privileged context to guide the current student's on-policy rollouts through token-level distribution matching. B-OPSD uses no ground-truth solutions during training. Results on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 show that both B-OPSD variants achieve higher average accuracy than OPSD at each of three Qwen3 model sizes. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes B-OPSD, an on-policy self-distillation method that replaces ground-truth solutions with self-generated problem briefs.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) conditions the teacher on ground-truth solutions, preventing its use when ground-truth answers are unavailable.
AI.method: An initial model or saved checkpoint generates a problem brief containing principles, applicability conditions, and pitfalls from the question alone, which a frozen teacher uses as privileged context to guide student rollouts via token-level distribution matching.
AI.result: On AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 across three Qwen3 model sizes, both B-OPSD variants achieve higher average accuracy than OPSD without using any ground-truth solutions during training.
AI.conclusion: Self-generated problem briefs enable effective on-policy self-distillation in label-free settings.

title: On Representational and Functional Alignment of Training Data Attribution Methods for Language Models
summary: Existing approaches to training data attribution derive influence estimates from different sources of information, including gradients, model-internal states, and surface-level similarity. However, comparisons between attribution methods remain incomplete, often relying on indirect evaluations through downstream task performance. In this work, we introduce a framework for directly comparing methods along three dimensions: functional alignment, which measures correlation between full attribution vectors; representational alignment, which captures structural similarity of the representations underlying attribution; and cross-method predictability, which evaluates agreement on local pairwise ranking decisions. We observe strong representational and moderate functional alignment within paradigms. Alignment across paradigms is low and task-dependent, yet stable across models. Our results suggest that the similar downstream performance observed across paradigms in prior work can be attributed to agreement on the relative importance of documents, rather than to agreement on rankings of the full training data.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a three-dimensional alignment framework to compare training data attribution methods for language models beyond downstream task accuracy.
AI.motivation: Prior comparisons of gradient-, representation-, and surface-based training data attribution methods rely on indirect downstream evaluations that obscure how their influence estimates actually relate.
AI.method: The authors evaluate functional alignment (correlation of full attribution vectors), representational alignment (structural similarity of underlying representations), and cross-method predictability (agreement on local pairwise rankings).
AI.result: Within-paradigm alignment is strong representationally and moderate functionally, whereas cross-paradigm alignment is low and task-dependent yet stable across models.
AI.conclusion: Similar downstream performance across attribution paradigms stems from agreement on relative document importance rather than agreement on full training-data rankings.

title: OmitEHR: Scalable Omission Detection in LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures, 15 tables. Accepted at Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026
summary: Health systems increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to draft summaries of patient medical records, yet evaluations now find omissions, the absence of clinically important information, to be the most common failure mode. Detecting omissions in an LLM-generated summary requires knowing which facts in the record are salient, a signal that existing methods hand-specify, ignore, or recompute at inference with costly LLM judges. We present OmitEHR, a reference-free omission detector that learns clinical salience from historical clinician-written summaries predating widespread LLM use. OmitEHR learns to predict which source-note sentences clinicians include in their summaries, then surfaces high-salience sentences not covered by an LLM-generated summary as candidate omissions. We apply OmitEHR to brief hospital course (BHC) summarization using 5,000 admissions from a large academic medical center. On held-out admissions, OmitEHR outperformed all evaluated baselines at predicting salient source sentences, including a prompted LLM judge. The full omission detection pipeline took 17.7 to 19.5 seconds and cost \$0.03 to \$0.13 per summary depending on the base model, 1.6 to 1.7 times faster and 5.6 to 6.7 times cheaper than scoring every source sentence with an LLM judge. In a blinded review of 25 admissions, two board-certified clinicians confirmed a mean of 5.6 clinically meaningful omissions per summary surfaced by OmitEHR, compared with 3.3 for a full LLM pipeline, counting candidates confirmed by at least one clinician. The efficiency and validity of OmitEHR make it a practical tool for health systems to flag omissions before a summary reaches the clinician.

AI.tldr: This paper presents OmitEHR, a reference-free omission detector that learns clinical salience from historical clinician-written summaries to flag missing facts in LLM-generated hospital course summaries.
AI.motivation: Omissions of clinically important facts are the most common failure mode in LLM-generated patient summaries, yet existing detectors rely on hand-specified rules or expensive LLM judges.
AI.method: OmitEHR trains on historical clinician-written summaries to predict which source-note sentences clinicians include, then surfaces high-salience sentences omitted by the LLM summary.
AI.result: Across 5,000 admissions, OmitEHR outperforms all baselines including a prompted LLM judge at 1.6x-1.7x faster speed and 5.6x-6.7x lower cost ($0.03-$0.13 per summary), and clinicians confirmed a mean of 5.6 meaningful omissions per summary versus 3.3 for an LLM pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Learning salience from historical clinical documentation enables fast, low-cost, and clinically valid omission detection for LLM summaries.

title: When Does Label-Free Deconfounding of Document Embeddings Work?
summary: Document embeddings encode spurious attributes that can distort semantic comparisons; yet supervised erasure requires metadata that is often unavailable. We systematically investigate label-free deconfounding across corpora and embedding models. Our results show that label-free methods improve semantic utility over unprocessed embeddings, while simple geometric approaches recover much of the supervised benefit, sometimes matching metadata-supervised erasure in linear confounder recoverability and semantic utility. We identify two distinct causes of ineffective erasure: poor proxy-confounder alignment and insufficient intervention coverage. Crucially, confounder recoverability and semantic utility are distinct dimensions of deconfounding success: utility can improve despite residual confounder information, while stronger suppression does not necessarily improve utility. Moreover, reduced linear recoverability can coexist with substantial nonlinear recoverability. Together, these findings distinguish confounder discovery from intervention effectiveness and highlight the importance of evaluating nuisance suppression alongside semantic preservation.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates label-free deconfounding of document embeddings and identifies when geometric erasure succeeds or fails without metadata.
AI.motivation: Document embeddings encode spurious attributes that distort semantic comparisons, but supervised erasure requires metadata that is often unavailable.
AI.method: The authors evaluate label-free deconfounding methods across multiple corpora and embedding models, measuring both linear/nonlinear confounder recoverability and downstream semantic utility.
AI.result: Label-free methods improve semantic utility over raw embeddings and simple geometric approaches sometimes match supervised erasure, but erasure fails under poor proxy-confounder alignment or insufficient intervention coverage, and reduced linear recoverability can coexist with substantial nonlinear recoverability.
AI.conclusion: Effective deconfounding requires evaluating both nuisance suppression (linear and nonlinear) and semantic preservation, as the two dimensions do not always move together.

title: A Comparative Evaluation of BERT-Based and LLM-Based Models for Indic Sentence Similarity
summary: The relative effectiveness of BERT-based encoders and large language model (LLM)-based embeddings for Indic semantic textual similarity remains insufficiently characterized. We compare eight BERT-based and five LLM-based models on the 1,500-pair STS Benchmark development set translated into ten Indic languages and on the native Marathi MahaSTS test set. IndicSBERT achieves the highest Pearson correlation in all ten translated language sets, with a macro-average of 0.843, followed by BGE-M3 at 0.792. Harrier-270M is the strongest LLM-based model on translated STS-B, with a macro-average of 0.751. On MahaSTS, IndicSBERT and Bhasha-Embed-v0 achieve Pearson correlations of 0.901 and 0.900, respectively, while EmbeddingGemma leads the LLM-based models at 0.871. The highest-scoring BERT-based model thus exceeds the highest-scoring LLM-based model in both settings, although the magnitude of the difference varies across benchmarks. These findings indicate that LLM-derived embeddings do not uniformly improve Indic sentence similarity over established encoders and motivate evaluation that accounts for language coverage, task supervision, and benchmark construction.

AI.tldr: This paper compares eight BERT-based and five LLM-based embedding models on Indic semantic textual similarity and finds that BERT-based encoders still outperform LLM embeddings.
AI.motivation: The relative effectiveness of BERT-based encoders versus LLM-based embeddings for Indic semantic textual similarity has not been systematically characterized.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 13 models on the 1,500-pair STS Benchmark translated into ten Indic languages and on the native Marathi MahaSTS test set using Pearson correlation.
AI.result: IndicSBERT achieves the highest Pearson correlation in all ten translated languages (0.843 macro-average) ahead of BGE-M3 (0.792) and top LLM Harrier-270M (0.751); on MahaSTS, IndicSBERT (0.901) and Bhasha-Embed-v0 (0.900) lead top LLM EmbeddingGemma (0.871).
AI.conclusion: Specialized BERT-based encoders currently outperform LLM-derived embeddings on Indic sentence similarity, highlighting the importance of language coverage and task supervision.

title: Leakage-aware calibrated decision-level fusion for mental-health text classification
summary: Decision-level fusion benefits from complementary errors, calibrated probabilities, and leakage-aware evaluation. We evaluated a heterogeneous transformer fusion framework on 262,276 proxy-labeled Reddit records covering anxiety, depression, schizophrenia, and suicidal ideation. In a stratified random split, MinHash-LSH identified 29.1% of test records as lexical near-duplicates of training data. Augmentation-lineage auditing found 50.2% lineage overlap with training, including 30.0% of records retained after lexical filtering. We therefore used lineage-disjoint partitions. Twelve encoders, comprising three seeds each of Bio-ClinicalBERT, MentalBERT, MentalRoBERTa, and RoBERTa-base, underwent cross-fitted validation for calibration and ensemble selection. A class-specific Complementarity Index (CI), defined as the Jaccard distance between members' correctly classified validation sets, was assessed against independent fusion gain. CI correlated with gain for depression (r=0.50) and suicidal ideation (r=0.68), but not anxiety; results for schizophrenia were mixed. The selected MentalBERT, MentalRoBERTa, and RoBERTa-base triad achieved macro-F1 0.844 [0.823, 0.863], MCC 0.779, and ECE 0.0033 after post-fusion recalibration, improving macro-F1 by 0.021 [0.007, 0.037] over the validation-selected best single encoder. Integrated-Gradients attribution diversity was 2.3 times greater in fusion-rescued cases. Removing divergence-driving words destroyed 58% of rescues, versus 12% under random removal. These findings show that lineage auditing detects dependencies missed by lexical filtering, while class-specific complementarity and post-fusion calibration reveal ensemble behavior obscured by aggregate accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a leakage-aware, calibrated decision-level fusion framework for mental-health text classification using lineage-disjoint splits and a Complementarity Index.
AI.motivation: Stratified random splits in mental-health datasets can harbor severe lexical and augmentation-lineage leakage, inflating single-model and ensemble evaluations.
AI.method: Auditing 262,276 Reddit records, the authors construct lineage-disjoint partitions, cross-fit 12 encoders (three seeds each of Bio-ClinicalBERT, MentalBERT, MentalRoBERTa, RoBERTa-base), and select a triad using a class-specific Complementarity Index (CI) with post-fusion recalibration.
AI.result: MinHash-LSH found 29.1% lexical near-duplicates and lineage auditing found 50.2% overlap; on lineage-disjoint splits, the selected triad achieved 0.844 macro-F1, 0.779 MCC, and 0.0033 ECE (+0.021 macro-F1 over the best single encoder), with CI correlating with gain for depression (r=0.50) and suicidal ideation (r=0.68).
AI.conclusion: Lineage auditing prevents hidden data leakage, and class-specific complementarity plus recalibration explains and improves decision-level ensemble gains.

title: CausalGloss: Multi-Evidence Action Control for a Simultaneous Mandarin Speech-to-ASL Gloss Cascade
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027
summary: Simultaneous Mandarin speech-to-American Sign Language (ASL) gloss translation requires deciding when an evolving utterance supports committing each gloss. Fixed Wait-k cannot adapt to source-gloss reordering, while training only on reference histories causes exposure bias. We present CausalGloss, an English-prefix-to-ASL-gloss action policy for a Mandarin-speech cascade. It combines lexical and semantic evidence, bounded delay, negation constraints, burst WRITE actions, and incomplete-history recovery. On a frozen 500-example How2Sign-derived benchmark with weak LLM-generated references, CausalGloss improves the fixed Wait-k frontier and nearly matches a three-seed TransLLaMA-style learned adaptive baseline at k = 5 in Token F1 (0.7047 versus 0.7067), with 54.4% lower LAAL. Against CLERC Epee human-gloss references, it achieves 0.649 Token F1 and Pareto-dominates three-seed TransLLaMA-style k = 5 and fixed k = 5, 7, reducing LAAL by 58.2-69.9%. Ablations separate timing from retention. A synthetic Mandarin-speech cascade preserves a smaller computation-aware latency gain, although outputs remain over-long. We also construct ChineseSpeech-ASLGloss-v1, a 19,924-utterance, 36.54-h controlled evaluation corpus.

AI.tldr: This paper presents CausalGloss, a multi-evidence action policy for simultaneous Mandarin speech-to-ASL gloss translation, along with a new 19,924-utterance evaluation corpus.
AI.motivation: Fixed Wait-k policies cannot adapt to source-gloss reordering in simultaneous Mandarin-to-ASL gloss translation, while training only on reference histories causes exposure bias.
AI.method: CausalGloss combines lexical and semantic evidence, bounded delay, negation constraints, burst WRITE actions, and incomplete-history recovery in an English-prefix-to-ASL-gloss cascade, evaluated alongside the new ChineseSpeech-ASLGloss-v1 corpus.
AI.result: On a frozen 500-example How2Sign-derived benchmark, CausalGloss achieves 0.7047 Token F1 with 54.4% lower LAAL than a TransLLaMA-style k=5 baseline (0.7067); against CLERC Epee human references, it achieves 0.649 Token F1 and reduces LAAL by 58.2% to 69.9%.
AI.conclusion: Multi-evidence action control substantially improves the latency-quality Pareto frontier for simultaneous speech-to-sign-gloss translation.

title: From Facts to Personas: Interpretable Role Unlearning in LLMs via Mixture-of-Experts
summary: LLMs are widely adopted in multi-role dialogue and persona simulation. However, their strong ability to imitate role-specific linguistic and behavioral patterns can introduce privacy risks, reinforce social biases, and lead to unsafe or uncontrollable outputs. To address these issues, we introduce the Role-playing Unlearning task, which aims to selectively forget the style and knowledge associated with target roles while preserving the language ability and behaviors of the remaining roles. Unlike prior unlearning tasks that focus solely on removing factual information, our task additionally requires forgetting persona-specific characteristics, making the control over model generation more fine-grained. We propose RoleMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts framework that maps different roles to more independent expert subspaces, improving role separation and structural interpretability. To further distinguish role-specific features, RoleMoE incorporates two complementary losses: a specialization loss that drives roles to adopt distinct expert distributions, and a disentanglement loss that encourages experts to develop distinct capability subspaces. This decomposed structure enables role unlearning to focus selectively on target-role experts. We finally propose RoleBench-Unlearn for evaluation, and experiments on multiple backbone LLMs show that RoleMoE enables precise and controllable role forgetting, while better preserving the linguistic quality, knowledge, and persona consistency of non-target roles. All code and datasets are publicly available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RoleMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts framework with specialization and disentanglement losses for interpretable role-playing unlearning in LLMs.
AI.motivation: LLMs' ability to imitate persona-specific styles and knowledge poses privacy and safety risks, yet prior unlearning methods target only factual knowledge rather than persona characteristics.
AI.method: RoleMoE maps roles to independent expert subspaces using a specialization loss (distinct expert distributions per role) and a disentanglement loss (distinct capability subspaces), enabling selective unlearning of target-role experts, evaluated on the new RoleBench-Unlearn benchmark.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple backbone LLMs show RoleMoE achieves precise, controllable forgetting of target-role style and knowledge while better preserving non-target-role quality, knowledge, and persona consistency.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing persona representations into specialized MoE subspaces enables targeted, interpretable role unlearning.

title: Real-World End-to-End Product Entity Resolution
summary: Product Entity Resolution (PER) in e-commerce is challenging due to unstructured text, formatting inconsistencies, promotional noise, and fine-grained product differences. We present an end-to-end evaluation of four zero-shot PER pipelines---Lexical Cascade, Semantic Cascade, Hybrid Fusion Cascade, and Generative-Lexical Cascade---across established benchmarks and introduce two real-world datasets characterized by cross-lingual noise and dense brand collisions. We evaluate lexical and dense blocking with cross-encoder, tensor-search, and Large Language Model verification, considering accuracy, runtime, and memory consumption.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an end-to-end evaluation of four zero-shot Product Entity Resolution (PER) pipelines across established benchmarks and two new real-world e-commerce datasets.
AI.motivation: E-commerce Product Entity Resolution is hindered by unstructured text, formatting inconsistencies, promotional noise, and fine-grained product differences.
AI.method: The authors evaluate Lexical Cascade, Semantic Cascade, Hybrid Fusion Cascade, and Generative-Lexical Cascade pipelines combining lexical/dense blocking with cross-encoder, tensor-search, and LLM verification.
AI.result: The study benchmarks accuracy, runtime, and memory consumption across standard benchmarks and two newly introduced real-world datasets featuring cross-lingual noise and dense brand collisions.
AI.conclusion: The evaluation clarifies the accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs of zero-shot blocking and verification cascades for real-world e-commerce PER.

title: Do Rule-Based Tools Help LLMs Translate Endangered Uralic Languages in the Prompt or over MCP?
comment: Accepted at the 11th International Workshop on Computational Linguistics for Uralic Languages (IWCLUL 2026), Munich. 9 pages plus appendices, 1 figure, 10 tables. Data and all model outputs: this https URL
summary: Komi-Zyrian, Moksha, Erzya and Udmurt have mature rule-based resources, among them finite-state analysers, constraint grammars and bilingual dictionaries, which language models do not use. We ask whether giving a model access to these resources improves machine translation from the four languages into English, and whether it matters how the access is provided: as analyses computed in advance and written into the prompt, or as tools that the model calls itself through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). We evaluate manually: an expert linguist read every English output of the strongest model under three conditions, 816 sentences in all, accepted or rejected each one, and named the main error in every rejected translation. With the analyses in the prompt, the number of accepted translations rises from 13 to 43 out of 272; with the tools attached it rises to 55. The gain comes from the bilingual dictionary. For Udmurt, whose dictionary has no English side, the prompt-based condition brings no gain at all, while for the other three languages an English gloss reaches the prompt for 74 to 80% of the source words. Tool calling is also much harder to get working than prompt injection. Of 31 open-weight models, 14 never call a tool, 11 of them because they cannot produce a usable call, and half of the calls that are made name a language the toolkit does not support. We release the data set, every model output and all tool-call logs.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether providing rule-based morphological and dictionary resources via prompts or MCP tool calls improves LLM translation of four endangered Uralic languages into English.
AI.motivation: Endangered Uralic languages have mature finite-state analysers and bilingual dictionaries that LLMs do not use, and it is unclear whether prompt injection or MCP tool calling is more effective.
AI.method: An expert linguist manually evaluated 816 English translations from the strongest model across three conditions (baseline, precomputed prompt analyses, and MCP tool calls) for Komi-Zyrian, Moksha, Erzya, and Udmurt.
AI.result: Accepted translations rose from 13/272 at baseline to 43/272 with prompt analyses and 55/272 with MCP tools, driven by bilingual dictionaries; Udmurt saw no prompt gain because its dictionary lacked English, and 14 of 31 open-weight models failed to produce usable tool calls.
AI.conclusion: Rule-based bilingual dictionaries substantially improve low-resource Uralic translation when accessible, though reliable MCP tool calling remains challenging for many open-weight models.

title: Text Speeding Itself Up: Recency and Restraint in Session-Local Drafting
summary: Speculative decoding lets a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large language model verifies in a single forward pass. When the verifier keeps a KV cache, verification is cheap and drafting must be nearly free. Session-local drafters, which predict from the prompt and the text generated so far, meet that bar without training. We compare a recency-weighted, backing-off, confidence-gated session memory against prompt lookup decoding in its reference form, which copies from the earliest earlier match, and in a variant that copies from the most recent one, with paired per-prompt bootstrap intervals throughout. On general, medical, and legal text with a Mistral-7B verifier, recency accounts for the speed: most-recent lookup gains up to 0.09 in speedup over earliest-match lookup on 500-token generations, and session memory's weighting and backoff add nothing measurable on top, at 30 to 40 times the drafting cost. Energy tells a different story. On medical and legal text, unselective drafters are 14% faster than plain decoding yet use as much energy per token, while drafters that abstain on weak evidence save 3 to 4 joules per 100 tokens; a three-token minimum match length on prompt lookup matches the confidence-gated session memory. Outputs are token-identical to greedy decoding in 94% of generations, with every divergence at a numerical near-tie. Under a repetition penalty, long-generation speedups shrink from 1.4-1.7x to 1.1-1.2x, but recency still helps and the length floor is the only drafter that saves energy in both domains.

AI.tldr: This paper compares session-local speculative drafters and shows that recency-based prompt lookup drives speedups while a three-token minimum match floor saves energy.
AI.motivation: When a verifier keeps a KV cache, session-local drafters must be nearly free, yet the relative contributions of recency, weighting, backoff, and confidence gating are unclear.
AI.method: Using a Mistral-7B verifier on general, medical, and legal text, the authors compare a recency-weighted, backing-off, confidence-gated session memory against earliest-match and most-recent prompt lookup decoding.
AI.result: Most-recent lookup gains up to 0.09 speedup over earliest-match on 500-token generations, while session memory's weighting/backoff adds no measurable gain at 30x-40x drafting cost; abstaining via a 3-token minimum match floor saves 3 to 4 joules per 100 tokens, and outputs match greedy decoding in 94% of generations.
AI.conclusion: Simple most-recent prompt lookup with a minimum match-length floor captures the speed and energy benefits of session-local drafting without complex session-memory overhead.

title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Unifying Representations in Neural Models (UniReps) co-located with NeurIPS 2026.(arXiv preprint)
summary: A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator. The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that probing and steering favor different hidden-state directions within and across language models, with steering consistently preferring directions closer to the mean difference.
AI.motivation: Probe directions are frequently reused for activation steering, but the direction that best detects a concept may not be the one that best modifies model behavior.
AI.method: Across three instruction-tuned model families, the authors sweep a one-parameter family from covariance-adjusted discriminant to mean difference for truthfulness and sentiment, evaluating probing, additive/rotation steering, cross-model linear transfer, and PopQA abstention.
AI.result: The best probe is not the best steering direction in 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations; linear-map probe transfer retains 81%-91% of above-chance probing performance whereas transferred mean-difference steering retains less effect in 11 of 12 pairs, and steering toward "unknown" on PopQA raises abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors versus 2-5 on confident errors.
AI.conclusion: Probing and steering rely on distinct geometric directions and transfer differently across models, so probe directions should not be assumed optimal for steering.

title: Evaluating and Improving Natural Language Autoencoders
summary: Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) are a method for generating natural language explanations of LLM activations. We develop evaluations based on auditing tasks that test the ability of NLAs to surface latent knowledge, identify whether a model was misled by a hint, and catch a silent fabrication. We also develop extensions to NLAs that let them use activation information from multiple layers and positions, let us apply them more effectively to long transcripts, and reduce the number of false claims they make. These extensions result in improvements on both our auditing evaluations and auxiliary evaluations adapted from prior work. We also use the evaluations to study how different auditing capabilities change over the course of NLA training, and find that although every evaluation improves early in training, extended training can hurt performance on some of our auditing evaluations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces auditing evaluations for natural language autoencoders (NLAs) and proposes multi-layer, multi-position extensions that improve activation explanations while revealing that extended training can degrade some auditing capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of NLAs do not adequately test their ability to surface latent knowledge, detect when a model was misled by a hint, or catch silent fabrications, and current NLAs struggle with long transcripts and false claims.
AI.method: The authors design auditing-based evaluations and extend NLAs to use activation information across multiple layers and positions, improving applicability to long transcripts and reducing false claims.
AI.result: The proposed extensions improve performance on both the new auditing evaluations and auxiliary evaluations adapted from prior work, while training-dynamics analysis shows that all evaluations improve early in training but extended training can hurt performance on some auditing tasks.
AI.conclusion: Multi-layer and multi-position extensions make NLAs more reliable for auditing LLM activations, though training duration must be balanced to avoid degrading auditing performance.

title: Formalizing Formal Semantics: The Formal Atlas
summary: In this paper we present the Formal Atlas, a system for the study of natural language semantics using proof assistants. Our aim is to formalize semantic accounts, check their predictions and compare the implemented theories. To this end, we connect source records and formal developments with an interactive application, where researchers can inspect proofs and modify supported Rocq files. Montague's PTQ and Gallin provide our main cases, followed by dynamic and type-theoretic comparisons, RSA and distributional semantics. We also discuss what it takes to formalize less explicit analyses. Lastly, we consider the use of AI, both for assistance in developing these resources and for inference systems that can make use of them. This work extends an earlier programme in proof-assistant semantics, with research and teaching as complementary uses.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the Formal Atlas, an interactive proof-assistant system for formalizing, checking, and comparing natural language semantic theories in Rocq.
AI.motivation: Natural language semantics lacks a unified, interactive environment for formalizing semantic accounts, verifying their predictions, and comparing different formal frameworks side by side.
AI.method: The authors connect source records and formal developments in an interactive application where researchers can inspect proofs and modify supported Rocq files, covering Montague's PTQ, Gallin, dynamic and type-theoretic semantics, RSA, and distributional semantics, while also considering AI assistance for resource development and inference.
AI.result: The system demonstrates how formal semantic theories and less explicit analyses can be implemented, inspected, and compared within a proof-assistant framework.
AI.conclusion: The Formal Atlas extends proof-assistant semantics to support both research and teaching by making formal semantic theories inspectable, comparable, and interactively verifiable.

title: Sada-ASR: A Production Multidialectal Arabic Speech Recognition System
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. Code: this https URL Dataset: this https URL
summary: Callers to Arabic customer-service lines speak their own dialect, while speech recognizers are built and evaluated mainly on Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). A recognizer that mishears the dialect breaks the call before anything else can help. We present Sada-ASR, the speech recognizer of EchoNova's production Arabic voice agent. On a 120-hour test set of MSA and eight dialects, it has the lowest word and character error rates of twelve systems, against eleven from Microsoft, ElevenLabs, Google, OpenAI, Speechmatics, IFM, Cohere, NVIDIA and Audar: 11.69% word error rate against 13.51% for the strongest, Microsoft's MAI-Transcribe-2 (a lead of 0.74 points on clips unaffected by that system's fixed number and script conventions), and 15.52% against 16.96% averaged over varieties. Its largest margins are on Omani (4.30 points), Egyptian (3.78) and Saudi (2.19) speech; it is level on Syrian and loses on Lebanese (24.96% against 23.05%), mostly because it writes Lebanese words in MSA forms and is less verbatim. On six public test sets its average word error rate under the leaderboard's current scoring is 17.17%, below every published figure we found, among them Falcon-ASR (20.92%), Jais-ASR (22.85%) and Audar-ASR-V1-Turbo (23.17%), though none of these states that it used that scoring, so the comparison is indicative. We describe the data pipeline and methodology behind Sada-ASR and release a 20-hour subset of the test set with our scoring code.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Sada-ASR, EchoNova's production multidialectal Arabic speech recognition system, which achieves the lowest overall word and character error rates across 12 systems on a 120-hour MSA and eight-dialect test set.
AI.motivation: Most Arabic speech recognizers are built and evaluated primarily on Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), causing customer-service voice agents to fail when callers speak regional dialects.
AI.method: The authors describe the data pipeline and methodology behind Sada-ASR for multidialectal Arabic recognition and release a 20-hour subset of the test set with scoring code.
AI.result: On a 120-hour test set covering MSA and eight dialects, Sada-ASR achieves 11.69% WER (versus 13.51% for Microsoft's MAI-Transcribe-2) and 15.52% averaged over varieties (versus 16.96%), with largest gains on Omani (4.30 points), Egyptian (3.78), and Saudi (2.19), while trailing on Lebanese (24.96% vs. 23.05%); on six public test sets it averages 17.17% WER under current leaderboard scoring, below Falcon-ASR (20.92%), Jais-ASR (22.85%), and Audar-ASR-V1-Turbo (23.17%).
AI.conclusion: Sada-ASR demonstrates strong production accuracy across diverse Arabic dialects, though dialect-specific transcription conventions such as Lebanese remain a challenge.

title: SemMask: Semantic-Prioritized Progressive Masking for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) are designed to enable globally parallel generation. However, in practice, they often exhibit pseudo-autoregressive behavior and a function-word-first bias, which undermines their performance on tasks such as text writing and code generation that benefit from global planning and parallel decoding. To address this, we propose SemMask, a novel fine-tuning paradigm that leverages a semantic-prioritized progressive masking strategy to encourage the model to decode high-information semantic tokens early and globally, thereby enhancing its global planning and parallel generation capabilities. Specifically, we first use the gradients of the original DLM with respect to each token to identify semantic tokens. During masking, these semantic tokens are preserved with priority, establishing a progressive generation order in which semantic tokens are decoded prior to function tokens. Meanwhile, we adjust the loss weight for semantic tokens to further reinforce their early prediction. Experimental results show that SemMask achieves quality comparable to strong autoregressive baselines on both text writing and code generation tasks, while providing superior semantic coherence. Notably, SemMask achieves higher accuracy with substantially fewer decoding steps, indicating that the early establishment of semantic structure improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SemMask, a fine-tuning paradigm for Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) that prioritizes semantic tokens during progressive masking to improve global planning, parallel generation, and the efficiency-accuracy trade-off.
AI.motivation: Although DLMs are designed for globally parallel generation, they often exhibit pseudo-autoregressive behavior and a function-word-first bias, which hurts performance on text writing and code generation.
AI.method: SemMask uses gradients of the original DLM with respect to each token to identify high-information semantic tokens, preserves them with priority during progressive masking so they are decoded before function tokens, and adjusts their loss weights to reinforce early prediction.
AI.result: On text writing and code generation tasks, SemMask achieves quality comparable to strong autoregressive baselines with superior semantic coherence, and attains higher accuracy with substantially fewer decoding steps.
AI.conclusion: Establishing semantic structure early via semantic-prioritized progressive masking enables DLMs to realize better global planning and a stronger efficiency-accuracy trade-off.

title: ROUNDS: Source-Framed Diagnostic Revision after Multi-Turn Clinical Evidence
comment: Accepted at Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026, Proceedings Track; to appear in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (PMLR). 17 pages
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical benchmarks, but does this performance translate into reliable diagnosis as a conversation unfolds? In diagnostic conversations, users can provide clinical findings across multiple turns, ask for a diagnosis without supplying answer options, and introduce opinions from others. Models must therefore form diagnoses from the available evidence and decide how to respond to subsequent advice. We introduce ROUNDS, a framework that evaluates these abilities after a fixed sequence of clinical evidence delivered over multiple turns. ROUNDS compares diagnosis with and without answer options, presents the same incorrect diagnosis under clinician and lay framing, and varies support for competing diagnoses in written five-clinician panels. Across seven models and 1,035 cases from five datasets, average accuracy was 76.9% with answer options and 57.0% without them. Clinician-framed misleading advice produced lower final accuracy than lay-framed advice in every model, with differences of 4.6 to 38.2 percentage points. Initially correct diagnoses more often became incorrect answers than abstentions, and many adopted the suggested disease. Conversely, accuracy increased as more panel members supported the correct diagnosis, including when the majority opinion remained unchanged. These findings reveal a gap between medical benchmark performance and reliable diagnosis in conversation: models respond to external opinions, but remain vulnerable to abandoning correct diagnoses without new clinical evidence.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ROUNDS, a multi-turn diagnostic evaluation framework showing that LLMs lose accuracy without answer options and frequently abandon correct diagnoses when presented with misleading clinician-framed advice.
AI.motivation: High scores on medical benchmarks do not establish whether LLMs can diagnose reliably in multi-turn conversations where answer options are absent and users introduce external opinions.
AI.method: ROUNDS delivers a fixed sequence of clinical evidence over multiple turns, compares diagnosis with and without answer options, presents identical incorrect diagnoses under clinician versus lay framing, and varies support in written five-clinician panels across 1,035 cases from five datasets and seven models.
AI.result: Average accuracy drops from 76.9% with answer options to 57.0% without them; clinician-framed misleading advice lowers final accuracy more than lay-framed advice in every model by 4.6 to 38.2 percentage points, with initially correct diagnoses more often turning into incorrect answers than abstentions, while panel support for the correct diagnosis increases accuracy even when the majority opinion is unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs remain vulnerable to abandoning correct diagnoses under authoritative external framing without new clinical evidence, revealing a gap between benchmark scores and conversational reliability.

title: SG-LegalClarify: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Legal Reasoning and Ambiguity Recognition in Singapore Law
summary: Singapore offers a distinctive testbed for legal reasoning by large language models (LLMs). Its legal system combines inherited English common law with jurisdiction-specific statutes, requiring models to distinguish local doctrine from generic common-law intuition. This setting also highlights the challenge of recognizing underspecification in lay legal queries, because the facts material to a legal outcome depend on the governing doctrine. Yet legal benchmarks rarely cover Singapore law or test this form of ambiguity recognition. To address these gaps, we introduce SG-LegalClarify, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law. SG-LegalClarify contains 1,100 lawyer-authored source questions spanning 10 legal domains, including 340 fully specified and 760 underspecified questions. Each underspecified question has a fixed hidden-fact assignment and a fully specified counterpart, yielding 1,860 evaluation instances. Responses are graded with lawyer-authored Issue, Rule, Application, and Conclusion (IRAC) rubrics. We evaluate 19 LLMs, closed-book and with web search, using a multi-turn pipeline in which models decide whether to answer or clarify, and a user simulator reveals hidden facts only when asked. We find the benchmark far from saturated: the best models satisfy only 69.8% of mandatory rubric items closed-book (average 53.8%) and 77.8% with web search (average 63.0%). Models also struggle to recognize when clarification is necessary. We will release the public split of our benchmark, the model outputs on it, and the evaluation pipeline to support future research.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SG-LegalClarify, a 1,100-question benchmark for legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law, showing that 19 evaluated LLMs remain far from saturation.
AI.motivation: Existing legal benchmarks rarely cover Singapore's hybrid common-law and statutory system or test whether models can recognize when lay legal queries are underspecified and require clarification.
AI.method: The authors construct 1,100 lawyer-authored questions across 10 legal domains (340 fully specified and 760 underspecified with hidden-fact assignments and fully specified counterparts, totaling 1,860 evaluation instances), grade responses with lawyer-authored IRAC rubrics, and evaluate 19 LLMs in a multi-turn clarify-or-answer pipeline with and without web search.
AI.result: The best models satisfy only 69.8% of mandatory rubric items closed-book (mean 53.8%) and 77.8% with web search (mean 63.0%), and models struggle to recognize when clarification is necessary.
AI.conclusion: SG-LegalClarify exposes substantial gaps in jurisdiction-specific legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition, and the public split, outputs, and pipeline will be released.

title: StaleBench: Isolating Stale Retrieval in Agent Memory, and Pricing the Fix
comment: Accepted to Findings of EACL 2027. 39 pages, 3 figures. Code and data: this https URL
summary: An agent that stores facts over time eventually stores several versions of the same fact. Asked a value-agnostic question - "which team does X play for now?" - a similarity retriever cannot prefer the current version, because every version matches the entity the query names. StaleBench isolates this stale-retrieval failure on 892 real updating facts, with currency labels from the source (Wikidata validity years via TempLAMA), never from a retrieval score. Our central result is that retrieval metrics can rank memory policies backwards: a retention policy and its retain-everything control return the identical statement at rank 1 for every test query, yet differ by 29.5 and 65.6 points in reader accuracy on two readers when no date is shown. Contamination@5, the metric we add, ranks them correctly where current@1 and current@5 do not. Withdrawing the lexical anchor that statements carry costs deployed keying mechanisms tens of points of freshness; entity resolution on both the write path and the query recovers most of the loss. Three deployed systems (Mem0, Graphiti, LangMem) and a reimplemented ERASE each handle supersession differently, and no single scoring convention describes all four. We release the data, a frozen evaluator, and reference baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces StaleBench, an 892-fact benchmark for stale retrieval in agent memory, showing that standard retrieval metrics can rank memory policies backwards and proposing Contamination@5 to fix it.
AI.motivation: When agents store multiple versions of a changing fact over time, similarity retrievers cannot prefer the current version for value-agnostic queries, and existing retrieval metrics fail to capture this failure.
AI.method: StaleBench isolates stale retrieval on 892 updating facts with Wikidata validity-year currency labels from TempLAMA, introduces the Contamination@5 metric, evaluates entity resolution on write and query paths, and compares three deployed systems (Mem0, Graphiti, LangMem) plus a reimplemented ERASE.
AI.result: A retention policy and its retain-everything control return identical rank-1 statements for every query yet differ by 29.5 and 65.6 points in reader accuracy when dates are hidden; Contamination@5 ranks them correctly where current@1 and current@5 fail, and entity resolution on both write and query paths recovers most of the freshness lost when lexical anchors are removed.
AI.conclusion: Stale retrieval requires currency-aware metrics like Contamination@5 and bidirectional entity resolution, as deployed memory systems handle supersession inconsistently.

title: Ambiguous Examples Help, But Full Data Wins: Revisiting Dataset Cartography for Extractive Adversarial QA
comment: 37 pages, 30 figures, 20 tables. Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EACL 2027. Code: this https URL
summary: Dataset cartography argues that training dynamics can reveal regions of a dataset that matter differently for learning: easy-to-learn examples aid optimization, hard-to-learn examples often expose annotation problems, and ambiguous examples contribute strongly to out-of-distribution generalization. A striking implication of the original work is that a model trained on only 33% ambiguous examples can outperform full-data training on several OOD evaluations, including a QNLI reformulation of SQuAD evaluated on Adversarial SQuAD. We revisit this claim in a stricter setting: open-ended extractive question answering, where models must predict answer spans rather than classify question-sentence pairs. For each encoder family, we compute clean-source SQuAD training dynamics, train on full, random, easy-ranked, ambiguous-ranked, and hard-ranked subsets, and evaluate robustness on adversarial-only AddSent and AddOneSent rows. Ambiguous-ranked 33% subsets beat random 33% subsets on exact-match accuracy in all 14 model-evaluation cells and on F1 in 12/14 cells. However, full-data training beats ambiguous-ranked training in 12/14 exact-match cells and 12/14 F1 cells, with mean full-minus-ambiguous gains of 3.40 EM and 4.10 F1. The most thoroughly replicated ELECTRA-small panel is also the main exception to the ambiguous-over-random F1 gains. These results show that clean-source cartography remains useful for reduced-data selection, but its OOD advantage does not carry over as a general replacement for full-data training in extractive adversarial QA.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits dataset cartography on open-ended extractive adversarial QA and finds that while 33% ambiguous-ranked subsets beat random subsets, full-data training still outperforms ambiguous-ranked training.
AI.motivation: Prior work claimed that training on 33% ambiguous examples outperforms full-data training on OOD evaluations using a QNLI reformulation of SQuAD, leaving open whether this holds in stricter open-ended extractive QA.
AI.method: The authors compute clean-source SQuAD training dynamics for multiple encoder families, train models on full, random, easy-ranked, ambiguous-ranked, and hard-ranked subsets, and evaluate robustness on adversarial AddSent and AddOneSent rows.
AI.result: Ambiguous-ranked 33% subsets beat random 33% subsets in all 14 exact-match cells and 12/14 F1 cells, but full-data training beats ambiguous-ranked training in 12/14 EM cells and 12/14 F1 cells with mean gains of 3.40 EM and 4.10 F1.
AI.conclusion: Clean-source dataset cartography remains useful for reduced-data selection, but its OOD advantage does not generalize as a replacement for full-data training in extractive adversarial QA.

title: Logical AI OS: A Training-Free Governance Layer Outside the Model for Instruction Following -- Benefits, Costs, Failures, and the Calibration of the Measuring Instrument Itself
comment: 18 pages, 5 tables, 3 figures. Technical report v3. Earlier reports in this line: doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23226740 (Measurement Layer) and the Validation Layer report. Data, model answers, per-item verdicts, annotations and the standalone checker: this https URL (tag v3.0-data). The governance-layer implementation is not released
summary: Small language models often fail explicit user requests (length, number of items, format, required or forbidden words, grammatical person, answer language). We measure a training-free governance layer placed outside the model: it reads the requests with rules, checks the answer mechanically, repairs it when a request is not kept, and hands back the original answer when the repair fails. The loop exists in prior work; our contribution is measuring its benefits, costs and failures, and reporting how the measuring instrument itself was calibrated. On four 4-bit Qwen-family models (3B, 7B, 14B, one 7B reasoning model) and 329 Chinese prompts: (1) answers that keep every request the layer read rise significantly (all comparisons p<0.0001), by 34 to 66 of 329 under the corrected checker and 52 to 92 after a length-control fix; a generic redo message brings no significant gain. (2) Exploratory: on 90 repair-triggered prompts, two AI annotators found the layer produced an acceptable answer where the bare model did not more often than the reverse (49:7; 18:12, not significant). (3) Costs: 43-66% more generation time; whole-answer rewriting makes a sizeable share of usable answers unusable. (4) Failures: rule-based reading reaches about 70% and 84% of a two-annotator ceiling on unseen phrasings; unsatisfiable requests make the reasoning model loop; model self-reports are unreliable (18 of 25 "fixed" items were not fixed). (5) Over half of the original checker's "violated" verdicts on structural requests were wrong; after correction the main result holds, and one comparison is downgraded. Conclusions are limited to this Chinese material, the Qwen family and sizes up to 14B. The governance implementation is not released; data, answers, verdicts and the checker are public.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates a training-free external governance layer for small language models' instruction following, measuring its compliance gains alongside latency costs, failure modes, and checker calibration errors.
AI.motivation: Small language models frequently violate explicit user constraints such as length, format, or forbidden words, and while external repair loops exist, their costs, failure modes, and measurement reliability have not been thoroughly quantified.
AI.method: The authors test a rule-based external layer that parses requests, mechanically checks outputs, and repairs violations on four 4-bit Qwen-family models (3B, 7B, 14B, and a 7B reasoning model) across 329 Chinese prompts, while auditing and calibrating the checker itself.
AI.result: Full-request compliance rises significantly (p < 0.0001) by 34 to 66 of 329 prompts under the corrected checker (52 to 92 after a length-control fix), at a cost of 43-66% more generation time and usable answers broken by rewriting; rule parsing reaches 70-84% of a two-annotator ceiling, model self-reports fail (18 of 25 "fixed" items remain unfixed), and over half of the original checker's structural violation verdicts were wrong.
AI.conclusion: External governance improves constraint compliance for small Chinese Qwen models up to 14B, but incurs substantial latency and rewrite-damage costs and requires careful calibration of the evaluation instrument itself.

title: Machine interpreting competitiveness: a discourse-sensitive comparison of meaning and target-language quality in English-Chinese simultaneous interpreting
comment: 88 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Includes Supplementary Information (40 pages)
summary: Machine interpreting (MI), or AI-enabled speech translation, is increasingly visible in professional and public-facing communication, yet its performance relative to human simultaneous interpreters remains insufficiently understood. Existing studies are often limited by a single discourse mode and evaluation frameworks that are not well aligned with interpreting as a discourse-level communicative activity. The present study compares five commercial MI systems with 26 human interpreters (14 professionals, 12 advanced students) on English-to-Chinese simultaneous interpreting across planned and unplanned discourse, focusing on meaning and target-language quality. In these materials, MI performance differed sharply between the two discourse modes. In the planned formal speech, the strongest system became highly competitive on meaning, entering the upper human range, and a second system also performed strongly. In the extemporaneous interview, however, no MI system approached the stronger human tiers. Code-level analysis further shows that similar overall scores often masked different error profiles. Human interpreters were more likely to preserve the broader communicative trajectory through selective omission, restructuring, and contextual inference, whereas even the best MI systems were more vulnerable to semantic distortion, discourse-tracking failures, and context-insensitive interpretation. On target-language quality, the human advantage proved more stable than on meaning. Unintelligible or nonsensical output and disfluency carryover emerge as particularly salient weaknesses in machine performance, especially in spontaneous discourse. Overall, the findings are consistent with a discourse-sensitive account of where MI appears competitive, where it remains limited, and why these distinctions matter for interpreting practice, interpreter education, and future MI development.

AI.tldr: This paper compares five commercial machine interpreting (MI) systems against 26 human interpreters on English-to-Chinese simultaneous interpreting, finding that MI competitiveness depends sharply on discourse mode.
AI.motivation: Prior evaluations of machine interpreting often rely on a single discourse mode and frameworks misaligned with interpreting as a discourse-level communicative activity.
AI.method: The authors evaluate five commercial MI systems and 26 human interpreters (14 professionals, 12 advanced students) across planned formal speech and extemporaneous interview discourse, analyzing meaning, target-language quality, and code-level error profiles.
AI.result: In planned formal speech, the strongest MI system enters the upper human range on meaning, whereas in the extemporaneous interview no MI system approaches stronger human tiers; human interpreters maintain a more stable advantage in target-language quality and use selective omission and contextual inference, while MI systems suffer from semantic distortion, discourse-tracking failures, unintelligible output, and disfluency carryover.
