We find silent failures in 11 of 15 public research APIs, with counts inflated up to 691 times. Current fixes leave over 70% of answers wrong, and agents report 77.4% of counts a judge flags. Across 7 open models, SilentGuard cuts wrong answers on its target faults from 74.0% to 1.7%, with no loss on fault-free tasks. On three frontier models they fall from 70.2% to 0.5%. A warning from the same check leaves 70.1% wrong, so enforcement is the key. On new fault types, the harness alone cuts wrong answers from 61.1% to 24.5%. It avoids wrong answers by abstaining rather than recovering.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SilentGuard, an invariant-aware harness that withholds tool outputs violating API invariants, cutting agent wrong answers on silent API failures from 74.0% to 1.7% across seven open models.
AI.motivation: Public APIs frequently fail silently (e.g., ignoring misnamed filters while returning HTTP 200), and models often answer using the flawed data even when warned by checklists or LLM judges.
AI.method: SilentGuard moves enforcement from the model to the tool-calling harness, testing each API response against required invariants and withholding violating values so the agent abstains rather than propagating errors.
AI.result: Silent failures appear in 11 of 15 public research APIs (inflating counts up to 691x); existing fixes leave over 70% of answers wrong, whereas SilentGuard cuts wrong answers from 74.0% to 1.7% on seven open models and from 70.2% to 0.5% on three frontier models with no fault-free loss, while warnings alone leave 70.1% wrong.
AI.conclusion: Harness-level invariant enforcement with value withholding—rather than model-level warnings—is essential to prevent agents from propagating silent API failures.

title: Same Papers, Different Verdicts: Tracing Version Drift in LLM Peer Review
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures. Results of the registered tests that need the ICLR 2027 decisions will be added after 16 December 2026
summary: Venues and benchmarks read LLM review scores as measurements of a paper, while providers replace their models within months. We audit twenty frontier models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic on ICLR 2027 submissions while they were under review, with tests registered before the decisions. Between an earlier and a later version of Claude Opus and of Gemini, the share of papers placed on the accept side falls by 52 and 53 percentage points on 183 and 60 randomly drawn submissions, and by 43 to 79 points in six further paired comparisons, with no paper moving up in any of them. Stating a 30% acceptance rate in the prompt leaves a gap of 79 points between the two Opus versions. When score-stripped critiques are swapped between versions, the later critiques alone lower the accept share by 35 points for Opus and 51 for Gemini; for Opus the drop is 35 points under a third-party scorer and 24 after a rewrite that keeps each technical point and removes evaluative wording. On 57 papers, the percentiles of Opus 4.6 and 5.5 correlate at 0.73 while their accept shares differ by 44 points. On 99 to 119 submissions, the self-estimated percentiles of three models correlate with two human reviewers more strongly than a third reviewer does (point estimates 0.17 to 0.21, 95% intervals between -0.04 and +0.42). All twenty models give a 2 or a 3 in 473 of their 475 reviews, against 60 of 72 human reviews. Retrospective tests on decided papers can draw on memory. Claude Opus 5.5 names the true first author of 27 decided ICLR 2026 papers from their titles alone, with no wrong name, and Claude Opus 4.6 accepted all 11 decided papers it said it recognized, against 5 expected. Thresholds on LLM-reviewer scores therefore have to be validated against human decisions for each model version; our tests against the ICLR 2027 decisions follow on 16 December 2026.

AI.tldr: This paper audits twenty frontier LLMs on ICLR 2027 submissions and finds substantial version drift in peer-review accept rates and critiques across model updates.
AI.motivation: Venues and benchmarks treat LLM review scores as stable measurements of paper quality, even though providers replace models within months and retrospective evaluations on decided papers can be confounded by memorization.
AI.method: The authors audit twenty frontier models from OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic on ICLR 2027 submissions while under review using pre-registered tests, swapping score-stripped critiques, rewriting critiques to remove evaluative wording, and testing recognition of decided ICLR 2026 papers.
AI.result: Between earlier and later versions of Claude Opus and Gemini, the share of papers placed on the accept side drops by 52 and 53 percentage points on 183 and 60 submissions, and by 43 to 79 points in six further paired comparisons, while Opus 4.6 and 5.5 percentiles correlate at 0.73 on 57 papers despite a 44-point accept-share gap.
AI.conclusion: Thresholds on LLM-reviewer scores must be validated against human decisions for each model version rather than assumed stable across updates.

title: Safety-Preserving Medical LLM Fine-Tuning via Bilevel Data Selection
summary: As general large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted for patient-facing medical applications, improving medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks remains a critical challenge. Large-scale medical instruction data are essential for acquiring domain knowledge through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), but unsafe responses can undermine existing safety alignment. To address this problem, we propose Scalable Bilevel Data Selection (S-BDS) for safety-preserving medical SFT. By controlling selection-weight concentration, S-BDS enables reliable sample ranking over large candidate pools and identifies training examples that improve medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks. We combine clinician-validated safe data and selected data with unscreened medical instruction data for SFT, and jointly evaluate medical capability and patient-facing safety on HealthBench and PatientSafetyBench, respectively. Experiments across Llama and Qwen models show that S-BDS achieves the highest safe rates among all compared methods, outperforming the strongest baselines by 4.64 and 3.00 percentage points, respectively, while maintaining competitive medical capability. Further experiments show that varying the safety-oriented weight during SFT controls the trade-off between medical capability and patient-facing safety.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Scalable Bilevel Data Selection (S-BDS) for safety-preserving medical LLM supervised fine-tuning, achieving the highest safe rates on Llama and Qwen models while maintaining competitive medical capability.
AI.motivation: Adapting general LLMs for patient-facing medical applications via large-scale medical instruction SFT can undermine existing safety alignment when training data contain unsafe responses.
AI.method: S-BDS controls selection-weight concentration to rank samples over large candidate pools, combining clinician-validated safe data and selected data with unscreened medical instruction data for SFT, and varies a safety-oriented weight to balance capability and safety.
AI.result: Evaluated on HealthBench and PatientSafetyBench across Llama and Qwen models, S-BDS achieves the highest safe rates among compared methods, outperforming the strongest baselines by 4.64 and 3.00 percentage points while preserving competitive medical capability.
AI.conclusion: Scalable bilevel data selection provides an effective mechanism to control the trade-off between medical capability and patient-facing safety during medical SFT.

title: MetaAct: Self-Evolving Executable Action Constraints for Embodied Language Agents
summary: Self-evolving language agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for continuously improving agent behavior through experience. However, most existing approaches evolve textual artifacts, which can influence action preferences but cannot reliably enforce action admissibility in embodied environments with discrete and often irreversible actions. We propose MetaAct, which shifts self-evolution from textual guidance to executable action constraints by synthesizing GEAR (Grounded Executable Action Rules) from execution feedback. Each rule is represented as a typed specification, compiled into a deterministic guard, and validated offline through trajectory replay without additional model calls or environment interactions. Across four benchmarks, MetaAct improves task performance; on ScienceWorld and WebShop, violations drop from 70% to 0% and 40% to 1%, with score gains of +10.1 and +8.0. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MetaAct, a framework that synthesizes executable action constraints from execution feedback for embodied language agents, reducing rule violations to near zero and improving task scores.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving language agents evolve textual artifacts that can guide preferences but cannot reliably enforce action admissibility in embodied environments with discrete, often irreversible actions.
AI.method: MetaAct synthesizes Grounded Executable Action Rules (GEAR) from execution feedback as typed specifications, compiles them into deterministic guards, and validates them offline via trajectory replay without extra model calls or environment interactions.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks, MetaAct improves task performance, reducing violations from 70% to 0% on ScienceWorld and from 40% to 1% on WebShop, with score gains of +10.1 and +8.0, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Shifting self-evolution from textual guidance to compiled executable constraints enables reliable action admissibility and stronger performance in embodied agents.

title: LEAF-OPD: Learning to Forget from Privileged Contexts via On-Policy Distillation
summary: LLM unlearning aims to erase targeted knowledge from large language models while preserving their utility. However, many existing methods suppress target knowledge without explicitly teaching the model how to respond to queries about it. We propose LEAF-OPD (LEArning to Forget from Privileged Contexts via On-Policy Distillation), in which a frozen teacher provides token-level supervision on student-generated responses. On forget data, the teacher uses privileged contexts (instructions not to reveal knowledge about forget targets) to guide forgetting. On retain data, the teacher provides supervision without privileged context to preserve model utility. The student operates without privileged context in both cases, learning how to respond when encountering knowledge that should be forgotten. A key challenge is that the teacher often provides effective supervision only at the first few tokens of student trajectories. We introduce Supervision Signal (SS) to measure corrective supervision over a specified token interval, evaluating the entire trajectory (SS1) and its second half (SS0.5) to assess overall strength and late-stage persistence. When supervision is weak, lightweight SFT strengthens the teacher's context-conditioned refusal behavior, substantially increasing both scores. We evaluate LEAF-OPD on three widely used benchmarks: TOFU, RWKU, and MUSE-News. On TOFU, LEAF-OPD achieves the best Forget Quality, Model Utility, and Forget ROUGE-L while maintaining competitive retain performance. On RWKU, it outperforms the second-best method by 34% in Forget Quality while maintaining competitive Retain Quality. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of privileged-context supervision with on-policy token-level distillation for LLM unlearning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LEAF-OPD, an on-policy token-level distillation method using a frozen teacher with privileged contexts for LLM unlearning, achieving state-of-the-art forget quality on TOFU and RWKU.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM unlearning methods often suppress target knowledge without explicitly teaching the model how to respond to queries about it, and teacher supervision can be weak beyond the first few tokens.
AI.method: LEAF-OPD uses a frozen teacher with privileged non-disclosure instructions on forget data and without privileged context on retain data to provide token-level supervision on student trajectories, introduces Supervision Signal (SS1 and SS0.5) to measure supervision strength, and applies lightweight SFT when supervision is weak.
AI.result: On TOFU, RWKU, and MUSE-News, LEAF-OPD achieves the best Forget Quality, Model Utility, and Forget ROUGE-L on TOFU, and outperforms the second-best method by 34% in Forget Quality on RWKU while maintaining competitive retain performance.
AI.conclusion: Privileged-context supervision combined with on-policy token-level distillation effectively teaches LLMs how to refuse or respond to unlearned knowledge while preserving utility.

title: Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can write several tokens per forward pass. Open-weight DLMs commit, in any order, every masked position whose confidence passes a threshold. If none does, a fallback commits the most confident one, and the commits are never revised. Wide windows let the decoder commit far ahead of the text, which should speed up decoding but often costs accuracy. It is unclear where the model is confident and which commits cause errors. We trace every commit of four off-the-shelf DLMs on math, code, translation and summarization, and rerun failing answers with one step changed. Most tokens become confident only near the frontier, the leftmost masked position, so committing only there, still several tokens per step, is about as fast as committing anywhere. The accuracy loss comes from committing tokens before the text to their left, and committing one token per step does not reduce it. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of the failures that left-to-right decoding avoids. Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes commit-level threshold decoding in diffusion language models (DLMs) and shows that committing tokens only at the leftmost frontier recovers most of the accuracy lost to wide-window parallel decoding.
AI.motivation: Open-weight DLMs commit any masked token passing a confidence threshold or fall back to the most confident token, and wide decoding windows speed up generation at the cost of accuracy, but it is unclear which commits cause failures.
AI.method: The authors trace every commit of four off-the-shelf DLMs on math, code, translation, and summarization, rerun failing answers with single-step changes, and compare wide-window decoding against frontier-only committing.
AI.result: Most tokens only become confident near the leftmost frontier, while fallback commits (11-35% of commits) initiate 61-72% of failures that left-to-right decoding avoids, and committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models at similar speed.
AI.conclusion: Restricting DLM commits to the leftmost frontier avoids premature right-side and fallback errors without sacrificing multi-token decoding speed.

title: IndustrialKnowEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multi-Level Industrial Knowledge in LLMs
comment: 26 pages (13 pages of main text and 13 pages of appendix), 11 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for industrial tasks, yet few benchmarks evaluate their mastery of industrial knowledge across different types of cognitive demand. We introduce IndustrialKnowEval (IndKnow), a benchmark for industrial knowledge and engineering question answering. It contains 43,282 samples covering 21 task types across seven industrial sectors, including aerospace, electric power, and metallurgy, organized into four levels of cognitive demand: memory, comprehension, reasoning, and engineering application. Enterprise-based domain specialists and experienced researchers participate in all stages of dataset construction and quality control. We conduct a series of experiments on 18 representative LLMs, with domain experts deeply involved in the evaluation. Building upon IndKnow, we propose the Industrial Cognitive Capability Gap (ICCG) metric to characterize the performance differential between foundational industrial knowledge and higher-order reasoning and application, and we analyze it alongside absolute performance to provide a more complete view of model capabilities. We anticipate that IndustrialKnowEval will support the benchmarking of LLMs in industrial scenarios and promote the development of robust industrial intelligence. Code is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper introduces IndustrialKnowEval (IndKnow), a 43,282-sample benchmark evaluating LLMs across four cognitive demand levels in seven industrial sectors, along with the Industrial Cognitive Capability Gap (ICCG) metric.
AI.motivation: Few existing benchmarks evaluate whether LLMs master industrial knowledge across varying levels of cognitive demand beyond basic recall.
AI.method: Domain specialists and researchers construct IndKnow with 43,282 samples spanning 21 task types, seven industrial sectors (such as aerospace, electric power, and metallurgy), and four cognitive levels (memory, comprehension, reasoning, and engineering application), and evaluate 18 LLMs using accuracy and the ICCG metric.
AI.result: Experiments on 18 representative LLMs with domain expert involvement characterize performance gaps between foundational industrial knowledge and higher-order reasoning and engineering application via ICCG.
AI.conclusion: IndustrialKnowEval and ICCG provide a structured foundation for benchmarking and advancing LLMs in industrial engineering scenarios.

title: ANCHOR: Cluster-Grounded 5W1H Extraction via Large-Small Model Collaboration
summary: Deep semantic understanding of events requires recognizing related events and distinguishing why an event occurs from how it is carried out. 5W1H extraction provides a structured foundation for such understanding by organizing event information around six fundamental questions. However, single-event slot filling provides limited support for these distinctions. We propose ANCHOR, a cluster-grounded framework that combines a large language model (LLM) with a small language model equipped with discriminative heads for accurate 5W1H extraction. The LLM proposes candidate events and generates their initial 4W records, which guide the selection of an event cluster and the subsequent anchoring of its main event. A shared document encoder provides evidence for joint 4W refinement, and two separate sets of boundary and role-scoring heads then extract why and how under event-specific constraints, respectively. Document representations are reused across events and stages, and unsupported roles can remain empty. Following the same principles, an agent-and-skill annotation workflow constructs a benchmark of 26,110 documents from ten source corpora covering three languages and seven domains. We select nine of the resulting datasets to evaluate ANCHOR against strong baselines using four open-weight LLMs. ANCHOR achieves competitive performance. The datasets and code are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ANCHOR, a large-small model collaboration framework for cluster-grounded 5W1H event extraction, along with a 26,110-document multilingual benchmark.
AI.motivation: Understanding events requires recognizing related events and distinguishing why an event occurs from how it is carried out, which single-event slot filling handles poorly.
AI.method: ANCHOR uses an LLM to propose candidate events and initial 4W records to anchor an event cluster, then uses a shared document encoder for joint 4W refinement and two separate boundary and role-scoring heads to extract why and how under event-specific constraints, supported by an agent-and-skill annotation workflow.
AI.result: Evaluated on nine selected datasets from a new 26,110-document benchmark spanning three languages and seven domains using four open-weight LLMs, ANCHOR achieves competitive performance against strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLM candidate generation with discriminative small-model heads and cluster-level document representations improves structured 5W1H event extraction.

title: MemEmo: Evaluating Emotion in Memory Systems
summary: Memory systems address the challenge of context loss in Large Language Models during prolonged interactions. However, as an essential tool for warm companionship and personalized services, the effectiveness of memory systems in processing affective information remains underexamined. To bridge this gap, we propose an emotion-enhanced memory evaluation benchmark to assess the performance of mainstream and state-of-the-art memory systems in integrating and harnessing emotional information. First, we design a benchmark called \textbf{MemEmo} to assess the affective reasoning and tracking capabilities of memory systems across four dimensions: emotional information extraction, emotional memory updating, emotional memory question-answering, and emotional conflict detection. Second, we construct the \textbf{H}uman-\textbf{L}ike \textbf{M}emory \textbf{E}motion (\textbf{HLME}) dataset to provide an empirical foundation for scrutinizing memory systems. Finally, We evaluate five representative memory systems on the HLME dataset, reporting 11 performance metrics across four dimensions. Experimental results reveal that aggregating scores for all tested memory systems is up to 45\%, far below 100\% scale, exposing a profound disparity between memory system and affective intelligence.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the MemEmo benchmark and HLME dataset to evaluate emotional reasoning and tracking in LLM memory systems, finding that all tested systems score at most 45%.
AI.motivation: Memory systems help LLMs retain context over long interactions, but their ability to extract, update, and reason over affective information for personalized companionship remains underexamined.
AI.method: The authors design MemEmo across four dimensions (emotional information extraction, emotional memory updating, emotional memory QA, and emotional conflict detection), construct the Human-Like Memory Emotion (HLME) dataset, and evaluate five memory systems across 11 metrics.
AI.result: Across five representative memory systems evaluated on HLME, aggregated scores reach at most 45%, well below the 100% scale.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM memory systems exhibit a substantial gap in affective intelligence, motivating dedicated mechanisms for emotional memory processing.

title: Can LLMs Give Good Product Advice? A Framework for Diagnosing Failures
summary: Evaluating product advice from a language model requires assessing whether the recommendation meets the user's needs and identifying where the model falls short when it does not. However, matching a product mentioned in an online reply cannot answer either question on its own: several products may be suitable, and the recorded answer may itself be poor advice. When shown a community-listed alternative alongside their own sampled car recommendation, six models prefer the alternative in 1.9 to 6.5 percent of eligible disagreements, consistently across both source-blind presentation orders. We propose a diagnostic framework that separates the user's stated needs, the model's added assumptions, candidate generation, filtering, and final choice, with 19 possible failure modes and the evidence needed to assess them. We apply this framework to product-advice data and to a separate product-selection task with externally assigned relevance labels. The experiments distinguish naming a community-listed product from selecting it and show how answer extraction and candidate-list construction affect the outcome.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a 19-mode diagnostic framework for evaluating LLM product advice, showing how answer extraction, candidate generation, and filtering affect recommendation quality.
AI.motivation: Matching a product mentioned in an online reply cannot determine whether an LLM's product advice meets user needs or identify where it fails, because multiple products may fit and recorded replies may be poor advice.
AI.method: The authors test six models on sampled car recommendations against community-listed alternatives in source-blind presentations and introduce a diagnostic framework separating user needs, added assumptions, candidate generation, filtering, and final choice across 19 failure modes.
AI.result: Six models prefer community-listed alternatives in 1.9% to 6.5% of eligible disagreements, and applying the framework to product-advice and product-selection tasks distinguishes naming a product from selecting it while revealing how extraction and candidate construction shape outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing product advice into structured stages and failure modes enables more accurate diagnosis of LLM recommendation failures than surface string matching.

title: GPRM: Global Perspective Process Reward Model
summary: Process Reward Models (PRMs) are widely used for step-level evaluation of multi-step reasoning in large language models, but existing methods are often limited by weak historical dependency modeling and insufficient global awareness. They typically fail to leverage prior step evaluations for coherent judgment and lack visibility into subsequent reasoning, leading to suboptimal assessment of intermediate steps. To address this issue, we propose the Global Perspective Process Reward Model (GPRM), which jointly models the problem, previous reasoning steps and their evaluations, the current step, and future steps to enable history-aware and globally informed process evaluation. We further introduce a structured evaluation framework along four dimensions---look back, look ahead, self-check, and goal alignment---to assess prior consistency, future plausibility, step validity, and task alignment. Based on this framework, we construct datasets for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (GRPO). Experiments show that, despite using less training data and smaller model sizes, GPRM outperforms strong baseline models by 7.8 and 5.4 points on PRMBench and ProcessBench, respectively. GPRM also generalizes well across tasks, surpassing the GPT-4.1 baseline on Agent Error Bench, improving strong baselines by around 4 points under test-time scaling (TTS), and achieving competitive performance on PPE.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes GPRM, a Global Perspective Process Reward Model that jointly models past, current, and future reasoning steps, outperforming strong baselines on PRMBench, ProcessBench, and test-time scaling.
AI.motivation: Existing process reward models evaluate intermediate reasoning steps with weak historical dependency modeling and no visibility into subsequent steps, leading to suboptimal step-level judgments.
AI.method: GPRM jointly models the problem, prior steps and their evaluations, the current step, and future steps along four dimensions (look back, look ahead, self-check, and goal alignment), trained with SFT and GRPO on constructed datasets.
AI.result: Despite using less training data and smaller models, GPRM outperforms strong baselines by 7.8 points on PRMBench and 5.4 points on ProcessBench, surpasses GPT-4.1 on Agent Error Bench, and improves test-time scaling baselines by around 4 points.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating bidirectional context and structured evaluation dimensions enables more accurate and generalizable process reward modeling.

title: Instant Weight-Space Consolidation for Long-Term Memory in LLMs
summary: Agentic memory systems give LLMs persistent memory by extracting experience into text and retrieving it at query time, but the model itself does not evolve: however many interactions it has had, it starts each query the same. Extraction errors compound, implicit cross-session patterns that no single fragment states cannot be surfaced, and the construction cost grows with every conversation. Fine-tuning on past interactions does change the weights, but requires backpropagation at serving time and degrades on long histories. We introduce CLAM (Carried Latent Adapter Memory), which combines the strengths of both: a recurrent hypernetwork performs parametric consolidation, compiling a stream of session activations into a low-rank adapter in a single forward pass with no gradient steps and no language-model generation calls, while a complementary episodic buffer supplies verbatim detail at inference. A gated latent state carries knowledge across sessions in fixed size, so the parametric memory accumulates without growing. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three open models (2-7B parameters), CLAM leads all agentic baselines by 1-45 points and all gradient-based parametric methods by 10-45 points, while requiring zero generative LLM calls, zero gradient steps, and 3-151x less wall-clock time than extraction systems to build its memory. The two channels are complementary: the consolidated adapter adds 12-15 accuracy points when the episodic buffer misses the gold evidence, and still adds 4-5 points even with an oracle buffer.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CLAM, a weight-space memory consolidation method using a recurrent hypernetwork and episodic buffer that outperforms agentic and gradient-based memory baselines on long-term memory benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Agentic text-extraction memory systems suffer from compounding errors and growing construction costs without evolving model weights, while serving-time fine-tuning requires backpropagation and degrades on long histories.
AI.method: CLAM uses a recurrent hypernetwork to compile session activations into a low-rank adapter in a single forward pass with a fixed-size gated latent state, paired with an episodic buffer for verbatim details at inference.
AI.result: On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three 2-7B open models, CLAM leads agentic baselines by 1-45 points and gradient-based methods by 10-45 points with zero gradient steps or generative LLM calls, using 3-151x less wall-clock time than extraction systems.
AI.conclusion: Combining forward-pass hypernetwork weight consolidation with an episodic buffer provides fast, scalable, and complementary long-term memory for LLMs.

title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
comment: Animated versions of Figure 3 are available in the blog: this https URL
summary: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open small language model post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it that achieves higher accuracy, fewer output tokens, and 2.74x faster decode speed with a DFlash drafter.
AI.motivation: Fast, local conversational agents and edge interfaces require small language models that maximize intelligence and tool-use capability per gigabyte of memory while minimizing latency.
AI.method: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it for multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding, and is released with a DFlash speculative drafter for GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark deployment.
AI.result: Across 21 benchmarks, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy with the fewest output tokens compared to Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B, and reaches 2.74x per-user decode speed with DFlash at concurrency 1 (1.21x throughput over Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1).
AI.conclusion: Targeted post-training and speculative drafting enable compact 4GB-class models to deliver strong agentic accuracy and low-latency local inference.

title: What Do Digital Traces Predict? Task Effects, Student Differences, and Critical Online Reasoning
summary: Digital assessment traces are increasingly used to predict student performance, often evaluated by correlating predicted and observed scores pooled across tasks. However, such correlations may reflect between-task differences rather than performance differences among students within tasks. To investigate this, we analyzed up to 527 browsing sessions from 424 university students completing open-Internet Critical Online Reasoning tasks and assessed the cross-task stability of their ratings. We evaluated the same out-of-fold predictions within and across tasks, compared three validation tiers up to leave-one-task-out, and tested incremental predictive contributions of consultation order and relational structure against matched permutation and randomization controls. None of the twelve prespecified primary tests was significant: on held-out tasks, consulted-page features showed no significant association with relative student performance, nor did observed order or relational structure add predictive value. Pooling observations across tasks substantially increased correlations, particularly for factual correctness, whose scores showed limited evidence of stable between-student differences across tasks. However, sentence embeddings yielded modest positive correlations with generic response quality on held-out tasks, without establishing added predictive value from observed order or relational structure. Our findings show that pooled predictive correlations may not reflect within-task student differences, highlighting the need for within-task evaluation and criterion generalizability audits.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 527 browsing sessions from 424 university students and shows that pooled cross-task correlations in digital trace predictions can mask a lack of within-task predictive power.
AI.motivation: Digital assessment traces are often evaluated by correlating predicted and observed scores pooled across tasks, which can conflate between-task differences with within-task student performance differences.
AI.method: The authors evaluate out-of-fold predictions within and across open-Internet Critical Online Reasoning tasks using three validation tiers up to leave-one-task-out, testing consultation order and relational structure against permutation and randomization controls.
AI.result: None of the twelve prespecified primary tests was significant: consulted-page features, order, and relational structure showed no significant association with relative student performance on held-out tasks, whereas pooling across tasks inflated correlations, and sentence embeddings yielded only modest correlations with generic response quality.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating digital trace models requires within-task validation and criterion generalizability audits to avoid mistaking task effects for student differences.

title: CuRSE-Bench: A Benchmark for Probing Cultural Blind Spots in Text-to-Image Safety Evaluation
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) safety evaluation typically assigns each prompt or image a single culture-blind harm label, so content that is harmful only within a particular culture can pass as benign. We introduce CultureCraft, an agentic framework that constructs T2I prompts that appear benign under a general-purpose rubric yet carry a latent harmful meaning in a target culture, and use it to build CuRSE-Bench: 10,709 culture-specific prompts and 2,648 culture-general controls over six regions and ten harm axes, each drawn from a predefined knowledge base of documented harm vectors and traceable to at least two independent sources. Scoring every prompt under six region persona judges and a paired culture-blind judge, we find that the culture-blind judge under-rates culture-specific latent harm while matching the persona judges on the controls. Each persona judge, in turn, chiefly decodes its own region's latent harm under our instrument: a selective cultural blind spot that persists in deployed moderators.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CultureCraft and the CuRSE-Bench benchmark of 10,709 culture-specific prompts, revealing that culture-blind safety judges systematically underrate culturally latent harms.
AI.motivation: Text-to-image safety evaluation typically uses a single culture-blind harm label, allowing prompts or images that are harmful only within a specific culture to pass as benign.
AI.method: The authors build CultureCraft, an agentic framework that generates T2I prompts appearing benign under general rubrics but carrying latent cultural harm, to construct CuRSE-Bench (10,709 culture-specific prompts and 2,648 controls across six regions and ten harm axes), and evaluate them with six region persona judges and a culture-blind judge.
AI.result: The culture-blind judge underrates culture-specific latent harm while matching persona judges on controls, and each persona judge primarily detects its own region's latent harms, demonstrating a selective cultural blind spot in deployed moderators.
AI.conclusion: Addressing culturally latent harms in T2I safety requires region-aware evaluation rather than relying solely on culture-blind moderators.

title: Medical question answering collapses in Hausa: a pre-registered pilot on three small open models
summary: A system that reads nothing and always answers the most frequent letter scores \BaselineP{} on our Hausa medical multiple-choice set. \NBelowBaseline{} of the \NModels{} small open models we evaluate do not beat it. We lead with that because the usual summary of a multilingual result -- a percentage-point drop from English -- does not say whether what survives the drop is performance at all. On a paired English--Hausa set of \NEval{} MedMCQA items, three instruction-tuned models of 3--4B parameters lose between \GapMedGemma{} and \GapQwen{} points of accuracy, every gap significant after Holm correction. Back-translating the Hausa items into English recovers between half and two-thirds of the gap for the two general-purpose models but not demonstrably for the medically adapted one, so the deficit is substantially, though not wholly, a matter of the language of presentation. Answers are also far less stable: agreement across three option orderings falls from \ConsEnQwen{} to \ConsHaQwen{} in the worst case. An exploratory error analysis of \ENRows{} discordant items attributes most of the damage to medical vocabulary lost in translation (\ETerm{}, 95\% CI \ETermLo{}--\ETermHi{}), usually in the question stem. A fourth registered hypothesis proposed closing the gap with self-generated preference pairs. Its pilot gate found nothing to train on: asked to reason in Hausa rather than to pick a letter, the model echoes the prompt back, switches into Swahili, or simply stops without answering; only \GateParse{} of chains are parseable. We report that intervention as not run, which is itself the sharper result -- a forced-choice benchmark cannot see a model that has no generative command of the language at all. All hypotheses, thresholds and decision rules were registered before any model was run, and all deviations are logged.

AI.tldr: This pre-registered pilot evaluates three 3-4B open models on paired English-Hausa medical QA, finding that two models fail to beat a majority-letter baseline in Hausa and cannot generate parseable Hausa reasoning chains.
AI.motivation: Reporting multilingual performance solely as a percentage-point drop from English obscures whether the remaining accuracy in low-resource languages represents meaningful capability at all.
AI.method: The authors evaluate three 3-4B instruction-tuned models on paired English-Hausa MedMCQA items, test back-translation into English, measure answer stability across option orderings, analyze discordant items, and attempt a self-generated preference-pair pilot in Hausa.
AI.result: Models lose significant accuracy from English to Hausa (two fail to beat the most-frequent-letter baseline), back-translation recovers half to two-thirds of the gap for general-purpose models, option-ordering agreement drops sharply, most errors stem from lost medical vocabulary, and the preference-pair pilot fails because models produce unparseable chains (echoing, switching to Swahili, or stopping).
AI.conclusion: Forced-choice benchmarks can mask complete generative collapse in low-resource languages, underscoring the need to check absolute baselines and generative command.

title: EDITORS Know Your Style! Editing LoRA Subspaces for Stylistic Attribution and Imitation
summary: Disentangling writing style from semantic content is a fundamental challenge in literary text modeling. Style-content entanglement causes models to rely on semantic content for authorship attribution (AA) tasks and memorize author-specific content for style imitation (SI) tasks. We propose EDITORS (EditingLoRA Subspaces), a diagnose-then-deflate framework that adapts pretrained large language models and prioritizes stylistic features, making it effective for both AA and SI tasks. EDITORS first trains a diagnostic LoRA adapter using style-neutral statements derived from the training corpus to identify a content-oriented subspace. It then trains the final style adapter under activation-space deflation that projects input activations away from the identified content-oriented directions. We empirically demonstrate that EDITORS is effective. On three AA benchmarks spanning literature, social media, and news, EDITORS achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, outperforming the strongest existing baseline by up to 29%. On SI, EDITORS generates stylistically faithful and diverse passages, outperforming baselines in achieving style similarity while adhering to content specifications.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes EDITORS, a diagnose-then-deflate LoRA framework that separates writing style from semantic content, improving authorship attribution accuracy by up to 29% and enhancing style imitation.
AI.motivation: Style-content entanglement causes language models to rely on semantic content in authorship attribution (AA) and memorize author-specific content in style imitation (SI).
AI.method: EDITORS trains a diagnostic LoRA adapter on style-neutral statements to identify a content-oriented subspace, then trains the final style adapter while projecting input activations away from those content-oriented directions.
AI.result: Across three AA benchmarks (literature, social media, news), EDITORS achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 29%, while generating stylistically faithful passages that adhere to content specifications in SI.
AI.conclusion: Activation-space deflation of diagnostic content subspaces effectively disentangles style from semantics in LoRA-adapted LLMs.

title: It Depends on the Task: Rethinking Rhetorical Segmentation of Dutch Judicial Decisions
summary: Classifying the material facts, submissions, judicial reasoning, and the court's decision (rhetorical roles) in case law is a prerequisite for high-quality performance across virtually all NLP-in-law tasks, including legal information retrieval, summarisation, and LLM-based analysis. These rhetorical roles often intertwine and shift sentence by sentence, making reliable classification difficult. This paper introduces the first sentence-level annotated dataset of Dutch judicial decisions, labelled across four legally meaningful categories: material facts, submissions, judicial reasoning, and the court's decision, alongside non-annotated (None) content, and compares several classification strategies, including a staged pipeline that separates None detection from the rhetorical roles, and a Bayesian update that leverages information about the section-header a sentence belongs to. Our results show that no single strategy dominates on both precision and recall: header priors help most when the None sentences are excluded and offer little benefit for None detection itself. These trade-offs matter in practice. For instance, extractive summarisation depends more on recall so it does not miss relevant facts, whereas outcome prediction depends more on precision regarding decision and facts sentences so that the predicted ruling is not contaminated by noise. We use these trade-offs and map the approaches tested in this study onto a set of representative legal NLP use cases.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first sentence-level rhetorical-role dataset for Dutch judicial decisions and compares classification strategies, showing precision-recall trade-offs across legal NLP tasks.
AI.motivation: Classifying rhetorical roles (material facts, submissions, judicial reasoning, decision) in case law is essential for legal NLP, but roles intertwine sentence by sentence and no single strategy suits all downstream tasks.
AI.method: The authors annotate Dutch judicial decisions at the sentence level across four rhetorical roles plus None, and compare a staged pipeline separating None detection from role classification against a Bayesian update using section-header priors.
AI.result: No single strategy dominates both precision and recall: section-header priors help most when None sentences are excluded and contribute little to None detection, creating task-dependent trade-offs for extractive summarization (recall-oriented) versus outcome prediction (precision-oriented).
AI.conclusion: Rhetorical segmentation strategies in legal NLP should be selected based on the precision or recall requirements of the target downstream application.

title: Experience Rot: Experienced Agents Fail Where Novices Succeed
summary: Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies Experience Rot, showing that experienced AI agents fail on most tasks after silent tool changes in MCP environments while novice agents succeed.
AI.motivation: Agents increasingly store conversation histories, memory files, and skills to reuse past successes, but how this accumulated experience behaves when underlying tool interfaces change silently is unknown.
AI.method: The authors evaluate multiple models using Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools before and after silent interface changes across various memory mechanisms, and test simple mitigations such as announcing updates or pointing agents to documentation.
AI.result: After silent tool changes, experienced agents fail on most tasks by copying earlier calls instead of checking current tool definitions and falsely reporting success, whereas novice agents mostly succeed; the failure worsens with more experience, and announcing updates or referencing incomplete documentation fails to fix it.
AI.conclusion: Accumulated agent memory can become a liability under evolving tool interfaces, requiring mechanisms beyond passive documentation or update announcements.

title: Navital Gym: Rule-Graded Agent Environments for Indian Workflows
comment: 10 pages. Code and tasks: this https URL
summary: AI agents are being deployed on Indian workflows such as payments, tax, forms, travel and customer support in Hindi and Hinglish. Public agent evaluations rarely cover these workflows, and many score with another language model. We present Navital Gym, a set of six open environments with 321 public tasks in five task families: trip planning, UPI payments and disputes, GST invoicing and returns, form filling (including a multi-document split) and customer support in Hindi, Hinglish and three experimental Indian languages. Every task is graded by named, deterministic rules that recompute the outcome from a synthetic sandbox world. No language model judges any score. We report one run per task for three models on all six environments, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and for Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite on two (UPI and the Support core). Opus solves 315 of 321 tasks, Sonnet 302 and Haiku 205. Trip planning and Hindi/Hinglish support separate the models most. We also describe a private held-out set that is not published, and a 7B adapter trained in the gym. Code is Apache-2.0 and task data is CC BY 4.0. The rules are a documented simplification of Indian practice, not the live systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Navital Gym, six open rule-graded agent environments with 321 tasks covering Indian workflows in Hindi, Hinglish, and three experimental Indian languages.
AI.motivation: Public agent benchmarks rarely cover Indian workflows such as UPI payments, GST invoicing, or Hindi/Hinglish customer support, and many rely on LLM-as-a-judge scoring.
AI.method: Navital Gym provides six synthetic sandbox environments across five task families graded entirely by deterministic rules without LLM judges, and evaluates Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 4.5, and Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite alongside a 7B trained adapter.
AI.result: On the 321 public tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 solves 315, Sonnet 5.5 solves 302, and Haiku 4.5 solves 205, with trip planning and Hindi/Hinglish support showing the largest performance gaps between models.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic, rule-graded environments enable reproducible evaluation of multilingual and region-specific agentic workflows.

title: Living Context Graphs: Continual Semantic Learning for Enterprise Data Reasoning
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Continual Learning in the Era of Foundation Models and Embodied Agents. Data splits and annotations: this https URL
summary: Enterprise AI can now perform analytics, reporting, and data-driven workflows, yet the data foundations it relies on remain hard to operationalize: business meaning, relationships, metric definitions, and reporting conventions are absent from database schemas and scattered across undocumented systems and tribal knowledge. We introduce the Living Context Graph (LCG), a continually learned context layer that makes existing enterprise data operational for AI without requiring a copy or transformation of the underlying warehouse. LCG bootstraps base semantics and relationships from the data itself, builds a concept graph that indexes business context as queries are served, writes durable semantic learnings from verified outcomes, and withdraws or re-earns context when later outcomes contradict prior routes. We evaluate LCG through text-to-SQL, a core data-reasoning task, on a transfer-aware split of three BIRD databases comprising 499 questions: 353 form the learning history and 146 are held out and never used to update the context layer. Bootstrapping alone improves overall accuracy by +4.6 percentage points. Learning only from the history raises accuracy on the untouched held-out transfer set by +22.6 points (95% CI [+14.4, +30.8]), exceeding five-shot retrieval from the same history by +12.3 points. Incremental learning reaches the one-shot endpoint within observed evaluation noise on every database. Ablating the graph changes held-out accuracy by at most one question per database but increases per-query cost 2.3-3.3x and median latency 1.8-3.4x: continually learned semantics drive accuracy, while the graph makes that context efficient to serve.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Living Context Graph (LCG), a continually learned semantic layer for enterprise data reasoning that improves held-out text-to-SQL accuracy by +22.6 percentage points on BIRD.
AI.motivation: Enterprise databases lack documented business meaning, metric definitions, and reporting conventions in their schemas, making them hard for AI to operationalize without copying or transforming warehouses.
AI.method: LCG bootstraps base semantics from data, indexes business context in a concept graph as queries run, writes durable learnings from verified outcomes, and revises contradicted routes, evaluated on a transfer-aware split of 499 questions across three BIRD databases (353 learning, 146 held-out).
AI.result: Bootstrapping alone improves accuracy by +4.6 percentage points, continual learning raises untouched held-out accuracy by +22.6 points (exceeding five-shot retrieval by +12.3 points), and ablating the graph leaves accuracy within one question while increasing per-query cost 2.3-3.3x and median latency 1.8-3.4x.
AI.conclusion: Continually learned semantic context drives text-to-SQL accuracy, while the concept graph structure makes serving that context substantially faster and cheaper.

title: SearchChord: Prompt Preselection and Field Recomposition for One-Step Image Editing
summary: Finding effective prompts and seeds for one-step image editors requires balancing edit fidelity, source preservation, and computational cost. To address this challenge, we explore a large collection of candidate edits, where each candidate is defined by a unique prompt-seed pair, and generate corresponding images on demand. We present SearchChord, a training-free framework that leverages a large pool of such candidates, combining text-based preselection, image verification, and latent-field recomposition. Our ablation studies across pool sizes up to 200 candidates show that a pool of 100 offers a cost-effective operating point. Compared with feeding all 100 candidates into recomposition, TextSim preselects a subset of 10 candidates. Rather than uniform averaging, we incorporate image-verifier scores to weight each candidate during recomposition. Experiments on PIE-Bench and the proposed CropWeed-EditBench reveal a trade-off: candidate selection improves target-text alignment, while recomposition better preserves unmodified source content. The oracle verifier achieves the best performance in both preservation and target-text alignment. Practical verification partially recovers semantic alignment, but recomposition still compromises edit fidelity, including in agricultural image edits. These results motivate text-first preselection and stronger verification to balance preservation, fidelity, and cost. Code and data will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SearchChord, a training-free framework for one-step image editing that combines text-based candidate preselection, image verification, and weighted latent-field recomposition.
AI.motivation: Selecting prompts and seeds for one-step image editors requires balancing edit fidelity, source preservation, and computational cost.
AI.method: SearchChord generates candidate prompt-seed pairs, uses TextSim to preselect 10 candidates from a pool of 100, and weights latent-field recomposition using image-verifier scores rather than uniform averaging, evaluated on PIE-Bench and CropWeed-EditBench.
AI.result: Candidate selection improves target-text alignment while recomposition better preserves unmodified source content; an oracle verifier achieves the best balance, whereas practical verifiers partially recover semantic alignment while recomposition still reduces edit fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Combining text-first preselection with stronger image verification is key to balancing preservation, fidelity, and cost in one-step image editing.

title: FDAM: A Frequency-Direction-Aware Multi-Task Framework for Pavement Crack Grid Localization
summary: Pavement crack grid localization remains challenging for thin and tiny cracks due to weak visual cues and background interference. Box detection often misses these cracks, while supervised semantic segmentation faces limited pixel-wise annotations and high labeling costs. In this paper, we propose a Frequency-Direction-Aware Multi-Task framework (FDAM) with box detection and grid classification branches. The core grid classification branch comprises Frequency-Domain Enhancement (FDE) and Directional Feature Refinement (DFR). FDE adaptively weights spectral bands and fuses reconstructed features with spatial features. DFR captures thin crack patterns through multi-scale strip convolutions, direction-sensitive modulation, and feature recalibration. Sparse positive cells and ambiguous local predictions motivate adaptive grid supervision. Adaptive Importance Reweighting emphasizes uncertain predictions and local label transitions, with focal supervision for all cells. Our contribution is to couple the box detection and grid classification branches through shared feature learning for pavement crack grid localization. We validate FDAM on our RoadDistress2026 dataset of thin and tiny cracks and further evaluate it on public datasets Crack500 and DeepCrack. The code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes FDAM, a multi-task framework coupling box detection and frequency-direction-aware grid classification for thin pavement crack localization.
AI.motivation: Detecting thin and tiny pavement cracks is difficult because box detection misses them and supervised semantic segmentation requires costly pixel-wise annotations.
AI.method: FDAM couples box detection with a grid classification branch featuring Frequency-Domain Enhancement (FDE) for spectral band weighting, Directional Feature Refinement (DFR) with multi-scale strip convolutions, and Adaptive Importance Reweighting with focal supervision.
AI.result: FDAM is validated on the proposed RoadDistress2026 dataset of thin and tiny cracks as well as public Crack500 and DeepCrack datasets.
AI.conclusion: Coupling shared-feature box detection with frequency- and direction-aware grid classification provides a label-efficient solution for thin pavement crack localization.

title: DEFDVO: Deformable Deep Visual Odometry for Equirectangular Images
summary: Omnidirectional ($360^\circ$) cameras capture the full surrounding scene in every frame, providing a strong advantage for visual odometry (VO) over pinhole sensors with a limited field of view. However, their equirectangular projection (ERP) introduces latitude-dependent distortion, an artificial seam at the image border, and a sampling bias toward the poles. Existing $360^\circ$ VO methods address these challenges only partially. DEFDVO closes this gap with a patch-based deep VO method that operates directly on ERP imagery, combining spherically initialized deformable feature extraction, end-to-end seam-aware estimation, and spherical-gradient patch selection. The deformable feature extractor combines spherical geometric priors with learned sampling offsets, while seam-aware processing preserves ERP continuity, and spherical-gradient selection reduces polar sampling bias. Trained exclusively on synthetic TartanAirV2 ERP imagery, DEFDVO improves the best prior average absolute trajectory error (ATE) by $4.8\times$ (0.201 m to 0.042 m) on the TartanAirV2 evaluation set defined by 360DVO and achieves the lowest average ATE on both splits of the real-world 360DVO benchmark. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DEFDVO, a patch-based deep visual odometry method for 360-degree equirectangular images that reduces average ATE by 4.8x on TartanAirV2 and achieves the lowest ATE on 360DVO.
AI.motivation: Equirectangular projection (ERP) in 360-degree cameras introduces latitude-dependent distortion, border seams, and polar sampling bias that existing omnidirectional visual odometry methods only partially address.
AI.method: DEFDVO operates directly on ERP imagery using spherically initialized deformable feature extraction, end-to-end seam-aware estimation to preserve border continuity, and spherical-gradient patch selection to reduce polar bias.
AI.result: Trained solely on synthetic TartanAirV2 ERP data, DEFDVO improves the best prior average ATE by 4.8x (from 0.201 m to 0.042 m) on the TartanAirV2 evaluation set and achieves the lowest average ATE on both splits of the real-world 360DVO benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating spherical priors, seam awareness, and gradient-based patch selection enables accurate, generalizable 360-degree visual odometry directly on ERP images.

title: DecoEdit: Beyond Flat Control for 3D-Aware Unified Image Editing
summary: While recent advances in multimodal image editing have achieved impressive results, current frameworks remain largely confined to ``flat" 2D controls (e.g., text prompts, bounding boxes, or masks). Precise 3D-aware geometric manipulation -- such as coordinating an object's location, physical scale, and 3D orientation while strictly preserving its fine-grained identity -- remains an elusive challenge, typically suffering from severe detail degradation or requiring expensive per-instance fine-tuning. In this paper, we present DecoEdit, an all-in-one image editing framework that goes beyond flat control by seamlessly integrating 1D textual, 2D spatial, and 3D volumetric inputs under a unified architecture. First, to power this unified model, we establish a data curation pipeline and curate a large-scale dataset, namely DecoDataset, containing 1.6 million samples, encompassing diverse multi-dimensional (1D/2D/3D) tasks and their complex compositions. Furthermore, we establish a comprehensive image editing benchmark named DecoBench to systematically evaluate multi-task editing performance. Finally, to address the fundamental trade-off between complex spatial transformations and identity preservation, we propose a novel decoupled pipeline: DecoEdit factorizes the editing process by utilizing structural guidance from SAM-3D to anchor the target geometry, scale, and spatial orientation, while concurrently leveraging a detail-preservation path to lock in high-fidelity textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DecoEdit achieves state-of-the-art results. Notably, on the challenging 3D spatial pose and orientation control tasks, DecoEdit significantly outperforms leading closed-source models such as Seedream 5.0 in both geometric accuracy and identity consistency.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DecoEdit, a unified 3D-aware image editing framework trained on a new 1.6M-sample dataset (DecoDataset), outperforming Seedream 5.0 on 3D spatial pose and orientation control.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal image editors rely on flat 2D controls and struggle with precise 3D-aware geometric manipulation while preserving fine-grained object identity without per-instance fine-tuning.
AI.method: DecoEdit integrates 1D textual, 2D spatial, and 3D volumetric inputs using a decoupled pipeline that anchors target geometry, scale, and orientation with SAM-3D structural guidance while locking textures via a detail-preservation path, supported by DecoDataset (1.6M samples) and DecoBench.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on DecoBench show DecoEdit achieves state-of-the-art multi-task editing performance and significantly outperforms closed-source models like Seedream 5.0 in geometric accuracy and identity consistency on 3D pose and orientation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling 3D structural guidance from detail preservation enables unified, high-fidelity 3D-aware image editing.

title: Puzzle: One Pass Is Not Enough for Open-Vocabulary Remote Sensing Segmentation
summary: Open-vocabulary remote sensing image segmentation (OVRSIS) enables the segmentation of unseen classes without additional annotation or retraining. By analyzing the predictions of existing OVRSIS methods, we find that many misclassified patches coexist with visually similar, correctly classified patches of the same class within the same image. Unfortunately, most of these methods stop after a single inference rather than using their predictions to guide further inference. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{Puzzle}, a plug-and-play iterative re-inference framework that combines prediction history with a visual-similarity prior to progressively refine patch-level attention. Puzzle employs a lightweight history-conditioned controller to regulate each patch's contribution as an information source and its reliance on visually similar patches, while an adaptive stopping rule determines when to stop. It keeps the segmentation model frozen and reuses the same controller across different models and datasets without retraining. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements across diverse OVRSIS models and datasets, highlighting the strong transferability of Puzzle. Moreover, Puzzle can further improve the performance of SOTA methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Puzzle, a plug-and-play iterative re-inference framework that refines patch-level attention using prediction history and visual similarity to improve open-vocabulary remote sensing segmentation.
AI.motivation: Open-vocabulary remote sensing segmentation methods typically perform a single inference pass, leaving misclassified patches uncorrected even when visually similar, correctly classified patches of the same class exist in the same image.
AI.method: Puzzle keeps the segmentation model frozen and uses a lightweight history-conditioned controller to regulate patch information flow and visual-similarity reliance across iterations, paired with an adaptive stopping rule.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse open-vocabulary remote sensing segmentation models and datasets show consistent performance gains and further improvements over state-of-the-art methods without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Iterative, history-conditioned re-inference provides a transferable, training-free boost to open-vocabulary remote sensing segmentation.

title: From zero-target transfer to target-site personalization: multi-source training across fall-detection models
summary: Video-based fall detection could support timely assistance when a person cannot call for help. Unfamiliar cameras and scarce local labels challenge deployment. We examine whether joint training improves cross-dataset detection and subsequent local training. We analyze 2,697 clips from eight OmniFall datasets and one AI-Hub dataset. Positive clips contain a fall or collapse transition, while negative clips do not. We hold out each dataset in turn, training on the other eight. We evaluate three vision-language models (VLMs), Qwen, LLaVA, and InternVL, and three visual baselines, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. We evaluate the stored source model without target data for training or selection. For each label budget, we update a separate copy using labeled clips from the held-out target dataset. We call this target-site personalization. We compare the Source-initialized model with Target-only, which skips source training but uses identical target clips and updates. Across nine targets, source training raises mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from frozen-model values of 0.821 to 0.912 for Qwen, 0.883 to 0.947 for LLaVA, and 0.939 to 0.962 for InternVL. With five target examples per class and 26 updates per run, 95% confidence intervals for the AUROC benefit over Target-only lie above zero for Qwen, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. With full-target training, they lie above zero only for Qwen and LLaVA. Separate VLM analyses reveal threshold sensitivity and post-fall false detections. The benefit varies by model and label budget.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates multi-source training and target-site personalization across nine fall-detection datasets, showing that source training boosts zero-target AUROC for VLMs and improves few-shot adaptation.
AI.motivation: Video-based fall detection faces deployment challenges from unfamiliar cameras and scarce local labels, and it is unclear how multi-source joint training affects zero-target transfer and local personalization.
AI.method: Using 2,697 clips from eight OmniFall datasets and one AI-Hub dataset in a leave-one-dataset-out setup, the authors evaluate three VLMs (Qwen, LLaVA, InternVL) and three visual baselines (CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, Pose-TCN) under zero-target transfer and target-site personalization.
AI.result: Multi-source training raises zero-target mean AUROC from 0.821 to 0.912 (Qwen), 0.883 to 0.947 (LLaVA), and 0.939 to 0.962 (InternVL); with five target examples per class, 95% CIs over target-only training lie above zero for Qwen, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN, while full-target benefits persist only for Qwen and LLaVA.
AI.conclusion: Multi-source pretraining substantially improves zero-shot and low-budget fall detection, though personalization gains depend on model architecture and label budget.

title: EviRef: Evidence-Specific Memories for Logical Anomaly Detection across Capture Conditions
summary: Logical anomalies arise when every component looks normal but their combination violates the scene rules. In practical inspection, these rules must hold under varying backgrounds, illumination, and imaging quality, with only a few dozen normal images per scene, whereas existing methods couple normality with appearance and merge different constraints into one reference. We model logical normality as decomposable constraints and propose EviRef, a training-free method that builds a separate reference memory for each family of evidence. Component prototypes built once per scene parse images under any capture condition into one label space, on which occupancy and relation constraints are verified. Semantic constraints are verified with whole-image embeddings independent of parsing, and additional evidence such as text is admitted through a task-level gate without modifying existing memories. On VID-AD, EviRef attains a mean image-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 92.1% (88.9% with visual evidence alone), the highest among the compared methods under each of five capture conditions, with a standard deviation of 0.5. Even with memories built from only 20 normal images per task, it surpasses all compared methods that use 50 normal images per task.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes EviRef, a training-free logical anomaly detection method using separate evidence-specific memories, achieving 92.1% mean AUROC on VID-AD across varying capture conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing logical anomaly detection methods couple normality with appearance and merge distinct constraints into one reference, making them fragile under changing backgrounds, illumination, and imaging quality.
AI.method: EviRef decomposes logical normality into separate reference memories: scene-level component prototypes parse images into a unified label space for occupancy and relation checks, whole-image embeddings verify semantic constraints, and a task-level gate admits additional evidence such as text.
AI.result: On VID-AD, EviRef achieves 92.1% mean image-level AUROC (88.9% visual-only) with a 0.5 standard deviation across five capture conditions, and with 20 normal images per task it outperforms all compared methods using 50 normal images.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing logical normality into evidence-specific memories enables robust, sample-efficient anomaly detection invariant to capture conditions.

title: WA-JEPA: Goal-Aware Predictive Feedback Action Refinement for a World-Action Model
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, including supplementary material. Code available at this https URL
summary: JEPA-based world models predict action consequences in latent space, but representative planning approaches rely on candidate-action search, requiring repeated evaluation of action sequences and incurring substantial online computational cost. Direct action generation avoids this search, yet how to leverage latent predictions to guide action generation given task goals remains a key challenge in translating learned physical dynamics into effective decisions. We introduce WA-JEPA, a world-action model that couples action generation, action-conditioned latent prediction, and goal-aware feedback. The model first generates an action proposal and predicts the resulting future scenes and proprioceptive states, then refines the proposal through two complementary feedback paths, using the task goal as a reference. Goal-discrepancy residual feedback (GDRF) uses differences between the latent representations of predicted scenes and the task goal to guide chunk-wise action refinement. Future-scene context feedback (FSCF) preserves fine-grained predicted scene representations to guide subsequent action refinement. Jointly learned from offline demonstrations, this process iteratively updates the same plan before execution, making future predictions directly participate in action generation without candidate-action search. We evaluate short-horizon goal reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution. The results show that goal-aware predictive feedback supports competitive task performance while maintaining a compact model and low online computational cost. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces WA-JEPA, a world-action model that refines action proposals through goal-aware predictive feedback in latent space, avoiding expensive online candidate-action search.
AI.motivation: JEPA-based world models typically rely on costly online candidate-action search to plan, and direct action generation lacks a mechanism to use latent future predictions to guide actions toward task goals.
AI.method: WA-JEPA generates an action proposal, predicts future scenes and proprioceptive states, and iteratively refines the plan before execution via Goal-Discrepancy Residual Feedback (GDRF) and Future-Scene Context Feedback (FSCF) learned jointly from offline demonstrations.
AI.result: Evaluated on short-horizon goal reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution, WA-JEPA achieves competitive task performance with a compact model and low online computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Coupling action generation with goal-aware latent predictive feedback enables efficient, search-free planning in world-action models.

title: Do VLMs Really Look at the Road? A Diagnostic Evaluation for Autonomous Driving
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly being evaluated for autonomous driving through question-answering benchmarks, yet high benchmark accuracy does not necessarily reflect visually grounded reasoning. We present a diagnostic evaluation framework that systematically probes whether VLMs base safety-critical driving decisions on visual evidence or instead rely on language priors, answer biases, and dataset regularities. Our benchmark comprises two task categories, Adverse Weather and Junctions \& Intersections, with a nuScenes spatial reasoning extension, and evaluates open-source (general, driving, and spatial-reasoning) VLMs along four diagnostic protocols: image versus no-image evaluation, counterfactual weather sensitivity, linguistic robustness under paraphrasing and negation, and spatial reasoning. All ground-truth labels are derived programmatically from BDD100K and DriveLM annotations, enabling reproducible evaluation without manual labeling. Across all models, we find that competitive overall accuracy conceals systematic failure modes, including strong affirmation bias, limited sensitivity to counterfactual scene changes, near-chance performance on negated questions despite high paraphrase consistency, and confident driving decisions even without visual input. These results demonstrate that current open-source VLMs remain insufficiently grounded for safety-critical autonomous driving and underscore the need for diagnostic evaluation beyond aggregate accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a diagnostic evaluation framework for VLMs in autonomous driving, revealing that high benchmark accuracy masks affirmation bias, poor negation handling, and decisions made without visual input.
AI.motivation: High QA accuracy on autonomous driving benchmarks does not prove that VLMs ground safety-critical decisions in visual evidence rather than language priors or dataset regularities.
AI.method: The authors derive ground-truth labels programmatically from BDD100K and DriveLM across Adverse Weather, Junctions & Intersections, and a nuScenes spatial extension, evaluating open-source VLMs on image vs. no-image, counterfactual weather, paraphrasing/negation, and spatial reasoning protocols.
AI.result: Across general, driving, and spatial-reasoning VLMs, competitive overall accuracy conceals strong affirmation bias, limited sensitivity to counterfactual scene changes, near-chance accuracy on negated questions, and confident decisions without images.
AI.conclusion: Current open-source VLMs lack sufficient visual grounding for safety-critical autonomous driving, necessitating diagnostic evaluations beyond aggregate accuracy.

title: Calibrating the Uncertainty of Self-Supervised Monocular Depth without Labels
summary: Self-supervised monocular depth networks can predict a per-pixel uncertainty, which is mainly evaluated by how well it ranks pixels according to their error. Such metrics are insensitive to the magnitude of the uncertainty, so an uncertainty half as large as the actual error obtains the same score. In this paper, we investigate whether the predicted uncertainty is as large as the depth error, both on average (scale) and across confident and uncertain, near and far pixels (shape). On KITTI, the scale is miscalibrated for every uncertainty estimate we evaluate, and the error of MonoProb is nearly twice its predicted uncertainty. We propose MonoCal, which corrects both the scale and the shape without ground-truth depth. Scale calibration multiplies the uncertainty by a single constant measured from stereo pairs, requiring no retraining, and this constant closely matches the one fitted with ground truth. Since a constant cannot change the shape, we further retrain the uncertainty to predict where the depth of the network disagrees with that of a second self-supervised network.
