We show that conventional metrics (CLIP Score, DINO similarity) are blind to this failure, and that abstract personality descriptors and scene-level emotion labels do not produce consistent improvements over neutral prompts across models. To systematically diagnose trait collapse, we introduce \textbf{ViStoryBench-Personality}, a story-level benchmark combining an expert-validated Visual Cues Lexicon (Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.757$) with a six-dimensional metric suite covering personality alignment, cross-scene stability, and behavioral coherence. Evaluating seven T2I systems, we confirm a persistent semantic gap between abstract trait labels and visual evidence, and find that visual identity consistency does not imply personality consistency. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{Trait-Behavior-Visual (TBV)}, a training-free prompting framework that decomposes personality traits into renderable visual constraints. TBV improves Personality Alignment Score by up to $+22.1\%$, with larger gains in models with stronger language-conditioning capacity.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies trait collapse in text-to-image storytelling, introduces the ViStoryBench-Personality benchmark, and proposes Trait-Behavior-Visual (TBV), a training-free prompting framework that improves Personality Alignment Score by up to 22.1%.
AI.motivation: Current text-to-image models maintain visual appearance across scenes but fail to depict consistent personality-relevant behavior, a failure missed by CLIP Score and DINO similarity.
AI.method: The authors build ViStoryBench-Personality combining an expert-validated Visual Cues Lexicon (Fleiss' kappa = 0.757) with six metrics for personality alignment, cross-scene stability, and behavioral coherence, and propose TBV to decompose abstract personality traits into renderable visual constraints without training.
AI.result: Evaluating seven T2I systems confirms a semantic gap between abstract trait labels and visual evidence where visual identity consistency does not imply personality consistency, and TBV improves Personality Alignment Score by up to +22.1%, with larger gains on models with stronger language conditioning.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing personality traits into concrete visual behaviors bridges the semantic gap in visual storytelling and mitigates trait collapse without model retraining.

title: JointQ: Joint Scale-and-Integer Quantization for Large Language Models
comment: 49 pages, 4 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: GPTQ is the de facto standard solver for layer-wise post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models, yet the solver itself has received less attention than weight preprocessing and cross-layer objectives. We target a bottleneck of GPTQ: its greedy procedure optimizes continuous group scales separately from the assignment of discrete integers. Evaluating each integer candidate with its closed-form optimal scale has been used for per-channel quantization; JointQ extends it to group-wise quantization, where a row's scales are coupled through the Hessian, and applies it to refine the GPTQ solution. Each local-search move changes one integer and recomputes its group's optimal scale in closed form, accounting for the other groups through the full Hessian; all scales are periodically re-solved jointly. The search starts from a row-wise selection among scale-refitted candidates including the GPTQ solution, so unregularized JointQ never has a larger layer-wise calibration error than GPTQ. JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement. Across four models and four settings, JointQ improves six-task average zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons and perplexity in 12 of 16. The mean accuracy gain increases from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel, and JointQ also improves average accuracy over GPTQ with MSE-based scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons, though rarely in G128. An ablation shows that JointQ's diagonal Tikhonov regularization mitigates severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation, so the largest gains are not due to the local search alone. Overall, JointQ's primary empirical benefit is downstream accuracy preservation in challenging low-bit and large-group regimes. Code is available in the OneComp library at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces JointQ, a drop-in local-search refinement for GPTQ that jointly optimizes group-wise scales and discrete integers using the full Hessian, improving zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons.
AI.motivation: GPTQ optimizes continuous group scales separately from discrete integer assignments, leaving a quantization bottleneck in low-bit and large-group regimes.
AI.method: Extending closed-form scale refitting to group-wise quantization where scales couple through the Hessian, JointQ performs local-search moves that update one integer and recompute its group's optimal scale in closed form, periodically re-solving all scales jointly, with diagonal Tikhonov regularization.
AI.result: Across four models and four settings, JointQ beats vanilla GPTQ on six-task average zero-shot accuracy in 14 of 16 comparisons (mean gain rising from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel) and perplexity in 12 of 16, and beats GPTQ with MSE scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Jointly refining coupled group scales and integer weights with Tikhonov regularization preserves downstream accuracy in challenging low-bit quantization while remaining a drop-in GPTQ replacement.

title: When the Cheapest Feasible Router Fails: Auditing Deployment Commitments in Cost-Aware LLM Routing
summary: Cost-aware LLM routing often selects the cheapest policy meeting empirical risk and coverage constraints. Yet a router that passes an audit can violate its fixed service contract on new requests, even when candidate policies are constructed independently. We study this deployment-commitment decision with disjoint construction, audit, and test samples. Across 19 RouterBench task families, the cheapest audit-feasible router deploys in 91.82% of opportunities but violates the held-out contract in 32.22% of deployments. We introduce Menu-Aware Routing Commitment (MARC), which qualifies policies using audit evidence and a serving-cost tolerance to retain the apparent winner, deploy a supported alternative, or defer. Its practical policywise variant (MARC-P) reduces observed conditional failure to 0.73% at 85.79% deployment, with higher serving cost; fixed-margin and formal risk-control procedures provide competitive alternatives. Nested audits show how added evidence changes deployable policy sets, and learned semantic routing exhibits the same commitment failure. These results establish deployment commitment as a distinct operational decision connecting router evaluation, service reliability, and inference cost.

AI.tldr: This paper studies deployment commitment in cost-aware LLM routing, showing that the cheapest audit-feasible router violates held-out service contracts in 32.22% of deployments across RouterBench, and proposes MARC-P to cut conditional failure to 0.73%.
AI.motivation: Routers selected as the cheapest policy passing an empirical audit frequently violate their fixed service contracts on new requests, even when candidate policies are built independently.
AI.method: Using disjoint construction, audit, and test samples across 19 RouterBench task families, the authors introduce Menu-Aware Routing Commitment (MARC) and its policywise variant MARC-P, which use audit evidence and a serving-cost tolerance to retain the winner, deploy a supported alternative, or defer.
AI.result: The cheapest audit-feasible router deploys in 91.82% of opportunities but violates the held-out contract in 32.22% of deployments, whereas MARC-P reduces conditional failure to 0.73% at an 85.79% deployment rate with higher serving cost; learned semantic routing exhibits the same commitment failure.
AI.conclusion: Deployment commitment is a distinct operational decision linking router evaluation, service reliability, and inference cost.

title: TrainExplorer: Autonomous LLM Post-Training via Plan-and-Decouple Exploration
summary: LLM-based agents can automate model post-training, accelerating progress toward recursive self-improvement. Despite their promise, existing approaches remain under-explored and face two main challenges: (1) strategy lock-in that limits exploration beyond the initial strategy; and (2) coupled execution that obscures the effects of individual modifications. To address these challanges, we propose TrainExplorer, a multi-agent framework for autonomous post-training, that incorporates strategy planning and execution decoupling, to achieve broaden strategy exploration. First, strategy planning draws on scientific literature to construct a candidate search space of training strategies. Then, decoupled execution enables single-component interventions and attribution to guide strategy exploration. Extensive experiments on PostTrainBench demonstrate that TrainExplorer achieves a weighted aggregate score of 39.02, outperforming Claude Code using the same LLM by 7.32 and surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol-powered Codex, which scores 36.23. Code will be available.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes TrainExplorer, a multi-agent framework for autonomous LLM post-training that decouples strategy planning from single-component execution, achieving a 39.02 score on PostTrainBench.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous LLM post-training agents suffer from strategy lock-in that restricts exploration and coupled execution that obscures the effect of individual modifications.
AI.method: TrainExplorer uses literature-grounded strategy planning to build a candidate search space of training strategies, paired with decoupled execution that performs single-component interventions and attribution to guide further exploration.
AI.result: On PostTrainBench, TrainExplorer achieves a weighted aggregate score of 39.02, outperforming Claude Code using the same LLM by 7.32 points and surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol-powered Codex (36.23).
AI.conclusion: Decoupling literature-guided strategy planning from single-component execution attribution enables broader exploration and stronger autonomous post-training performance.

title: GaugeRoPE: RoPE-Compatible Executable Latent Attention
summary: Latent KV cache compression reduces memory footprint by mapping historical keys and values into compact representations. However, generic compressed key states require reconstruction to native dimension before applying RoPE and computing attention scores, adding sequence-scaling overhead to the decode path. We characterize when a latent KV representation can serve directly as the execution state of pretrained RoPE. For RoPE-based transformers, exact static linear execution of the rotary key path requires the latent-to-native map to preserve the pretrained RoPE action through an intertwining relation, restricting exact mixing to coordinates that share the same RoPE frequency. Guided by this characterization, we build GaugeRoPE, a training-free executable latent KV representation. It combines a RoPE-compatible carrier that preserves the rotary action with an approximate position-independent residual key--value (RKV) correction for complementary key and value information, both evaluated without per-token dense historical K/V reconstruction. On Mistral-7B, GaugeRoPE achieves $5.85\times$ KV compression while maintaining quality close to the full-cache baseline. Additional MHA results validate the construction beyond GQA. GaugeRoPE achieves up to $2.48\times$ the decode throughput of the vanilla uncompressed baseline through direct latent execution.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes when latent KV caches can execute RoPE directly without dense reconstruction and introduces GaugeRoPE, achieving 5.85x KV compression and up to 2.48x decode throughput on Mistral-7B.
AI.motivation: Generic latent KV cache compression requires reconstructing keys to native dimension before applying RoPE and computing attention, adding sequence-scaling overhead during decoding.
AI.method: The authors prove that exact static linear execution of RoPE requires the latent-to-native map to preserve the rotary action via an intertwining relation (restricting mixing to same-frequency coordinates), and build GaugeRoPE, a training-free representation combining a RoPE-compatible carrier with an approximate position-independent residual key-value (RKV) correction.
AI.result: On Mistral-7B, GaugeRoPE achieves 5.85x KV compression with quality close to the full-cache baseline and up to 2.48x decode throughput over the uncompressed baseline, with additional MHA results validating the construction beyond GQA.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing RoPE intertwining in latent KV representations eliminates per-token dense K/V reconstruction and enables fast, training-free compressed decoding.

title: ReconPotBench: Evaluating LLM Honeypots in Multi-Round Linux Reconnaissance
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to build interactive honeypots, yet existing evaluations mainly assess isolated command outputs and cannot determine whether a system remains believable when later commands depend on earlier results. We present ReconPotBench, a multi-round benchmark for Linux reconnaissance honeypots. It contains 1{,}032 three-round reconnaissance interactions across eight reconnaissance categories, with reference outputs collected from a real Linux environment. Under a unified testing protocol, we compare Cowrie, open-source LLMs, and closed-source LLMs along three dimensions: round-level authenticity, cross-round contextual consistency, and hacker-oriented reconnaissance value. Results show that multi-round evaluation exposes failures hidden by single-round testing, as authenticity declines with interaction depth and both open-source and closed-source LLMs struggle to maintain coherent state across rounds. LLM-based honeypots nevertheless outperform Cowrie in authenticity and reconnaissance value, while Cowrie remains more consistent because of its rigid templated behavior. Category-level analysis further shows that tasks requiring systems to preserve network relationships across rounds are harder than tasks centered on explicit entities such as ports. ReconPotBench enables reproducible evaluation of LLM honeypots across authenticity, entity consistency, and hacker-perspective utility in dependent multi-round interactions. The dataset is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ReconPotBench, a 1,032-interaction multi-round Linux reconnaissance benchmark for LLM honeypots, showing that authenticity declines with interaction depth and LLMs struggle to maintain cross-round state consistency.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-based honeypots test isolated single-round commands and fail to measure whether honeypots remain believable when later commands depend on earlier outputs.
AI.method: ReconPotBench comprises 1,032 three-round Linux reconnaissance interactions across eight categories with real Linux reference outputs, evaluating Cowrie, open-source LLMs, and closed-source LLMs on round-level authenticity, cross-round contextual consistency, and hacker-oriented reconnaissance value.
AI.result: Multi-round evaluation exposes failures hidden in single-round tests: LLM authenticity drops with depth and both open- and closed-source LLMs struggle with cross-round state (especially preserving network relationships), though LLMs still beat Cowrie on authenticity and reconnaissance value while Cowrie stays more consistent due to rigid templates.
AI.conclusion: ReconPotBench provides a reproducible multi-round benchmark demonstrating that stateful consistency across dependent commands remains a key challenge for LLM honeypots.

title: Necessary for What? Auditing Demographic Disclosure to LLM Synthetic Respondents
comment: 29 pages, 10 figures, 11 tables; Code: this https URL
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly answer surveys on behalf of real panelists, and each panelist's recorded demographic attributes (e.g., age, education, ethnicity) are often placed in the prompt on the premise that richer profiles make more faithful synthetic respondents. While data minimization limits personal data to what a purpose requires, a synthetic survey serves several purposes at once, from predicting individual answers to estimating how opinions are distributed and comparing groups. We ask which of these purposes require the respondent's record, and whether improved estimates support sound conclusions about groups. We vary whose profile a model receives, where it comes from, and how many fields it contains, in two U.S. surveys with eleven open-weight and three hosted models, and compare each model with a statistical model fit to the same information. We make four contributions. First, we show that the record adds little to individual predictions and that, for the open-weight models, most of its gain in population estimates remains when it is replaced by census data or a synthetic persona. Second, we find that group comparisons improve only with the respondent's own record, and that even then the models' group differences rest more on the demographic label in the prompt than on the individual respondent, which the usual check of reproducing known group differences does not reveal. Third, we find that the models make groups look more alike than they are, keeping differences in circumstances while flattening or reversing differences in attitudes, most sharply for religious affiliation and ethnic origin, both special categories of personal data. Fourth, we outline an audit that a survey organization can run on questions it has already fielded to decide which estimates may use the record.

AI.tldr: This paper audits demographic disclosure in LLM synthetic survey respondents across two U.S. surveys and 14 models, finding that personal records add little to individual predictions and cause models to flatten or reverse attitudinal group differences.
AI.motivation: Rich demographic profiles are routinely placed in prompts for synthetic survey respondents on the assumption they improve faithfulness, raising data-minimization concerns when different survey purposes may not require personal records.
AI.method: Across two U.S. surveys, eleven open-weight models, three hosted models, and a statistical baseline, the authors vary whose profile is provided, its source (real record, census data, or synthetic persona), and the number of fields, and outline an audit for survey organizations.
AI.result: Personal records add little to individual predictions, census or synthetic personas retain most population-estimate gains for open-weight models, group comparisons improve only with the respondent's own record yet rely more on demographic labels than individual traits, and models flatten or reverse attitudinal differences (especially for religion and ethnicity).
AI.conclusion: Survey organizations should audit existing questions to determine which estimation purposes genuinely require personal demographic records rather than defaulting to full disclosure.

title: RAMP: Rethinking Multimodal Evaluation through Answer Readout Protocols
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are often evaluated by converting model outputs into discrete answers. The conversion protocol determines which scores become predictions and can strongly influence the reported results. We introduce RAMP (Readout Aware Multimodal Protocol), a systematic framework that compares direct yes/no token logits, surface-form scores, and typed or reversed A/B interfaces under fixed model checkpoints and paired visual questions. On 500 POPE adversarial questions, typed versus bare readout changes accuracy by $-20.2$ percentage points for SmolVLM-256M, $-16.4$ for TinyLLaVA-1.1B, and $+1.8$ for Qwen2.5-VL-3B. Paired transitions reveal extensive prediction changes even when the net accuracy difference is small: 79 of 104 binary ChartQA items change correctness for SmolVLM-500M, despite a $+1.0$-point net difference. We further analyze prompt wording, candidate forms, option position, cross-task effects, and calibration. An independent offline replay reproduces 16,140 first-token decisions from saved raw scores with exact agreement. Our findings establish answer readout as a measurable component of multimodal evaluation and provide a reproducible protocol for analyzing model comparisons.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RAMP to compare answer readout protocols in multimodal LLM evaluation, showing that switching between typed and bare readouts alters POPE accuracy by up to 20.2 percentage points and flips 79 of 104 binary ChartQA items for SmolVLM-500M.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLM evaluations convert model outputs into discrete answers, yet the choice of readout protocol strongly skews reported scores and is rarely analyzed systematically.
AI.method: RAMP compares direct yes/no token logits, surface-form scores, and typed or reversed A/B interfaces under fixed checkpoints and paired visual questions, analyzing prompt wording, candidate forms, option position, cross-task effects, and calibration.
AI.result: On 500 POPE adversarial questions, typed vs. bare readout changes accuracy by -20.2 percentage points for SmolVLM-256M, -16.4 for TinyLLaVA-1.1B, and +1.8 for Qwen2.5-VL-3B; on binary ChartQA, 79 of 104 items flip correctness for SmolVLM-500M despite a +1.0-point net difference, and offline replay reproduces 16,140 first-token decisions with exact agreement.
AI.conclusion: Answer readout is a major, measurable variable in multimodal evaluation that must be controlled and reported alongside model comparisons.

title: When the Bill Falls: Reusing the Old Index Defers,Never Avoids, Re-encoding in Complete Embedding-Model Migration
summary: Upgrading the embedding model behind a vector index requires re-encoding the corpus. Recent work reuses the old index through adapters or window re-ranking. Across sixteen model pairs on passage and code corpora, plus eleven on Natural Questions (NQ), we find three results. First, reuse never avoids re-encoding: if migration must complete, every strategy eventually encodes every document; reuse only changes when that work is paid and the quality served meanwhile. Second, adapters should be compared with the old model, not only the new one. Of five adapter variants, only same-family LLM bridges beat the old model, and only by a negligible margin. Third, window re-ranking cost can be priced from the old index alone; pre-registered replays on all 8,841,823 passages confirmed the prediction on all three tested pairs. Workload skew also matters: across 36 further pre-registered Zipf replays, the planned family matched on 32. These findings yield three pre-migration rules: whether reuse is worthwhile, which strategy to use, and how deep a window to take. The depth rule priced every window that reached target quality to within 4 parts in 10^5 of the corpus. On NQ, a pre-committed plan selected the family on 10 of 11 pairs and priced every window exactly. Quality inputs transferred less reliably across corpus scale, so the model gap and window quality loss must be measured on the serving index.

AI.tldr: This paper studies complete embedding-model migration across 16 passage/code pairs and 11 Natural Questions pairs, showing that index reuse only defers re-encoding and deriving three pre-migration planning rules.
AI.motivation: Upgrading an embedding model behind a vector index requires re-encoding, and recent reuse methods (adapters, window re-ranking) lack clear guidance on whether they avoid work or how to configure them.
AI.method: Through pre-registered replays on 8,841,823 passages and 36 Zipf workload replays across 16 passage/code pairs and 11 NQ pairs, the authors evaluate five adapter variants and window re-ranking cost models.
AI.result: Reuse never avoids full re-encoding for complete migration; only same-family LLM bridges beat the old model and by a negligible margin; window re-ranking cost can be priced from the old index alone (confirmed on all three tested pairs and 32 of 36 Zipf replays), and the depth rule priced every target-quality window within 4 parts in 10^5 (and 10 of 11 NQ pairs).
AI.conclusion: Three pre-migration rules determine whether reuse is worthwhile, which strategy to pick, and window depth, though quality inputs must be measured directly on the serving index.

title: DetourBench: Trajectory-Level Evaluation of Interactive Agents with Exact Minimum-Action Bounds
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Evaluation of Interactive Agents
summary: Benchmarks judge language-model agents mainly by whether they reach the correct final state, not by how they got there. Endpoint scoring cannot separate an agent that retrieved exactly the evidence a decision required from one that read most of the environment, nor an agent that never located the evidence from one that stopped a single action short. Settling this needs a reference cost, and authored solutions establish only that a task is solvable, not that no shorter route exists. We present DetourBench, which constrains the environment until that minimum is computable. Each task is a finite, partially observable transition system with unit-cost accesses whose resources become globally addressable after discovery. Exhaustive search yields the full-information minimum action count $L_0$ with a replayable witness; from graph-recoverable terminal states it also yields exact residual work $R_T$, which separates an episode that stopped one access short from one that wandered, while an irreversible wrong commitment is recorded as having no finite residual distance rather than assigned one. Success, attainment, residual progress, and normalized detour are reported separately. Across 375 scored episodes --- five model endpoints, 25 integrated tasks, three repeats --- success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and orders the models differently. Among recoverable failures, residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and from irreversible commitment. We open-source the instances, oracle witnesses, and evaluation harness at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DetourBench, a trajectory-level agent benchmark with exact minimum-action bounds and residual work metrics, showing that conditional attainment reorders five model endpoints compared to endpoint success alone.
AI.motivation: Endpoint scoring cannot distinguish agents that retrieve minimal evidence from those that exhaustively read the environment, nor near-complete failures from wandering or irreversible mistakes.
AI.method: DetourBench models tasks as finite, partially observable transition systems with unit-cost accesses and globally addressable discovered resources, using exhaustive search to compute the exact minimum action count L_0 and exact residual work R_T from graph-recoverable states.
AI.result: Across 375 episodes (five model endpoints, 25 tasks, three repeats), endpoint success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and reorders models; residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and irreversible wrong commitments.
AI.conclusion: Exact minimum-action bounds and residual work enable rigorous trajectory-level evaluation of interactive agents beyond binary endpoint success.

title: MolReps: Taking SELFIES, Making SMILES, Teaching LLMs
summary: The same molecule can be expressed in multiple, syntactically distinct representations, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs) can recognize and relate these equivalent encodings. We introduce MolReps, a pipeline that generates 9,600 question-answer pairs across ten representations for conversion, normalization, and 2D structure recognition. Post-training on MolReps improves text-only and multimodal models, MolQwen3-4B-Instruct (MQ3-4B-I) and MolQwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (MQ3-VL-4B-I), from $4.01\%$ to $75.13\%$ and from $7.11\%$ to $73.14\%$ (InChIKey match) on the molecule-overlap test set, respectively. On the molecule-disjoint test set, post-training increased validity from $20.35\%$ to $58.12\%$ for MQ3-4B-I and from $17.19\%$ to $59.34\%$ for MQ3-VL-4B-I. However, InChIKey match remained low, decreasing from $3.86\%$ to $3.09\%$ and from $6.44\%$ to $2.29\%$, respectively. Furthermore, the resulting models achieve a relative $27.84\%$ improvement in average over their base model on MolRepBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating molecular property prediction. These results show the effectiveness of targeted post-training for enhancing molecular representation understanding and its potential to improve downstream molecular tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MolReps, a 9,600-QA dataset across ten molecular representations, showing that post-training boosts molecule-overlap InChIKey match from 4.01% to 75.13% and yields a 27.84% relative gain on MolRepBench.
AI.motivation: Molecules can be written in multiple syntactically distinct encodings (e.g., SELFIES, SMILES), yet it is unclear whether LLMs can recognize and relate these equivalent representations.
AI.method: The authors build MolReps with 9,600 question-answer pairs covering conversion, normalization, and 2D structure recognition across ten representations, and post-train MolQwen3-4B-Instruct (MQ3-4B-I) and MolQwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (MQ3-VL-4B-I).
AI.result: On the molecule-overlap test set, InChIKey match rises from 4.01% to 75.13% (MQ3-4B-I) and 7.11% to 73.14% (MQ3-VL-4B-I); on the molecule-disjoint set, validity rises from 20.35% to 58.12% and 17.19% to 59.34% while InChIKey match remains low (3.09% and 2.29%), and average MolRepBench performance improves by 27.84% relative to base models.
AI.conclusion: Targeted post-training on equivalent molecular encodings substantially improves representation understanding and downstream molecular property prediction, though cross-molecule exact generalization remains challenging.

title: From Recursion to Convolution: Parallel Self-Improvement for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent self-improvement enables agents to improve through interaction and feedback. However, sequential dependencies across agents and refinement rounds can propagate errors, increase computational costs, and limit parallelism. Moreover, refining individual features or agents in isolation can overlook their dependencies and restrict collective coordination. To address these challenges, we propose ConvRSI, a framework for parallelizing multi-agent self-improvement through convolution. ConvRSI couples intra-agent convolution, which jointly refines related agent features, with inter-agent graph convolution, which aggregates messages according to the collaboration topology. Both stages operate in latent space, enabling parallel updates without repeatedly decoding and re-encoding intermediate messages. Experiments on MATH-500 show that ConvRSI achieves 5.04% performance improvement while reducing 17.27% inference cost, and 45.11% latency compared with RecursiveMAS. It also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing their topologies as adjacency matrices. These results demonstrate the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. Our code and datasets are provided in this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ConvRSI, a latent-space convolutional framework for parallel multi-agent self-improvement, achieving 5.04% higher performance, 17.27% lower inference cost, and 45.11% lower latency on MATH-500 than RecursiveMAS.
AI.motivation: Sequential multi-agent self-improvement propagates errors, inflates compute, and limits parallelism, while refining agents or features in isolation ignores their dependencies.
AI.method: ConvRSI couples intra-agent convolution (jointly refining related agent features) with inter-agent graph convolution (aggregating messages over collaboration topologies represented as adjacency matrices) directly in latent space without repeated decoding and re-encoding.
AI.result: On MATH-500, ConvRSI improves performance by 5.04% while reducing inference cost by 17.27% and latency by 45.11% compared with RecursiveMAS, and supports diverse collaboration topologies.
AI.conclusion: Convolutional co-evolution in latent space enables faster, cheaper, and more accurate multi-agent self-improvement.

title: Jev-as-a-Reward: Validating Probabilistic Safety Judges for Reinforcement Learning
summary: Probabilistic safety judges return the probability of a safety label and cheaply score reinforcement learning rollouts. A confidence gate sends only uncertain verdicts to a stronger LLM judge, which leaves confidently passed harm in a blind spot. Policies can exploit this blind spot, and commercial judges release new versions. We propose a protocol that validates such a judge before and during training, separates the share of confidently passed harm from its amount, and re-validates it after each judge change. We apply it to two versions of Jev, a commercial decision-only judge, and to an open guard classifier. Under the probability reward of Jev, passed harm shrinks in all 11 runs under the primary reference, mostly more slowly than caught harm, and concentrates in the blind spot. Binarizing this judge meets the escape criterion on Llama, and the open guard classifier shows an escape signal in one seed under a second reference. Guard classifiers share this blind spot, and even frontier LLM judges catch at most one of 10 human-labeled confident misses. Without a trained reward model, the probability reward with a helpfulness term lowers HarmBench attack success on Llama-3.1-8B from 0.287 to at most 0.033 at the final checkpoint.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a validation protocol for probabilistic safety judges in RL, showing that confidence-gated judges leave confidently passed harm in a blind spot and that a probability reward with helpfulness lowers Llama-3.1-8B HarmBench attack success from 0.287 to at most 0.033.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic safety judges cheaply score RL rollouts, but routing only uncertain verdicts to stronger judges leaves confidently passed harm unmonitored, creating a blind spot that policies can exploit across judge versions.
AI.method: The authors introduce a protocol that validates judges before and during training, separates the share of confidently passed harm from its amount, re-validates after judge updates, and tests it on two versions of Jev and an open guard classifier.
AI.result: Under Jev's probability reward, passed harm decreases in all 11 runs under the primary reference but concentrates in the blind spot; binarizing Jev meets the escape criterion on Llama, the open guard classifier shows an escape signal in one seed, frontier LLM judges catch at most 1 of 10 human-labeled confident misses, and adding a helpfulness term lowers HarmBench attack success on Llama-3.1-8B from 0.287 to at most 0.033.
AI.conclusion: Continuous validation of confidently passed harm is essential when using probabilistic safety judges as RL rewards, as both commercial and open guard classifiers share blind spots.

title: TRACK: Tool-Augmented Reasoning over Time Series for Fault Diagnosis in Power Management System
summary: Fault diagnosis in power management systems running multiple loads relies on experts manually inspecting current and voltage waveforms, which fails to scale across deployed units. We present TRACK, which pairs a time series encoder with a Small Language Model to produce structured, physics-grounded diagnostic reports, calling tools for exact, verifiable calculations. It operates on-device, keeping proprietary sensor data local and avoiding expensive API calls. We introduce a rubric-based framework that evaluates these reports by scoring structure, signal fidelity, physics reasoning, diagnosis, and actionability through per-criterion verdicts. On a 15-class multi-load simulated benchmark, TRACK achieves over 95% fault-category accuracy and generalizes to out-of-distribution faults, whereas the best encoder-probing baseline reaches only 58% accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TRACK, an on-device system pairing a time-series encoder with a Small Language Model and tool calls for power-management fault diagnosis, achieving over 95% accuracy on a 15-class benchmark vs. 58% for encoder probing.
AI.motivation: Manual inspection of current and voltage waveforms for multi-load power-management fault diagnosis does not scale, and cloud APIs risk exposing proprietary sensor data.
AI.method: TRACK combines a time-series encoder with an on-device Small Language Model that invokes tools for exact calculations to generate physics-grounded diagnostic reports, evaluated via a rubric scoring structure, signal fidelity, physics reasoning, diagnosis, and actionability.
AI.result: On a 15-class multi-load simulated benchmark, TRACK exceeds 95% fault-category accuracy and generalizes to out-of-distribution faults, compared to 58% accuracy for the best encoder-probing baseline.
AI.conclusion: Tool-augmented Small Language Models enable accurate, private, and verifiable on-device fault diagnosis from time-series waveforms.

title: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated via truthful evidence in open channel
summary: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated through open channels such as social media, even when the information they receive is truthful. When agents fill gaps between fragments with self-induced relationships, they may accept those relationships as established facts and pass the resulting rumours to others. Drawing on cognitive theory of narrative understanding and film theory of montage, we introduce Generative Montage to operationalize this failure, termed narrative overfitting, by coordinating agents to arrange truthful fragments into misleading narratives. Across 1,090 rumour targets from six Twitter events, agents often accepted rumours overconfidently, with overall acceptance exceeding 65 percent in twelve of fourteen models. Acceptance remained above 50 percent after majority voting or review of the same evidence, showing how errors can reach downstream decisions. To explain this susceptibility, fragment interventions identify posts that influence belief within complete narratives. Synthetic controls then show that similar response patterns arise from valid evidence, separating belief influence from evidential support. This distinction motivates Grounded Monitor, a proof-of-concept neuro-symbolic runtime monitor that checks direct evidential support to guide agents' judgements, improving decision accuracy by 5.6 to 29.0 percentage points across original and anonymized settings. These findings expose a cognitive route to rumour amplification and support monitoring inferred relationships before agent-generated conclusions guide public decisions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Generative Montage to show that arranging truthful social-media fragments induces narrative overfitting in LLM agents (>65% rumour acceptance in 12 of 14 models), and proposes Grounded Monitor, improving decision accuracy by 5.6 to 29.0 percentage points.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can be manipulated via open channels even when all received information is truthful, because they fill gaps between fragments with self-induced relationships and propagate the resulting rumours.
AI.method: Drawing on narrative cognition and film montage, Generative Montage coordinates agents to arrange truthful fragments into misleading narratives across 1,090 rumour targets from six Twitter events; the authors then build Grounded Monitor, a neuro-symbolic runtime monitor checking direct evidential support.
AI.result: Overall rumour acceptance exceeds 65% in 12 of 14 models and stays above 50% after majority voting or evidence review; fragment interventions and synthetic controls separate belief influence from evidential support, and Grounded Monitor improves decision accuracy by 5.6 to 29.0 percentage points across original and anonymized settings.
AI.conclusion: Monitoring inferred relationships for direct evidential support is necessary to prevent rumour amplification when agents reason over truthful but fragmented open-channel evidence.

title: Stream of Belief: Eliciting Collective Intelligence through Latent Belief Dynamics
summary: In this work, we view multi-agent reasoning as a process of seeking a collective equilibrium of implicit belief dynamics and introduce Stream of Belief (SoB), where agents maintain continuous latent beliefs and iteratively refine them through communication and reflection. Our method seeks a collective belief state of a multi-agent system where further communication induces no meaningful information propagation. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the generalization of SoB across tasks and model families. More Broadly, our results suggest a new perspective on scaling multi-agent reasoning from belief dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Stream of Belief (SoB), a multi-agent reasoning framework where agents maintain and iteratively refine continuous latent beliefs through communication and reflection until reaching a collective equilibrium.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent reasoning can be framed as converging on a collective belief state, yet standard approaches lack a continuous latent belief-dynamics formulation.
AI.method: In SoB, agents maintain continuous latent beliefs and iteratively update them via inter-agent communication and reflection until further communication yields no meaningful information propagation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that SoB generalizes across multiple tasks and model families.
AI.conclusion: Framing multi-agent reasoning as latent belief dynamics offers a new perspective for scaling collective intelligence.

title: Classical structural priors improve neural molecular representations in molecule language models
comment: 40 pages. This is the originally submitted version. The final version, revised after peer review, is published in J. Chem. Inf. Model. (2026): this https URL
summary: Classical molecular similarity is central to chemical information systems, yet molecule-language models trained on paired structure-text data do not necessarily organize molecular embeddings according to graded structural relationships. Here we introduce Structure-Aware Guided Alignment (SAGA), a training-only regularizer that uses Centered Kernel Alignment to align neural molecular representations with fingerprint-based Tanimoto similarity, without adding parameters or requiring fingerprints at inference. In MolCA and Atomas, SAGA improves molecule-text retrieval, shifts non-exact retrieval toward closer structural analogues, and increases average scaffold-split property-prediction performance, while molecular description and text-to-molecule generation are improved or preserved in single-run ablations. These results show that established chemoinformatics priors can make molecule-language representations more chemically faithful while retaining their multimodal utility.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SAGA, a training-only CKA regularizer aligning neural molecular embeddings with fingerprint-based Tanimoto similarity, improving molecule-text retrieval and scaffold-split property prediction in MolCA and Atomas without inference overhead.
AI.motivation: Molecule-language models trained on paired structure-text data often fail to organize molecular embeddings according to graded classical structural similarity.
AI.method: Structure-Aware Guided Alignment (SAGA) uses Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) during training only to align neural molecular representations with fingerprint Tanimoto similarity, adding no parameters and requiring no fingerprints at inference.
AI.result: In MolCA and Atomas, SAGA improves molecule-text retrieval, shifts non-exact retrieval toward closer structural analogues, and boosts average scaffold-split property prediction, while preserving or improving molecular description and text-to-molecule generation in single-run ablations.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating classical chemoinformatics similarity priors during training makes molecule-language representations more chemically faithful while retaining multimodal utility.

title: AnachroBench: Evaluating Historical Consistency in Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Existing Large Vision-Language Model benchmarks primarily evaluate visual understanding in general everyday scenarios, leaving historical consistency with a specified era and country largely underexplored. To address this gap, we propose AnachroBench, a controlled discriminative benchmark for evaluating historical consistency in visual scenes. It contains 1,600 image pairs from eight countries spanning the late 19th to the early 20th century, each pairing an original historical image with an anachronistic version containing a seamlessly inserted modern object. AnachroBench evaluates three aspects: Inserted Object Perception, which tests whether models detect the inserted modern object; Era-Country Consistency, which assesses whether the scene is consistent with the specified era and country; and Conditional Era-Country Consistency, which measures consistency judgments only when the inserted object is correctly perceived. A false consistency judgment occurs when a model perceives the modern object but still judges the scene as historically consistent. Overall, AnachroBench reveals a gap between inserted object perception and era-country consistency judgments, providing a targeted evaluation of this behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper presents AnachroBench, a 1,600-image-pair benchmark for evaluating historical consistency in Large Vision-Language Models, exposing a gap between perceiving inserted modern objects and judging era-country consistency.
AI.motivation: Existing LVLM benchmarks focus on everyday scenes and leave historical consistency with a specified era and country largely untested.
AI.method: AnachroBench pairs 1,600 historical images from eight countries (late 19th to early 20th century) with anachronistic versions containing a seamlessly inserted modern object, evaluating Inserted Object Perception, Era-Country Consistency, and Conditional Era-Country Consistency.
AI.result: Models frequently exhibit false consistency judgments, perceiving the inserted modern object yet still judging the scene as historically consistent, revealing a gap between object perception and historical reasoning.
AI.conclusion: AnachroBench provides a targeted discriminative benchmark for diagnosing perceptual vs. historical-consistency reasoning gaps in LVLMs.

title: A Crowd-Audited Atlas of Implicit Bias in LLM-Powered Agents
summary: Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) express implicit biases in high-publicity, one-off decision scenarios such as hiring and intelligence assessment. However, as people increasingly employ autonomous, LLM-powered AI agents that make decisions on their behalf in doing day-to-day tasks, it is of critical importance that we understand how implicit biases, based on sociodemographic assumptions, emerge across a broad milieu of workaday decision scenarios. We used the 17 domains of daily activity in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) to generate an atlas of 506 decision scenarios in which LLMs --- endowed with personas representing different races, gender identities, and political ideologies --- expressed significant implicit bias. Next, in a crowdsourced audit, 500 participants made 8,010 binary choices about which implicitly biased decision scenarios most deserved further review. We found that participants prioritized decision scenarios that had broad relevance (e.g., about food choices), were high stakes (e.g., about health), and where all members of a simulated sociodemographic group made unanimous decisions (because it was a clear indication of stereotyping). They were less swayed by the magnitude of an observed disparity or the specific ATUS domain the decision scenario represented. When examining the rationale behind their prioritization choices, we found that participants often interpreted disparities as traits of demographic groups and judged whether those traits seemed plausible, often based on their own internalized stereotypes. We discuss implications for building personalized AI agents, digital twins, social simulations, and for using crowdsourced bias audits.

AI.tldr: This paper builds an atlas of 506 implicitly biased daily decision scenarios across 17 ATUS domains and conducts a crowdsourced audit with 500 participants (8,010 choices), finding that people prioritize broad-relevance, high-stakes, and unanimous-stereotyping scenarios.
AI.motivation: Prior LLM bias work focuses on high-publicity one-off tasks like hiring, leaving implicit sociodemographic biases in everyday autonomous agent decisions underexplored.
AI.method: Using the 17 American Time Use Survey (ATUS) domains, the authors generate 506 decision scenarios where persona-endowed LLMs (race, gender, political ideology) show significant implicit bias, then have 500 crowd participants make 8,010 binary prioritization choices and analyze their rationales.
AI.result: Participants prioritized scenarios with broad relevance (e.g., food), high stakes (e.g., health), and unanimous decisions within a simulated demographic group, rather than disparity magnitude or specific ATUS domain; participants also frequently interpreted disparities as plausible group traits using internalized stereotypes.
AI.conclusion: Crowdsourced bias audits must account for both scenario salience and raters' own internalized stereotypes when prioritizing implicit biases in everyday AI agents.

title: Beyond Bilingual: Studying Quadrilingual Code-Switching with Conversational AI
summary: Multilingual speakers choose languages by topic and conversation partner. Large language models (LLMs) support these languages unequally. Research on code-switching with conversational AI has mostly examined bilingual pairs of well-resourced languages. In Curaçao and Aruba, many people use Dutch, English, Spanish, and the low-resource Creole Papiamentu/o. In a preregistered study, 42 university students held two five-minute chatbot conversations, one about university life and one about local food and culture. Surveys assessed language background, AI use, and switching comfort. 20 international students in Curaçao formed a comparison sample. Participants switched between turns and rarely mixed languages within a message. English dominated both conversations. Participants switched more often in the cultural conversation, where Papiamentu/o and Spanish rose from 15% to 24% of messages. Self-reports showed no lower comfort switching with the chatbot than with a person. Conversational agents must follow turn-by-turn language changes and handle local low-resource languages well.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a preregistered study of quadrilingual code-switching (Dutch, English, Spanish, Papiamentu/o) with conversational AI among 42 university students and 20 international students, finding turn-by-turn switching and higher minority-language use in cultural topics.
AI.motivation: Research on code-switching with conversational AI has focused on high-resource bilingual pairs, leaving quadrilingual settings with low-resource Creoles like Papiamentu/o understudied.
AI.method: In a preregistered study in Curaçao and Aruba, 42 local university students and 20 international comparison students held two five-minute chatbot conversations (university life vs. local food and culture) and completed background and comfort surveys.
AI.result: Participants switched languages between turns rather than within messages, English dominated overall, Papiamentu/o and Spanish rose from 15% to 24% of messages in the cultural conversation, and self-reported comfort switching with the chatbot was no lower than with a human.
AI.conclusion: Conversational agents serving multilingual communities must track turn-by-turn language shifts and support local low-resource languages.

title: Do Embedding-Map Distances Guide LLM Ideation? Four Tests Against What Came Next
comment: 48 pages, 5 figures. Code, data pointers and pre-registrations: this https URL
summary: A popular ideation recipe treats an embedding map of existing work as a guide: pick points far from everything and decode them into ideas. I test four ways such distances could guide ideation against what appeared later. (1) Far random directions are not text: no later item reaches a raw cosine above about 0.10 with one (after centring or whitening, 22 of 24 cells stay out of reach), and an LLM decoder shown a target's neighbours, with score-only feedback, writes those neighbours in all six target sets. A neighbour-free search writes coherent text at median cosine 0.57 and 0.47 to interior gaps, beating the nearest existing item on 15 and 14 of 20, but only 0.07 and 0.06 to far points. (2) On k-means cells of a past-only map, the registered hole score mostly tracks cell size and position; three density-based gap scores forecast which cells grow fastest at or below chance (AUC 0.30 to 0.66) and add nothing to momentum in Steam and arXiv, with patents inconclusive; more isolated new Steam games are slightly better reviewed. (3) LLM continuations of arXiv papers stay closer to the source than papers that cite it, under three user prompts and against proposal rewrites (gpt-4o) and April-December 2023 papers (OLMo). Critique lengthens this step beyond content-free revision, replicated on 150 new papers. Revealing a real follow-up's title turns the ideas by 0.032 along a follow-up-specific direction beyond revision; reviewer, oracle and distance feedback add 0.13, 0.08 and 0.34 of that turn (upper bounds 0.46, 0.46, 0.70), and their turn is not separable from revision or their longer step. (4) For inspiration material graded by distance, no inverted U was detected, on an anticipation margin that tracks format more than content. Original tests were registered before running, follow-ups (thirteen requested in two AI-agent reviews) after the main results; all are dated only by local git commits.

AI.tldr: This paper tests four ways embedding-map distances are used to guide LLM ideation against future outcomes, finding that far random directions do not decode to real text and density-based gap scores predict cell growth at or below chance.
AI.motivation: A common ideation recipe treats embedding maps of prior work as guides by picking points far from existing items, yet its assumptions have not been tested against what actually appeared next.
AI.method: Across four preregistered tests (plus 13 follow-ups) on Steam, arXiv, and patents, the authors test whether far random directions match later items or decode coherently, whether density-based gap scores forecast cell growth, whether LLM continuations match citing papers, and whether inspiration distance shows an inverted-U effect.
AI.result: No later item reaches raw cosine above ~0.10 with far random directions; neighbour-free search decodes interior gaps (median cosine 0.57, 0.47) but fails on far points (0.07, 0.06); three gap scores forecast growth at or below chance (AUC 0.30-0.66) and add nothing to momentum; and LLM continuations stay closer to sources than citing papers while distance feedback's turn is not separable from revision.
AI.conclusion: Embedding-map distance and density-hole heuristics do not reliably guide novel, realistic LLM ideation beyond existing momentum and revision effects.

title: AuXSpec: Learning to Autoformalize Program Specifications via Executable Postconditions
summary: Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended behavior. Prior approaches obtain this feedback through explicit proofs or separately implemented code with formal correspondence proofs, both expensive. We introduce AuXSpec, a Lean framework that pairs declarative postconditions with executable counterparts, obtained through type class resolution when possible and otherwise defined separately with an equivalence proof. Test cases can then evaluate declarative specifications by execution, letting us use agreement as a reinforcement-learning reward. Using AuXSpec, we synthesize 3,037 LeetCode problems and expand training to 19.5K samples through expert iteration on Codeforces. Experiments show that training Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B with the execution-based reward improves SpecGen pass@4 on AuXSpec-Test 0.7% $\to$ 82.7% and 14.3% $\to$ 84.3%, and the 27B model outperforms all frontier models. On the out-of-domain Verina benchmark with its original prompts, both models improve 7.0% $\to$ 90.5% and 21.9% $\to$ 90.5% and surpass VeriSpecGen-30B-A3B, the prior state of the art among open-source specification models, on pass@1 (theirs 47.6% vs. ours 73.7% and 84.5%) and pass@4 (theirs 63.9% at pass@10 vs. ours 90.5%). We release the weights of the trained 9B and 27B models and the 3,037 problems with test cases, including the 300-problem AuXSpec-Test benchmark with expert review and correctness proofs for future evaluation. Models and data: this https URL. Website: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AuXSpec, a Lean framework pairing declarative postconditions with executable counterparts for RL with test-case execution rewards, boosting Qwen3.8-27B pass@4 on AuXSpec-Test from 14.3% to 84.3% and on Verina from 21.9% to 90.5%.
AI.motivation: Autoformalizing natural-language problems into formal specifications in Lean is bottlenecked by the high cost of obtaining scalable feedback via explicit proofs or separate verified code.
AI.method: AuXSpec pairs declarative postconditions with executable counterparts via type class resolution or equivalence proofs, using test-case agreement as an RL reward on 3,037 LeetCode problems expanded to 19.5K samples via Codeforces expert iteration.
AI.result: Training Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B improves SpecGen pass@4 on AuXSpec-Test from 0.7% to 82.7% and 14.3% to 84.3% (27B beating all frontier models), and on out-of-domain Verina from 7.0% to 90.5% and 21.9% to 90.5%, surpassing VeriSpecGen-30B-A3B on pass@1 (73.7% and 84.5% vs. 47.6%) and pass@4 (90.5% vs. 63.9% at pass@10).
AI.conclusion: Executable postconditions provide a scalable, verifiable RL reward for training open-source autoformalization models, with models and the 300-problem AuXSpec-Test benchmark released.

title: Illusion of Explainability: A Sanity Check for Spectral Band Attribution in Satellite Time-Series Crop Classification
comment: Accepted at the 4th Computer Vision for Earth Observation (CV4EO) Workshop at WACV 2027
summary: Attribution methods are commonly validated through convergence across methods and consistency with domain knowledge, yet neither criterion establishes whether identified features are necessary for a task. This limitation is particularly relevant in multispectral remote sensing, where overlapping spectral information makes individual bands potentially substitutable. We investigate this gap in crop-type classification using GradientSHAP, Shapley sampling, and Occlusion on a U-TAE segmentation model trained on Sentinel-2 time series from the PASTIS benchmark. All three methods identify vegetation-sensitive spectral regions consistent with domain knowledge, while Shapley and Occlusion exhibit strong ordering sensitivity in deletion and insertion tests. However, these properties do not reliably predict retraining performance. Aggregate attribution consensus masks substantial per-class disagreement, with pairwise mean Spearman correlations ranging from 0.09 to 0.79. Models retrained from scratch using the five lowest-ranked bands perform comparably to or better than those using the five highest-ranked bands. Furthermore, attribution rankings from an independently trained model with identical configuration and seed identify a different top-five subset that yields better retraining performance. Analysis of all 252 five-band subsets reveals consistently low effective dimensionality (1.35 to 2.62), suggesting substantial spectral redundancy. These findings demonstrate that plausible and apparently faithful attribution rankings do not necessarily identify task-relevant bands for improved retrained performance, highlighting the limitations of band-level feature attribution in spectrally redundant input spaces.

AI.tldr: This paper sanity-checks spectral band attribution (GradientSHAP, Shapley sampling, Occlusion) on Sentinel-2 crop classification, showing that models retrained on the five lowest-ranked bands perform comparably to or better than those using the top five.
AI.motivation: Attribution methods are commonly validated by cross-method convergence and domain-knowledge alignment, which does not establish whether attributed features are actually necessary for the task in spectrally redundant inputs.
AI.method: The authors evaluate GradientSHAP, Shapley sampling, and Occlusion on a U-TAE model trained on PASTIS Sentinel-2 time series, testing per-class rank correlation, retraining on top-5 vs. bottom-5 bands, and analyzing all 252 five-band subsets.
AI.result: Aggregate consensus hides per-class disagreement (pairwise mean Spearman 0.09 to 0.79); models retrained on the bottom-5 bands match or beat top-5 models; an identical-seed retrained model yields a different top-5 subset with better retraining; and all 252 subsets show low effective dimensionality (1.35 to 2.62).
AI.conclusion: Plausible and consistent band-level attribution rankings do not reliably identify task-necessary features in spectrally redundant satellite time series.

title: HIVE-ECIA: Identity-Aware Historical Evidence Acquisition for Bandwidth-Efficient Multi-Object Tracking
summary: Panoramic multi-object tracking (MOT) requires reliable identity association across a 360° field of view, yet bandwidth-constrained operation forces a trade-off between low-resolution (LR) identity ambiguity and costly high-resolution (HR) transmission. We propose HIVE-ECIA, an identity-aware framework that selectively retrieves historical HR evidence to recover fragmented identities without modifying detection boxes or the underlying tracker. An ECIA Base-Guided query policy determines when additional HR evidence is warranted; HIVE ranks historical LR observations to select an informative retrieval timestamp; and ECIA Full integrates the retrieved HR crop through learned gated fusion and conservative identity safeguards. We further introduce DualPano-MOT, a real-world dual-fisheye panoramic evaluation dataset featuring controlled pedestrian interactions, panorama-seam challenges, and occlusions, with model-assisted, manually verified tracking annotations. On held-out QuadTrack sequences and zero-shot DualPano-MOT, HIVE-ECIA improves identity association across four MOT trackers without tracker-specific retraining. Across these trackers, identity switches decrease by up to 21.8% and 23.4%, while the largest IDF1 gains reach 3.81 and 6.74 percentage points, respectively. Under an offline JPEG-based acquisition model, our framework reduces encoded data volume by 89.2% and 79.3% relative to continuous Full-HR acquisition.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes HIVE-ECIA, a framework that selectively retrieves historical high-resolution crops for panoramic multi-object tracking, cutting identity switches by up to 23.4% while reducing encoded data volume by 79.3% to 89.2%.
AI.motivation: Bandwidth-constrained panoramic multi-object tracking faces a trade-off between low-resolution identity ambiguity and expensive continuous high-resolution transmission.
AI.method: An ECIA Base-Guided policy decides when HR evidence is needed, HIVE ranks historical LR observations to pick an informative timestamp, and ECIA Full fuses the retrieved HR crop via gated fusion and identity safeguards; the authors also introduce the DualPano-MOT dataset.
AI.result: On held-out QuadTrack and zero-shot DualPano-MOT across four trackers without retraining, HIVE-ECIA reduces identity switches by up to 21.8% and 23.4%, boosts IDF1 by up to 3.81 and 6.74 percentage points, and cuts encoded data volume by 89.2% and 79.3% vs. continuous Full-HR acquisition.
AI.conclusion: Selective historical HR evidence retrieval resolves panoramic identity ambiguity at a fraction of full-resolution bandwidth without modifying underlying detectors or trackers.

title: Remember, Replay, Adapt: Learning from Past Experience in Online Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Existing feedback-based methods for online vision-and-language navigation (VLN) primarily learn from current episode outcomes, leaving previously acquired feedback underutilized. Inspired by human episodic memory, we propose R2A, an online VLN adaptation framework that continually reuses successful and failed navigation experiences for policy learning. Specifically, Success-Failure Memory (SFM) retains successful and failed navigation episodes with acquired feedback and retrieves task-relevant experiences based on incoming instructions, enabling historical feedback to guide subsequent navigation. Prior-Anchored Adaptation (PAA) learns from these experiences by reinforcing successful trajectories and suppressing failed ones relative to a frozen pretrained policy, while regularizing behavioral drift. Together, these modules enable continual feedback reuse and stable policy adaptation without source-domain data or expert supervision. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks, REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE, and five navigation backbones demonstrate consistent performance gains. On the REVERIE validation unseen split, R2A improves DUET's SR from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces R2A, an online vision-and-language navigation framework that stores and reuses past successful and failed episodes, raising DUET's REVERIE validation unseen SR from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.
AI.motivation: Existing feedback-based online VLN methods learn only from the current episode's outcome, underutilizing previously acquired navigation feedback.
AI.method: R2A combines Success-Failure Memory (SFM), which stores and retrieves task-relevant past episodes by instruction, with Prior-Anchored Adaptation (PAA), which reinforces successful trajectories and suppresses failed ones relative to a frozen pretrained policy while regularizing drift.
AI.result: Across REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE and five backbones without source-domain data or expert supervision, R2A consistently improves navigation, raising DUET's REVERIE validation unseen SR from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.
AI.conclusion: Episodic reuse of past successes and failures anchored to a frozen prior enables stable, data-free continual adaptation in online VLN.

title: HEmIF-Bench: Benchmarking H&E-to-mIF Models BeyondVirtual-StainFidelity
summary: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-to-multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) generators predict spatial protein expression from routine histology, yet pixel-level marker reconstruction does not establish downstream utility. We present HEmIF-Bench, evaluating five frozen generators across eight datasets spanning molecular, cellular, tissue, and patient scales. HEmIF-Bench decouples internal encoder features from generated outputs, benchmarking both against the pathology foundation reference UNI2. Mirroring the clinical workflow where pathologists rely on mIF to define cell phenotypes, delineate tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) and germinal centers (GCs), and stratify patient risk, we evaluate external CD3 recovery, single-cell classification, dense nuclear segmentation, TLS/GC segmentation, and patient survival prediction. Across the benchmark, foundation-model-based MIPHEI-ViT leads among the generators, while non-foundation models show task-specific strengths. Comparing the two routes reveals that internal encoder features generally outperform generated outputs, and larger output marker panels do not guarantee stronger downstream utility across datasets. Moreover, neither internal encoder features nor generated outputs consistently surpass frozen UNI2. These findings show that pixel-level stain fidelity does not equate to downstream utility, and that generators trained at current paired-data scales have yet to surpass large-scale pure-H&E foundation models. With the expansion of paired translation cohorts and the advancement of foundation-based generative architectures, HEmIF-Bench establishes a definitive benchmark for tracking when H&E-to-mIF generation crosses the threshold to deliver genuine value beyond routine histology for tumor microenvironment analysis and precision oncology.

AI.tldr: This paper presents HEmIF-Bench, evaluating five frozen H&E-to-mIF generators across eight datasets, finding that pixel-level stain fidelity does not equate to downstream clinical utility and generators do not consistently surpass frozen UNI2.
AI.motivation: H&E-to-mIF generators predict spatial protein expression from routine histology, yet pixel-level marker reconstruction does not establish whether they improve downstream clinical tasks.
AI.method: HEmIF-Bench decouples internal encoder features from generated outputs across five frozen generators and eight datasets, benchmarking both against the pure-H&E foundation model UNI2 on CD3 recovery, single-cell classification, nuclear segmentation, TLS/GC segmentation, and survival prediction.
AI.result: Foundation-model-based MIPHEI-ViT leads among generators while non-foundation models show task-specific strengths; internal encoder features generally outperform generated outputs, larger marker panels do not guarantee better utility, and neither route consistently beats frozen UNI2.
AI.conclusion: HEmIF-Bench establishes a multi-scale benchmark showing that current H&E-to-mIF generators have yet to surpass large-scale pure-H&E foundation models on downstream oncology tasks.
